Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What distinguishes a top AI development company from other AI software companies in the industry?
Answer: The top AI companies have billions of dollars in funding, allowing them to buy an enormous number of GPU servers and train the biggest and most expensive AI models. That's what distinguishes them. You may think I'm half-joking, but that's literally the main reason why these companies are on top. Anthropic has 600 or so employees, many of them brilliant engineers that are paid top dollar. Still, salaries only account for less than 20% of operating costs whereas GPU infrastructure accounts for ~80%. That’s why their language model Claude is currently the top LLM. xAI recently raised $6B in the largest funding round of any startup ever, only a year after its founding. With billions in the bank, the company is planning to train the next iteration of its Grok model on 100,000 H100 GPUs, which would make it the most expensive AI model ever trained and would probably catapult it to the top of leaderboards. The vast majority of AI companies can not afford to compete in this race. There are still many viable alternative strategies for AI startups out there, but they don’t provide the same insane growth rates as training ginormous frontier models.

Question: Are software engineering and hardware engineering dead because of AI?

Question: What large or significant problems does AI promise to solve but actually never will?

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Will DevOps go away because of AI?
Answer: Technically speaking, DevOps is just a set of practices centered around the idea that the team that builds the software should also be the one that deploys and supports it. I don’t think that’s going away. If anything, AI tools will make it even easier for dev teams to deploy and support their own software. However, there’s the bastardized version of DevOps where dedicated “DevOps Engineers” are responsible for setting up and maintaining CI/CD pipelines, which is really just another way of separating Dev and Ops again. That practice could very well disappear in the next few years. Modern tools have already made it pretty easy to set up CI/CD pipelines. You spend a few hours setting it up initially and then it makes your life a lot easier for the remaining software development life cycle, with the pipeline itself requiring minimal maintenance. I’m pretty sure we’ll have AI tools within the next few years that automate even the initial setup, which would really put into question why any organization would need DevOps Engineers.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: In machine learning, do "the bitter pill" and the no-free-lunch theorem contradict each other?
Answer: They don't. I would even say they're two sides of the same coin. The Bitter Lesson states that general techniques will win out in the end as compute capacity increases. The No Free Lunch theorem states that any two optimization techniques are equivalent when averaged across all possible problems. The consequence of both those statements is that any short-term optimization algorithms for solving specific problems will be rendered irrelevant by more powerful general models in the future. Essentially, it means that most of today's machine learning research has temporary benefits at best and is most likely completely useless. That's a bitter pill for many of us.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What is a good diet that isn't hard? I need to lose 5 kgs.
Answer: There is only way to lose weight, and that is to consume fewer calories than you burn. There are many diets that can help to achieve this indirectly. For instance, the keto/low-carb diet limits the amount of carbohydrates you consume which indirectly tends to limit the number of calories. Periodic fasting limits the number of hours during the day that you allow yourself to eat, which again indirectly tends to limit caloric consumption. The easiest diet in my experience is to just eat normal food but count the calories to make sure you are in a caloric deficit. That way, you are always in control. By eating the food you actually want instead of imposing some arbitrary rules like “no carbs” or “no breakfast” it becomes a lot easier because it doesn't feel like you're torturing yourself.

Question: How can self-taught programmers have the same level of understanding (or logic) as computer science students who took advanced college courses?

Many of us started gaining that experience when we were very young, in our preteens. So of course someone who has been programming since childhood is going to have a higher level of understanding than someone who just completed a CS degree and never did any programming outside of that. The difference between having a CS degree or not is that you pick up many of the theoretical fundamentals “for free”, whereas someone who never attended college will have to read up on their own. But again, programming is a practical skill, and experience matters more than theoretical knowledge.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What is meant by a "multi-modal foundation" in the context of artificial intelligence?
Answer: Multi-modal means that the AI model supports multiple data types, such as text, image, video and sound, both as input and output. A foundation model is one that is trained on a very wide variety of data and can be applied to a very wide variety of problems. GPT-3 introduced the term Large Language Model (LLM) to the world. The model was huge, with 175 billion parameters, and it only supported language. Last year, LLMs started incorporating vision to be able to respond to, and generate, images. With the release of GPT-4o, we now have models that support audio as input and output, and a primitive form of video support, by taking frequent image snapshots of a live video feed. As these models add ever more modalities and consistently have billions of parameters, it no longer makes much sense to call them Large Language Models. We needed a new term, and foundation model seems to have caught on. Others have called them Large Multi-modal Models (LMMs), but that doesn't roll as easily off the tongue.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: When developing a micro SaaS, is it crucial to come up with a completely innovative idea that no one has thought of before, or can you build upon existing solutions by adding unique features or twists to create a competitive advantage?
Answer: No, not at all. Good ideas are more or less worthless for any startup, and that's no less true for a micro SaaS. What matters is execution and speed. For a typical SaaS startup, the recipe for success might be 1% idea, 69% execution and 30% speed. For a micro SaaS, it's more like 1% idea, 19% execution and 80% speed. After all, a micro SaaS is basically an attempt at a quick cash grab. You don't want to grind it out at microstakes for years. You want to get immediate traction to either gain some early profits at very high margins or make an early exit for a small amount. If the business idea is not scalable and the company dies after a couple of years, that's fine, because you already had your payday. You don't need any unique ideas to achieve this. You can “steal” someone else's idea or just seize an obvious opportunity in the market. The key is that you ship like a bat out of hell. If your code quality is very poor, that's fine too.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What is the best science fiction film ever so far?
Answer: Being a lifetime science fiction fan and movie buff, it's obviously really hard to pick a favorite. That being said, it's a weird genre. Most of the sci-fi films ever made are bad. And not just a little bad, but laughably abysmal. But the ones that are good, can be really good. I'd say that most of the best sci-fi movies are adaptations of novels. The recent Dune: Part One (2021) and Dune: Part Two (2024) were amazing. Another Denis Villeneuve film, Arrival (2016), was also really, really good. It's based on a short story, but I guess that counts as an adaptation. The Martian (2015) was great. Excellent novel, great film. Jurassic Park (1993) is one of my all-time favorites. Decent book, magical film. Contact (1997) is an underrated one in my opinion. And while we're on the subject of 90s-era sci-fi, I'd like to mention Starship Troopers (1997), which I controversially thought was better than the novel and is a personal favorite of mine. And of course, we shouldn't forget the OG of sci-fi movies, 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968). Speaking of Stanley Kubrick, I guess A Clockwork Orange (1971) counts as sci-fi as well. Its sequel, Aliens (1986), was pretty awesome too. Finally, the original Star Wars trilogy (1977–1983) holds a special place in my heart. I'm finding it borderline impossible to pick just one.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How do you modify an AI algorithm to score higher on benchmarks?
Answer: You can do benchmark hacking by training and validating your model on well-known benchmarks, and then intentionally fine-tuning it to overfit on those specific benchmarks either through post-training, hyperparameter tuning or some other method. When major AI labs release new flagship LLMs, they will usually publish their scores on the same 10 open benchmarks, such as MMLU, GPQA, HumanEval etc. That's why I'm always reluctant to give too much weight to self-published benchmark scores. The real test is how a model performs in the wild when encountered with novel problems.

Question: Should a start-up raise funds if the founders aim for an acquisition valued at $5-10 million?
Answer: Probably not, as that would be quite a small acquisition. Let's say you have two co-founders who are diluted down to 20% each and the company is acquired for $5M. They would only be taking out a million each before taxes. Considering the time and effort usually required to take a startup from idea to exit, and the fact that success is not guaranteed, you really want a bigger payday for it to be worth it. The basic idea of founding a startup is that both the risk and reward is very high. Of course, if the startup has to do a small funding round to survive at a difficult stage, you probably do it. But I wouldn't start out with strategy of being funded to a small exit.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Reaching a $100K MRR within 12-18 months of a product launch in a B2B SaaS seems to be the ideal growth rate recommended by most investors. How can founders structure their startup, product, and sales before launching to hit those numbers?
Answer: There is no ideal growth rate. You want to grow as fast as possible obviously. In the past, there was a consensus that you needed to get to that magic milestone of $1M ARR within a certain timeframe, or else your startup would not be fundable. Since then, several B2B Saas companies have squashed that myth by demonstrating that a startup can be a late bloomer and still become wildly successful. How many of the companies in the following chart do you recognize? I recognize a few of them, and certainly Figma, since I use their product on a daily basis. Figma took over 3 years to launch the product, another year to get their first customer and another year to get to $1M ARR. Today, the company is valued at $12.5B. Another success story is Loom. You’d think the outlook was not great considering it took the company over 3 years to go from first customer to $1M. But in the end it became a unicorn. To answer the question, I think founders should structure their startup in a way that’s appropriate for its level of traction and funding. You don’t have to gamble everything on going broke or going home. The name of the game is survival. It’s possible to win in the end even if you don’t achieve blitz scale at first.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: It’s my first year of software engineering at university. My uncle wanted me to pick electrical engineering, and he said I will be unemployed because software engineering won’t be in demand in the future. What do you think about it?
Answer: I doubt that your uncle, unless the rest of us, is able to accurately predict the future many years ahead. I have a lot of experience working in predictive modelling, and I know that the best way to forecast a complex phenomenon is to extrapolate the current trend. The current trend is that the demand for software engineers is increasing, as it has been doing for several decades. There are no strong signals that this trend is turning. That your uncle thinks otherwise is what I would call a weak signal. I also happen to have a degree in electrical engineering, yet I have devoted my career to software. Hardware has been commoditized to a much greater degree than software. As a result, many electrical engineers such as myself have turned to software instead, where there are many more jobs available. Another reason, or the main reason, that I switched to software engineering is that I enjoy it a lot. If you truly enjoy something, that's probably the right path to take, regardless of what your friends, family and strangers on the internet think.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How much does it cost to build a SaaS product?
Answer: The initial cost of building a SaaS product is high, but not exorbitant. Typically a few million dollars. The challenge is that SaaS companies only become profitable through economies of scale, and it takes time to build up a large enough customer base. That’s why SaaS startups go through a phase known as the cash flow trough, when costs increase faster than revenue. (Illustration by David Skok) The irony of this is that the more the company invests in engineering and sales, the faster the growth will be, and the more profitable the company will be eventually. However, that leads to an even deeper cash trough initially. Most startups want to invest to fuel that rapid growth, but raising enough capital can be challenging, and they don’t want to give up too much equity early either. So it depends. The cost of the product relies more on the founders’ ability to raise funding and less on the complexity of the product. Of course, a SaaS product is never really “finished”. It continues to be in perpetual development, and the costs increase over time. But that can be more than offset by the nearly endless scaling opportunities offered by SaaS. Once SaaS companies reach maturity, they become cash machines.

So yes, I suspect people working in this domain will simply be called Software Engineers. Google has been doing that all along.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What is the easiest and least stressful job someone with a computer science degree can get?
Answer: Software developer. Okay, I can already sense people being triggered before I've even clicked submit, but hear me out. If - and that's an actual if- you are someone who has a talent for writing code, who actually enjoys it, who is intrinsically motivated to master the craft, then it almost doesn't feel like a job. You’re doing it because you love it. The money is just a bonus. In a well-functioning software org, developers are shielded from company politics and unnecessary meetings. They’re mostly left alone to do their job, because it provides a lot of value to the company. Now, you might be one of those developers who works on a horrible legacy system with annoying micromanagers and you might think I’m crazy. But when done right, being a developer is about as chill of a job as they come. Sure, the technical challenges are not always easy. You can be stuck scratching your head over some bug for days. But eventually you figure it out. Because unlike people, code is logical. It’s a fun kind of difficulty. One that’s intellectually stimulating. When you’re a manager that has to lay off half your department or you’re a sales rep desperately trying to hit the monthly quota, that’s also difficult. But that’s difficult in an entirely different way. It’s not fun. Unless you’re a psychopath. Software development is fun. And that takes away the stress.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What did Ilya see?
Answer: No, Ilya didn't “feel the AGI”. What Ilya saw was that OpenAI's executive management led by Sam Altman and Greg Brockman gradually decided to prioritize commercialization over his superalignment team that was researching ways to prevent AGI from having a harmful impact on society. Initially, OpenAI was supposed to dedicate 20% of its compute budget to the superalignment group. However, as the compute budget grew, and as ChatGPT was being rolled out to customers worldwide, that was starting to make less sense. Basically, there were two factions inside OpenAI's leadership. The effective altruists (also known as the doomers), led by Ilya Sutskever, Jan Leike and other board members. And the accelerationists, led by Altman and Brockman. In a coup attempt, Ilya's crew decided to fire Altman. However, that quickly backfired, as it turned out that the vast majority of the ~700 employees at OpenAI stood behind their CEO and were willing to follow him over to Microsoft unless the board reinstated him as CEO. So Altman was invited back in, and the board was reshuffled. After OpenAI's announcement of GPT-4o this week, Ilya and Leike resigned. Since Altman has been making statements recently that “society will figure out alignment”, it should come to no one's surprise that OpenAI now seems to be shutting down the superalignment team entirely.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: As a software engineer, does a software engineering title matter to you?
Answer: Sure, they do matter. If you're going to be looking for a new job in the future, you want your LinkedIn profile to tell a convincing story. I once interviewed someone with less than one year of experience who titled himself as Senior Software Architect. It was hard to take the guy seriously. Another time, I saw someone with 7 years of experience at the same company who still had the title of Junior Engineer. In the back of my mind, I couldn't help but think “your employer has screwed you over for promotions for 7 years, why haven't you left yet?” Nonsensical titles like Jedi Master or Ninja Rockstar don't tell me anything and don't really help the candidate either. On the other hand, if I see a CV with Junior Software Engineer -> Software Engineer -> Senior Software Engineer, that makes it very easy for me as a hiring manager to understand without the candidate having to go through hoops to explain. So yes, I care about having a title that's aligned with my job, because that makes me more employable and my role easier for others to understand.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Which IT job role do you foresee as the most likely to become prevalent for individuals seeking full remote positions in the upcoming years: Machine Learning engineer, Data scientist, Data engineer, DevOps engineer, or software engineer?
Answer: Some of these jobs have become somewhat riskier career choices due to developments in AI. Specifically in the areas of Natural Language Processing and Computer Vision, there are now pretrained foundational models that can solve many problems in a no-shot or few-shot approach that would have required bespoke models in the past. There are efforts being made to apply pretraining to other fields, like robotics. In the areas where pretrained models and generative AI can be applied at scale, there will be less need for data scientists to come up with custom models, data engineers to collect data for them and machine learning engineers to deploy them. Instead of 100 companies creating 100 big models, we'll have one company creating a huge model and 99 companies using it with simple prompt engineering or minimal finetuning. A team of software engineers skilled at prompt engineering will get you very far. Another specialized role is that of the DevOps engineer. I would bet good money on that role being among the first software engineering roles to be affected by AI. DevOps is inherently about automation and thus easier to automate than many other tasks. I think the most robust role going forward will be that of the general-purpose software engineer. By all means, dive into data science and ML, but I would recommend going broad rather than narrow. Get into software engineering, learn how to build APIs and user interfaces and distributed systems. Pick up a wide variety of skills that will allow you to solve a wide variety of problems and you will be adaptable and ready to make yourself useful in a rapidly changing world.

Question: Wouldn't so-called general artificial intelligence allow creation of Von Neumann machines or self-replicating spacecraft? On the face of it, that seems quite impossible.
Answer: The absence of von Neumann probes has been proposed as a solution to the Fermi paradox. This is the so-called Hart-Tipler conjecture: The idea that there is no other intelligent life in the galaxy, since any advanced civilization could construct von Neumann probes and explore the entire galaxy in less than a million years. One explanation for why we appear to be alone is that there is some Great Filter that prevents alien life from evolving to a high level on the Kardashev scale. A common speculation is that artificial intelligence is that filter. That somehow every lifeform that develops AI ends up self-destructing soon after. A chilling thought…

Question: How do I hire a software engineer for startups in 2024?
Answer: It's become a lot harder. In the past, you only needed to offer interesting technical challenges, a small equity stake, some empty promises, unlimited coffee and maybe a foosball table. But startups have become ubiquitous in the tech industry, and engineers are not so gullible anymore. These days you basically need to offer market salary, a decent options package, interesting technical challenges and some evidence that your business plan has the potential to succeed. If we look at macro trends, startups are struggling to raise funding and revenue multiples are way down since the peak in 2021. Meanwhile, Big Tech is doing better than ever before. So why would a software engineer work for your startup when they can go and work for Microsoft or Nvidia instead? To find software engineers for your startup, you have to grind recruitment and work actively on marketing targeted towards techies. And you need to allocate a proper salary budget and options pool.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Can a SaaS company have a net profit margin of 50%?
Answer: While many mature SaaS companies could sustain a 50% profit margin if they wanted to, only a few of them do. The main goal of for-profit entities is to maximize shareholder value, not profit margins. Rule of 40 In SaaS, we talk about the “rule of 40”. You want your combined profit margin and growth rate to exceed 40%. But ideally, you want both to be in the double digits. Rule of 40 Index as of May 2024 [1] The last couple of years, the SaaS market has been pretty rough. The Rule of 40 Index shows that out of 84 publicly traded SaaS companies, only 7 companies currently have an R40 score of >40 (the bubbles on the upper right side of the cutoff line). Back in 2021, this would have been more balanced. On the current list, there is only one company (Paycom) with a profit margin >50%. Case study: DropBox vs. HubSpot An interesting case study that illustrates why SaaS companies are not chasing higher profit margins is DropBox vs. HubSpot. Here are their current numbers: HubSpot DropBox While both companies are pulling in a huge $2.5B in ARR, HubSpot is trading at a much higher valuation than DropBox despite having a smaller profit margin. If we consider that DropBox is sitting at $3B cash, their ARR multiple net of cash is a measly 2x, while HubSpot is trading at a very strong 13x multiple. DropBox would love to trade some of its profit for that strong growth rate HubSpot has, which would increase its market cap, but it’s easier said than done. On the other side, HubSpot could fire a thousand sales reps and see its profit margin shoot through the roof at the expense of growth if it wanted to, but again, that probably wouldn’t do the stock price any favors.

Question: Which country has the purest Germanic blood, Norway, Sweden, Denmark, or Iceland?

Question: Why do software companies release software that then regularly need updating/upgrading, rather than making it right in the first place?
Answer: Oh boy. Any piece of software that’s even just a little bit complex will have tons of bugs. Why? Because the state complexity of a program quickly blows up to epic proportions as more moving parts are added. Why can’t we just have 100% code coverage in our tests, you might ask. Of course, we could do that, but that’s not the same as covering all edge cases, which is essentially impossible. That’s why we always have to keep fixing bugs as they are discovered. Another reason for updating the software is to improve it by adding new features, which is generally expected to happen with some frequency in the world of web-based products and SaaS

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: If I create a QR-based attendance SaaS, would you buy it?
Answer: I don't know. I assume you're trying to validate your startup idea. Word of advice. Just because a bunch of people tells you it's a great idea, and that they would buy your app if you made it, that doesn't mean they would actually buy it. People are generally (too) nice, so they will tell you want to hear. There are different tiers of difficulty in SaaS: If you get to tier 4, the rest is comparably easy. If you don't get there, you don't have a business. If you make the world's best QR-based attendance app, you have a business for sure. It's all about execution. To validate if you're going to get there, make an MVP and try to sell it to at least one customer. One. That's the first step.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is it possible that no limit hold’em isn’t solvable by AI/computer due to differences in best bet sizes versus different players?
Answer: Heads-up (HU) Limit Texas Hold ’Em was weakly solved by Cepheus in 2015. Cepheus has an expected loss of only 0.000986 big blinds per hand against an unexploitable Nash equilibrium strategy. As you point out, the varying bet sizes in No Limit Hold ’Em complicates matters. As far as I know, NLHE hasn't been solved in any way even for HU play. Introducing more players would complicate it even further. Now, even if you could solve the game, you have to keep in mind that the Nash equilibrium strategy is not the same as best play. It's just the optimal way to play against another player that also employs Nash equilibrium. Against a fish, playing like that could actually be pretty bad, because the fish plays in a highly exploitable way, allowing for more efficient counter-strategies.

Question: Would a 2000 to 2100 rated player score a single win in a hundred match against Magnus Carlsen?

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How do you learn AI and machine learning?
Answer: AI/ML is a highly empirical, practical field. Yes, there is a science behind it, but the science can pretty much be summed up by this: The best results in AI/ML are achieved by throwing things at the wall and seeing what sticks. As a result, the top researchers are usually those who have the coding chops (and big datasets and compute budgets) to be able to rapidly iterate on their experiments. If you want to get good at this game, it's very much a case of learning by doing. I guess you could say that about anything, but it's especially true in ML. You don't need the big datasets and GPU clusters when you're just starting out. A good mini project would be to write your own transformer-based language model from scratch. You can make a small one that runs on your laptop, and you'll learn a ton in the process.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: You are an older developer, and a new manager comes in and tells you to implement a six-month feature in four weeks. They constantly shout at you and micromanage you. How would you respond if you were the old developer?
Answer: Managers telling developers to implement a six-month feature in four weeks is completely normal. It's common for managers to say stupid shit like “I have a small task for you. I want you to implement X. It shouldn't take too long.” Whenever I heard this as a developer, inside me I was thinking “the fuck do you know how long it takes?!” But then you learn to ignore it and just do the work. If the six-month task takes longer than four weeks, whatever. It's not like you didn't warn them. Shouting is not something I really encountered, but heated discussions are a necessary component of entrepreneurial companies in my opinion. If everything is nice and cozy all the time, it means one of two things. Either employees fear management, which is really bad, or they don't care, which is even worse. Micromanagement is tricky. Some developers have no problem being micromanaged as long as it's done respectfully. They even prefer it. But for most developers, it's not the right recipe. Personally, I despise being told what to do, and even worse, how to do it. Whenever someone told me what to do, my knee-jerk reaction was to do the exact opposite. Admittedly not a great personality trait, but I dealt with it by taking on roles with a great deal of freedom.

Question: Why are so many raving about The AI Singularity, given that it won't happen in their lifetime, if ever? Is this because they have simply no idea what today's "AI" actually is?

I think we're actually in the midst of the singularity, but I think it will take a decade or two before we have superintelligent AI that surpasses humans in essentially all intellectual domains. Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What potential use cases can you imagine for Meta AI's Llama 3 open source model?
Answer: Llama 3 is great for fast inference in applications that require low latency, such as in conversational AI. It's also great for fine-tuning. Scaling laws With LLMs, there are so-called scaling laws. Basically, given a fixed compute budget, how many parameters should a model have and how much data should it be trained on to achieve optimal performance, or level of intelligence. Kaplan In 2020, OpenAI introduced the Kaplan scaling laws[1] upon which the training of GPT-3 was based. GPT-3 was trained on 300B tokens and had 175B parameters, for a ratio of 1.7:1 of tokens to parameters. Chinchilla Later, Google showed in the Chinchilla paper [2] that previous LLMs were vastly overparameterized given their compute budgets. Chinchilla outperformed GPT-3 with only 70B parameters (the same size as Lllama 3) by training on 1.5T tokens, with a ratio of 21:1. But there is another type of performance, and that is inference speed, measured in tokens generated per second, T/s. MosaicML As pointed out in later research [3]by a team at MosaicML, the Chinchilla scaling laws don't account for inference. The paper suggests increasing the size of the training set when there is a high inference demand. Llama 3 Meta has a very large number of users and thus spend more compute on inference than training. The team behind Llama 3 took that into account by training the model on 15T tokens. That's a factor of 214:1 for the 70B model and 1875:1 for the smallest 8B model. What you end up with are models that are very capable compared to their size and inference cost. Llama 3 8B has comparable capabilities to Llama 2 70B, while Llama 3 70B is comparable to GPT-4, a 1.8T-parameter monster. When running on Groq's proprietary inference-optimized hardware, Llama 3 8B generates 800 T/s and the 70B model generates 300 T/s. Compare that to GPT-3.5 turbo, which has long been one of the most capable mid-sized LLMs, but only generates something like 50 T/s. Conversational AI use case For the conversational AI platform I'm building this has plenty of use cases related to real-time voice conversations and we're currently rolling out Llama 3 as a replacement for ChatGPT for many of our most latency-sensitive prompts. Fine-tuning Finally, Llama is open-source, and anyone is free to download it and fine-tune it. That opens up many opportunities that are not there with proprietary models.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: If an eng to claims they understand long-term architecture but not stayed long enough to see their own decisions play out over several year then are they really a junior developer with X years of experience? Why not?
Answer: We've all met that engineer who had one year of experience, repeated ten times. It's become a meme, but of course there is a certain truth to it. When someone has hopped from project to project in quick succession over a long career, it's certainly a bit of a yellow flag to me, but it doesn't always mean they're a bad developer. The architect Some developers simply love to work on greenfield projects. When things start to fall in place, they get bored and leave for the next thing. While that's not great from the employer's perspective, these people also get a lot of experience initiating new projects. They can become really efficient at setting up the basic structure of a software project with everything that entails, and eventually they become expert architect craftsmen that you'll love to have around in the beginning stages of a new project. Despite not having experienced the full life cycle of a product, they will build their systems to be maintainable because they simply know their craft very well. The jack of all trades Another type of developer is the jack of all trades who has been around the block for a long time and has seen every technology under the sun. These guys are great to have around in large, messy organizations. They are fixers. You have a problem, they fix it. It doesn't matter how esoteric the problem is. The freeloader Now this is the person you want to avoid. Some developers join lots of new projects, always as a team member and never as a tech lead or solo developer. They stay for a while until the rest of the crew figures out that they're not really contributing. Then they jump to the next thing. Their CVs will look great, despite having only short assignments. But this is really a case of having one year of experience, repeated ten times.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is working in startups only for high-achievers?
Answer: Not necessarily, but early-stage startups can’t afford any dead meat. What it means for employees You can’t hide in a startup. Everything is out in the open. In large corporations, you can breeze along and pretend to be working, or only do the very minimum, and you’ll generally be fine. In a startup, that will quickly get exposed and dealt with. This doesn’t mean you need to be among the best in your field or work crazy hours. But you need to put in an effort and justify your compensation by clearly demonstrating the value you bring to the table through actual results. What it means for founders Because of strict budget constraints and the small number of employees, every hire is super important and needs to bring a high ROI. Importantly, this does not mean that startups should make cheap hires as a default to save costs. If a senior engineer costs $200k/year but provides 3x the value (or more) of a junior engineer that costs $100k/year, then the startup cannot afford to hire the junior. The cost is smaller but the ROI is too low. In practice, this means that startups should often make relatively expensive hires, which can seem counterintuitive when they’re strapped for cash. VC funded startups are a special category because they generally have much larger budgets, which can create the illusion that they can hire more leniently. What happens quite often is that the organization becomes bloated by hiring too many mediocre employees and they run the company into the ground before reaching profitability.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What is reinforcement learning? How is it used to teach AI agents complex tasks?
Answer: In layman's terms, reinforcement learning is when you train an AI agent in an environment where it can be rewarded and punished for taking right or wrong actions. By getting that feedback, it knows “I should do more of this” and “I should do less of that”. You have already told the AI what you want it to achieve. By observing how it gets rewarded and punished, it learns to understand how it can achieve it.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: If we can’t terraform Mars, then where is humanity supposed to go when the Earth becomes uninhabitable or when the Sun turns into a red giant possibly swallowing Earth?
Answer: Earth is a planet that when left to itself produces the perfect environment for humanity to thrive. The only thing we need to do to retain this paradise is to not try to actively destroy it on a global, industrial scale. If we can't even do that, then we have no business whatsoever trying to terraform Mars, a planet which has an extremely hostile environment for us. The only thing Mars has going for it is that it's the least hostile of all the other objects in the Solar System. But that's not saying a lot. If we screw up Earth, we might as well just give up and go extinct, leaving the planet for a species that's better equipped to run things.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is it possible to make a SaaS where data will be stored on the client?
Answer: You can use local storage such as cookies to store data in a web browser client, but ideally it should be kept to a minimum and you need to be totally transparent about what data you store. This is something all enterprise SaaS customers ask about.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Have you considered using LLMs provided by OpenAI (e.g. GPT4) or Google (e.g. Gemini) to improve your product? What stood out to you comparing OpenAI versus Google?
Answer: I’m running technology and product at a conversational AI company, so yes, I’m considering using different LLMs left and right. It’s quickly becoming a full-time job just to keep up with all these new models! I recently added the Claude suite of models from Anthropic and DBRX from Databricks to our technology stack. Yesterday, I was evaluating Command R+ from Cohere and all of a sudden OpenAI released a new version of GPT-4 turbo. Today, Mistral just dropped Mixtral 8x22B. It’s enough to drive a man crazy! But these are exciting times we live in. What stands out to me about OpenAI is that whenever they drop a new model, it almost always sets a new standard for everyone else to follow. Despite being trained two years ago, GPT-4 is still the gold standard that every other LLM is being compared to. Through its collaboration with Microsoft, OpenAI is also able to deliver features that are important to business customers like me, such as performance, availability, security, data privacy, content moderation and ease of integration. Google's response to OpenAI's advancements has been surprisingly lackluster for a company that used to dominate the AI space. After several failed launches, they finally seem to have a decent LLM in Gemini. But even their most impressive release of Gemini 1.5 was completely overshadowed by OpenAI's launch of Sora later on the same day.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is there a document that explains which LLM model is best for a given task? How do we know whether for example Claude is better for artistic input, while ChatGPT4 is better for coding problems (random example, not necessarily true)?
Answer: There are public benchmarks. For instance, Claude 3 Opus scores 84.9% on the HumanEval dataset which consists of 164 original programming problems, while GPT-4 only scores 67.0%. Whenever a new SOTA model is released, the team or company behind it tends to brag about its score on various public benchmarks, such as Anthropic did here. Now, if you have been in the machine learning game for a while like some of us have, you would know that these scores should be taken with a grain of salt, for several reasons: A better test is to see how the model performs “in the wild”. The LMSYS Chatbot Arena Leaderboard is a good place to check out that. There, top LLMs are evaluated by humans in head-to-head counters and an Elo rating is calculated. Of course, this does not specify what use cases they are best at, since the human evaluators can use any prompt they like. So in reality, it can sometimes be pretty difficult to know. You have to benchmark the models against your own use cases. As for coding, I am fairly confident that Claude 3 Opus is far superior to GPT-4, simply because I’ve used it myself a lot and have been told the same by many others.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What potential advantages does Cohere's Command-R model offer compared to ChatGPT created by OpenAI?
Answer: It arguably offers a better performance-to-latency ratio than the ChatGPT suite of models. It’s slightly slower, but clearly stronger than, GPT-3.5 turbo and much faster than GPT-4 turbo. It also has a really cool superpower. By adding just a single parameter to the API request, you can get the model to google your question and provide citations.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: From how many experts does LLM training using a mixture of experts (MoE) start slowing down compared to training LLMs without MoE?
Answer: Training an MoE LLM should generally be faster than a dense model, assuming the training set, number of epochs and number of parameters in each model are the same. Unless you increase the number of experts to the point where the routing overhead gets ridiculous. But I suppose you're asking about the speed of convergence. It really comes down to the individual model and setup then. As in, how efficiently can you spread out training across multiple GPUs. In short, how well is your training run designed. Keep in mind, MoE models can overfit more easily. In any case, MoE models tend to be slightly weaker than their dense counterparts of the same size. Their main advantage is the significant speedup offered at inference time.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is $47 per month expensive for a SaaS product?
Answer: For B2C it certainly is. Many great consumer products charge $10 per month or even less. For B2B it's kind of average. It's not uncommon for high-end B2B licenses to cost in the hundreds of dollars per seat or more. But big enterprises will typically negotiate substantial volume discounts. At the end of the day, the total contract value matters more than the price per user. There are also low-end B2B products that can cost as little as $10 per user month, but usually not lower than that.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How often does a SaaS product need to be improved or updated?
Answer: Every single day. Or at least every working day. If you have a SaaS product, you have at least one full-time software engineer (if not, what's wrong with you?). If that person is not improving and updating the product, what are they even doing? With modern CI/CD and cloud deployments, you have no excuse for not releasing to production all the time.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: If I want to prepare for a senior software engineer interview in a good company, and I have a lot of practical experience, do I still need to master "leetcode" type of questions, or my experience is enough?
Answer: Depends on your definition of a good company. Do you mean those huge tech companies? The Magnficient Seven, with their hordes of tens of thousands of code monkeys? Then yes, you need to practice LeetCode type questions. When I'm interviewing software engineers, however, I don't give them those types of questions. Why? Because to me, that's like interviewing math professors and asking them to solve a linear equation with two unknowns on the blackboard. Quite frankly, I have higher standards. Make no mistake, I vet my candidates hard, I just use different methods. Then again, I'm hiring a core team of just a few engineers, not tens of thousands. If I worked in one of those humongous code factories, I would probably use more standard interviewing techniques. All of this to say, there are companies out there, good companies, that don't put much emphasis on your ability to solve data structures and algorithms problems on a whiteboard while the hiring manager is watching you and taking notes. But they aren't necessarily the ones you've heard of.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How can a tech startup be made successful?
Answer: That’s a very broad question, but if we break it down to the basics, it’s relatively straightforward. The startup needs to offer products and/or services that can generate revenue. Beyond that, there are two core principles that modern startup theory generally agrees on. Product-market fit The product/service needs to appeal enough to customers that they are willing to pay for it. Repeatable, scalable and profitable

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Can generative AI and LLM get much better? Should we prepare for another AI winter?
Answer: We are only at the beginning. The algorithms are becoming better and more efficient, the datasets are improving, GPUs are becoming much faster and the funding into the field is exploding. All of this is happening at once, putting us right in the middle of an exponentially climbing curve. I suspect OpenAI will release an LLM within less than a year that will make current SOTA models look like toys. It'll be like the PlayStation compared to the Super Nintendo. People have been talking about a new AI winter for over a decade. They said the same thing with GPT-2. It was such a huge model, 1.5 billion parameters. How could it scale any further. Well, guess what. Three years later, we had GPT-4 with 1.8 trillion parameters, over a thousand-fold increase. And the performance difference is night and day. The evolution of AI is going from strength to strength and is showing no signs of slowing down.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: At what point will artificial Intelligence pass the Turing test?
Answer: It's not obvious to me that we'll ever pass the Turing test. In a real Turing test, the human evaluator knows that they are tasked with trying to distinguish an AI from a human, and the AI needs to be indistinguishable to pass the test. Doing that is probably much harder than achieving superintelligence. Let's make an analogy to chess. We've had superhuman chess engines since the mid-2000s. The current generation of top chess engines are much stronger than what we had back then. Miles ahead of the best humans. Yet I, a lowly amateur, not even a titled player, can still distinguish a chess game played by a computer from one played by a human top player. The chess played by computers feels different. Alien. Stronger? Sure. Able to trick and beat any human? Absolutely. But recognizably weird. I suspect it will be like that with conversational AI too.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What career is future proof from AI?
Answer: There is no career that's future proof from being impacted by AI. Literally not a single one. AI is soon going to permeate every layer of business and society whether we like it or not. Trying to ignore that fact is probably not a great career move.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Would you go out of your way to see a movie again and again?
Answer: In junior high school, there was a year that I watched a Star Wars movie every day after school. Since there were only three of them at the time, I ended up watching them quite a few times. I didn't really need to go out of my way, since the VHS tapes were lying next to the TV ready to go and I didn't have a life yet. I needed to rewind the tapes I guess. I haven't repeated that experiment since. To be honest, it got a little repetitive. I'm not even sure I have watched any other movie more than 10 times.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Why is Gen AI good for business?
Answer: Gen AI is a dream for businesses because: The ROI of Gen AI compared to traditional supervised model development is through the roof.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Outsourcing labor to cheaper countries and shipping the goods back to wealthy countries was a game changer since the 1980s. But, with AI and robots, man-hours per product goes down while design and robot training goes up. Will this kill outsourcing?
Answer: Let's make one thing clear. It's not a lack of technology that's preventing the Western world from homesourcing manufacturing of goods. Industrial robots have been around for over 50 years. They don't require modern AI to operate. No, the main reason China is the leader in manufacturing is simply that the cost of labor is lower than the cost of installing and maintaining industrial robots for most types of goods. There are some exceptions for very expensive and complex goods like cars, where robots are more cost-efficient than humans. However, you still need humans to operate a robotic factory, so the car factories tend to get outsourced to China anyway. The introduction of smart factories and industry 4.0 could potentially lead to more homesourcing as the number of employees needed is reduced even further, but it's not going to kill outsourcing just yet.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is Hans Niemann the real deal capable of overtaking Magnus Carlsen as the world's best chess player or an overhyped & overrated GM who secretly cheated to make himself look very good?
Answer: Hans Niemann is the real deal. He is ranked 45th in the world with a FIDE rating of 2688 and a peak FIDE rating of 2708. That makes him a genuine super GM. He is also merely 20 years old, and has a potentially bright career ahead of him. While Niemann has been caught cheating online in the past, there is no solid evidence that he has cheated to obtain his current over-the-board rating. Is he capable of overtaking Magnus Carlsen as the number one player in the world? No. He might overtake Magnus one day simply because he is 12 years younger, but it's not going to happen while Magnus is number one. Niemann is an incredible talent, but not quite at the level needed to become the world's very best player. Especially while Magnus is still in his prime.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How much does drinking alcohol (not to the point of getting drunk nor even tipsy) impact muscle recovery and muscle growth? If you drink both after working out and on the next day will that impact gym results?
Answer: Alcohol in your system severely inhibits protein synthesis since your body will prioritize breaking down the alcohol. Timing Going to the gym before drinking (which many people do) is a lot worse than going to the gym the day after drinking (which not so many people do). If you work out before drinking, your body will be preoccupied with alcohol metabolism during the time it should be recovering. On the other hand, if you work out the next day when the alcohol is out of your system, it won't really affect recovery, although it will impact your performance in the gym. Amounts Naturally, the more you drink, the worse it is. But there is really no amount that's “safe”. If you drink something like 3–4 units or more, the workout will probably have a negative effect on your body, since your muscles will break down more than they recover. If you drink just a single unit, the workout will most likely still have a positive muscle-building effect, but it will be worse than if you didn't drink anything. Working out and going on an immediate binge is definitely inadvisable. Other factors To make matters worse, alcohol makes you sleep worse, which also has a negative effect on recovery. Alcoholic beverages also contain “empty” calories that tend to give you excess bodyfat when those calories could instead have been spent on nutritious food.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: It is said that programming requires a certain aptitude. According to you, what is this aptitude that people talk about? What were the traits you personally have ?
Answer: High general intelligence, or g. Now, before you start writing your angry comments, let me just state that I don't mean to say that professional programming requires genius-level intelligence or anything of the sort. A fairly normal intelligence is enough to be a successful programmer, but it does help a lot if you're a standard deviation or two above the mean. Intelligence is one aspect that's pretty important to succeed as a programmer. Another major factor that's arguably even more important is the intrinsic motivation to study and learn how to program computers. That being said, it's much more likely for someone to gain that intrinsic motivation if they are intelligent enough that it comes easy to them. When you are good at something, it's naturally more enjoyable. Now you can proceed with your angry comments.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: As a young software engineer, how is my career outlook in 5-10 years time during this current AI boom?
Answer: Nobody really knows. The opinions of people who claim to know what the future will bring on a longish timescale should be regarded with a great deal of skepticism. On one side, there is a large group of people who claim confidently that AI will never replace software engineers. It's just another tool that will make us more efficient, like all the other programming tools that came before it. On the other side, you have those that claim that all software engineers will be gone in 5 years. I'm highly skeptical about both of these extremes. They just seem unlikely to me. I believe we'll see something in the middle. Software engineers will become more efficient thanks to AI (that's already happening) and employers will gradually let AI tools take over more of the programming work, starting with the simplest tasks. This will most likely lead to software developers being displaced. But again, I don't really know. Even though my background and experience makes me qualified to make pretty good guesses, it's pure speculation. If I were to make one career advice, it would be this: Be adaptable and don't be resistant to progress and change. Embrace new technologies and make yourself useful. If you do that, you should be alright.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How many years does it take for a SaaS company to reach $1-2mm ARR?
Answer: The median SaaS startup goes from first customer to $1M ARR in 2 years and 9 months according to ChartMogul's 2023 growth report. The best-in-class startups get there in less than a year, while the laggards take more than 4 years. Keep in mind two things when comparing your startup with these metrics, though: If your startup is on a trajectory to $1M at all, that's a big win. SaaS is a marathon, not a sprint. Once the machine gets rolling and you get to economies of scale, it's an incredibly lucrative business model that can just keep compounding.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Are the algorithms now used by MS and Google on LLM AI too wasteful of power? From the story of DeepMind alphago, via algorithm improvement, it not only greatly reduces the calculation amount but also get better results (at least 50% of power waste)?
Answer: Current LLMs are absolutely too wasteful, but the technology is progressing at incredible rates. The new DBRX model from Databricks is better than GPT-3.5 Turbo while being a slightly smaller model with 132B parameters and having a mixture-of-experts architecture that means only 36B parameters are active per inference request. That makes it far more computationally efficient and thus more energy-efficient. The new Blackwell generation of GPUs from Nvidia support 4-bit precision floating-point operations, meaning a quarter of the computation is needed per matrix multiplication compared to the 16-bit architecture of the current Ampere generation. Blackwell also supports liquid cooling, reducing power consumption even further. This is Huang's law, the observation that performance advancements in GPUs are far outpacing advancements in CPUs. We'll soon have LLMs far more capable than the ones we have today running at a much lower wattage. The end game is that foundation models will be running in real-time on edge devices.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What prompted Elon Musk to announce the decision to make XAI's AI chatbot Grok open-source?
Answer: Someone pointed out the irony in Musk suing OpenAI for keeping their models proprietary while not open-sourcing his own model, Grok. A day or so later, the model was up on GitHub.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How do you think Databricks' new DBRX generative AI model compares to GPT-4?
Answer: It's not as good as GPT-4, but that's not what I would compare it to. DBRX has two important qualities that GPT-4 doesn't have: For a model that's slightly more performant than GPT-3.5 turbo while also being faster, that makes it arguably the top LLM for real-time use cases at the moment.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How do I structure a startup team at the early stage?
Answer: Start with defining the different functions in your company. Look into the future and try to imagine what the departments of your org will be when it has 50 or 100 employees. Maybe it looks something like this: If you're two team members in the founding team, you pick three functions each. For instance, one co-founder could do sales, marketing and ops, while the other handles product, engineering and customer success. This would be a typical CEO/CTO split for a business-oriented and technical co-founder duo. If you're three, you pick two functions each etc. When hiring employees, they report directly to the person in charge of their respective function. Hire an engineer? They report to the CTO. Hire a sales rep? They report to the CEO. Pretty simple. Once either of the functions have enough people that they can no longer share two pizzas, the team needs a manager. You either promote within the team or hire externally. Then you add additional layers of management as the company scales. This is a fairly straightforward playbook that works for most startups.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: If you've read the novel, is "2001" by Arthur C. Clarke worth reading?
Answer: If you're a fan of science fiction like me, I would consider 2001 essential reading. It's one of the landmark works of one of the greatest SF writers of the 20th century in his prime. 2001 was one of the first SF novels I ever read as a kid, and I have very fond memories of it, having read it twice (thrice?). It's mysterious and captivating, and tackles typical sci-fi themes like aliens and AI in an original and interesting way. It was written specifically for Kubrick's movie, but stands well on its own. In fact, I gained a greater appreciation of the movie after having also read the book, because some of the plot points in the movie were far from obvious to 12-year-old me. I would personally rank 2001 as Clarke's second best novel after Rendezvous with Rama, which is one of the all-time classics of the genre. Others would rank Chilhood's End or Fountains of Paradise ahead, but I think 2001 is more universally appealing. Even for the casual sci-fi reader who only enjoys the occasional novel now and then, I would shortlist 2001 as one of the 20 or so titles I would recommend to pretty much anyone.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What are appropriate titles to give to the high level tech talent at a startup?
Answer: The founding engineer is usually given the CTO title. While the job of a founding engineer at an early-stage startup is very different from that of a CTO at a mature company, it's an established practice to use it for several reasons. Having a CTO on board gives confidence to investors, outward credibility to partners and customers and can be helpful when attracting tech talent. The next engineering hires after that should in my opinion simply be called Senior Software Engineer even if they are high-end talents. Titles like Lead Software Engineer, Tech Lead, Engineering Manager, Head of Engineering and VP of Engineering should be preserved for when the company adds additional layers of management. You don't want to give those titles up front because you don't yet know whether you want to promote managers internally or hire them externally as you scale up. Some engineers are either not a good fit to step into a management position or they simply don't want to.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How fast do programmers really code? Is it as fast as we see in the movies? Is that possible?
Answer: Some type fast. Others don't. It's really not the typing speed that matters.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Does it mean as an entrepreneur you are weak since you have to hire people stronger than you? If that's the case, please make it make sense to me, if not, so the merit of the entrepreneur is overrated?
Answer: Entrepreneurs are superstars. If they’ve brought the company from zero to… something, they’ve already done the hardest job there is in the world of business. A successful entrepreneur who can hire a first sales manager that is half as good as them is on the right track. Of course, every entrepreneur will tell you that they’re hiring people that are smarter than them. Saying anything else is an insult to employees and investors. But the truth is they’re often not.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: If AI robots talked to each other, would they become smarter?
Answer: Possibly, yes. Reinforcement learning through self-play has shown incredible results with models like AlphaZero that learned how to play chess and beat the best chess engines in the world. In principle, there is no reason why this learning paradigm wouldn't work with conversations instead of gameplay. The challenge lies in defining good utility functions. In games they are obvious. The goal is to win the game. But you could imagine a scenario where AIs are working on science and engineering problems and share their results with each other. Let's say you let multimodal AIs design the new engines for every team on the Formula 1 grid. Between each season, they share their findings with each other through conversations. The loss function is how much time the car spends around the circuits. It would probably work, with the caveat that the learning itself would need to happen in virtual worlds in practice. The real world is just too slow.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: I am considering purchasing a Volvo XC90 plug-in hybrid (electric range of 30.4 miles). I am interested in hearing about people's experiences with plug-in hybrids. Are they becoming irrelevant? I would appreciate your advice on this matter.
Answer: I’ve driven an XC90 plug-in hybrid as my main vehicle for five years. First of all, it’s an excellent car. Volvos are expensive, but man, they are really, really good. While it may not be the most spectacular car in the world, it just checks all the boxes for me, having a family of five. That being said, if I were to buy a new car today, I would almost certainly go for the EX90 fully-electric vehicle instead. It is the same size as the XC90 and has a range of 373 miles. It’s also built on a dedicated EV platform, with all the advantages that entails. Now, the reason I bought the plug-in hybrid five years ago was primarily due to tax exemptions for hybrids here in Norway. The flagship T8 hybrid was actually cheaper than the T6 gasoline model here. (I also bought it because 400 hp is cool, obviously, but don’t tell my wife). To be honest, the 30-mile electric motor in the car is kind of pathetic. It gets me to work and back, but that’s about it. It’s also pretty hard to not use any gas even for short commutes when you’re driving a puny 90 hp electric motor and have a 310 hp gas motor just waiting for you at the slightest push of a pedal. Even in the so-called Pure mode, the gas engine kicks in quite easily. When I go for long drives or holidays, I never bother bringing the charger. The future is fully electric anyway. Hybrids are just a transitional phase. They’re going to be banned in the future. I’m keeping mine for the time being, though. Like I said, it’s an amazing car.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: As a software engineer, have you seen POC code being pushed to production without being production ready?
Answer: “Production ready” is a matter of definition and kind of a misused term in my opinion. Modern CI/CD and trunk-based development When I've developed a new feature and it seems to be working, I don't see anything obviously wrong with it and it passes my unit tests, I ship it to production. If some critical bug turns up, I roll back, but it usually doesn't. More often, some minor thing will come up and I use a “fix forward” strategy instead. This is one of the key ideas of trunk-based development and contiuous delivery. The lead time for bug fixes is fast, because you're already working against origin/master. That does not mean I'm trying to “fail fast” or “break things” as so many teams pride themselves on. I'm trying to avoid failing and breaking things as much as I can. But failures eventually happen, and when they do, I minimize their impact. The old way “Production ready” used to mean slow release cycles and big bang deployments. Everything had to go through pull requests, code reviews, QA sign-offs and all kinds of processes before the code would be allowed to touch production. You know what often happened? Instead of introducing one or two bugs to production, a release might introduce 50 bugs. Merge hell was a thing too. Imagine being a SaaS company today and telling your customers “we can develop the feature this week but we'll have to wait to end of next quarter to release it”. That's no good.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Will tech companies still hire entry-level software engineers?
Answer: For sure. Even if we were to imagine a company that let AI do all of the programming, they would still be hiring computer science graduates. Understanding how software and computers work is very valuable in a tech company, even if you’re not doing any actual coding. Having that background is useful whether you’re a product manager, UX designer, data analyst, sales engineer or any other non-coding tech role. And in the meantime, software engineers are still needed to churn out code as well.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What are the major takeaways from the Nvidia GTC conference?
Answer: The one major takeaway is that the new Blackwell architecture allows for much faster, more cost-effective and more energy-efficient training of - and inference by - generative AI models. Data centers have only recently begun rolling out the H100 GPUs that run on the Hopper architecture, and this new B200 unit completely blows it out of the water. Most of the world’s AI infrastructure is still running on A100s using the Ampere architecture, which is the generation before Hopper. The other crazy update is that the NVLink system now allows for 1.8 TB/s inter-GPU communication per connection in a setup with up to 576 (!) GPUs. The previous generation was limited to 8. A single rack with 72 Blackwell GPUs can run up to 1.4 exaFLOPS. That is insane! To put that into perspective, the world’s fastest supercomputer (which cost $600 million) runs at 1.2 exaFLOPS[1]. That’s right. You’re looking at a rack that’s faster than any supercomputer in the world. I didn’t physically attend the conference, but I watched the 2-hour keynote by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. To be honest, some of it was the typical hot air that tech CEOs spout to increase shareholder value. Like, “we’re going to build a digital twin of the world”. But there is no denying that Nvidia is delivering the goods when it comes to computing hardware.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Would anyone want an AI-powered content assistant? I am a solo developer and wondering if this is worth my time to build.
Answer: There is a demand for AI-powered content assistants, but it's a highly saturated market. The reason for that is simple. You only need a lightweight wrapper on top of an LLM like ChatGPT or Claude to provide content. It's really easy to build. You could even say that the LLMs are content assistants without any additional logic on top. In fact, millions of people use ChatGPT for this very use case every day. Jasper (jasper.ai) took an early lead in this space by being the first GPT wrapper to launch as a content assistant tool in 2021. By October 2022, its valuation had already ballooned to $1.5B. You'd think that the huge success of GenAI in the last couple of years would have elevated Jasper to even greater heights. But no. Its most recent valuation was $1.2B, a drop from 2022 due to disappointing growth. There could be all kinds of reasons for Jasper's failure to grow, but I think the crux of it is that you need to provide substantially more value on top of GenAI models to succeed as a startup in 2024 compared to 2022. By all means, you can probably copy Jasper's business model, stick a lower price tag on your product and get some customers if you're really good at sales and marketing. But that's a race to the bottom. There are so many business opportunities for AI-powered startups at the moment. Content assistants honestly seems like one of the least promising ones.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What are the trade-offs involved in choosing between a monolithic architecture and a microservices architecture for a large-scale distributed system, and how do you decide which one to use?
Answer: With microservices, you get flexibility at the cost of complexity. Let's throw around some concrete examples to illustrate. Example 1: A system is developed by a team in Europe, while a sub-module of the system is being developed by a team in East Asia who uses a different programming language and deploys their code while the developers in Europe are asleep. Microservices are great because the services are independently deployable. Example 2: A system processes billions of lightweight messages a day (think IoT or social media) while also running a heavy analytics batch job once a day. In this case a service-based lambda architecture with a hot and a cold path would be a typical choice. It would make no sense to run the real-time stream processing job on the same infrastructure as the batch job since they have totally different scaling requirements. Example 3: A simple enterprise app with a CRUD backend and SPA frontend has 100 million users. It's developed by a single team using a unified tech stack. A monolithic architecture would be a good choice here to avoid unnecessary complexity and network overhead. Just because it's a large-scale distributed system doesn't mean you need to split it up.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Should I continue studying software engineering as AI is going to take my job?
Answer: I take it you don't have a job yet. It's not really possible for AI to take something you don't have. Myself, I have studied math, physics, electrical engineering, economics, management and journalism. None of those fields of study are directly related to my primary job. Yet they have provided me with various problem-solving skills that have turned out to be useful in every job I've had. My point being that if you acquire knowledge as part of your higher education, it will probably be useful to you in ways you hadn't imagined.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How "good" were you after 1-3 years of full-time experience as a software engineer?
Answer: When I was hired for my first full-time software engineering job, I essentially couldn't write code. I had to learn on the job. After 1 year, I was basically still a beginner. After 3 years, I was becoming quite decent. However, that year I got a new colleague who was very experienced and also really, really good. A true 10x engineer. He taught me a lot. A couple of years later when I had 5 years of experience I was a heck of a lot better than before.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How did Tesla become the top-selling car company in Norway? It gets very cold in Norway like in Alaska.
Answer: Because unlike what the fossil fuel lobbyists will tell you, EVs work perfectly fine in extremely cold weather. Besides, Norway is not nearly as cold as Alaska, even though we're on the same latitudes. Norway is a coastal nation that gets warmed up by hot Atlantic currents. The climate is not as harsh as you'd expect. The main reason Teslas became popular in Norway, however, is that EVs are not taxed as heavily as ICE cars.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: According to Nvidia CEO Jen-Hsun "Jensen" Huang, coding is dead. Do you agree?
Answer: Of course it's not dead. There are tens of millions of people around the world who are paid to write code on a daily basis. They are paid well too. Jensen said that kids shouldn't learn to code. While I understand his motivations and I agree with him that AI is going to transform the way we program computers, I still think it's an irresponsible thing to say. The world will still need software engineers for the foreseeable future, even if AI is going to gradually take over more of the programming work. Any young person today who is interested in computer science should study it and learn how to write code. There will be work for them in the future, even if the job might not look exactly like the same as it does now.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What should be the main focus of a software engineering student in the last year of graduation?
Answer: In order of importance: 1. Finishing strong. 2. Finding a job. 3. Learning how to write code.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: If someone is obese, what should they do at the gym? I am currently doing 4x strength training a week and 2x cardio, but after every strength day, I also do 15 minutes of cardio.
Answer: If you are obese, you should focus more on what you do outside of the gym. Specifically, what you do in the kitchen. You can go from obese to lean simply by adjusting your diet, without doing any exercise whatsoever. You can also stay obese even with a great training program if you don’t adjust your diet. What you can’t do is lose a lot of weight without restricting your diet. Don’t get me wrong. I’m not saying exercise doesn’t help. It just matters very little for weight loss compared to your diet.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is it true that no programmers will be needed within 5 years due to AI?
Answer: I'm fairly bullish compared to most people on AI taking over programming work. However, I can't imagine a path for AI to replace all programming jobs in less than five years. First of all, I don't think the capabilities of the best AI systems will be advanced enough to perform some of the more complex work. Realistically, we might see two or three more generations of LLMs in that time. By extrapolating current trends, I can see the next generation being on par with a decent junior developer in terms of pure code-writing ability. The generation after might be on the level of a senior engineer. Writing code is only half the story, though. We need agents with built-in automation to plan and organize development work. That's going to take more time. Besides, there will probably still be those weird edge cases that fall just outside the capabilities of the best models even three or four generations down the line. Finally, the rollout and deployment of AI agents on a mass scale is going to take a long time. There are industries that are so conservative and archaic you wouldn't believe it. Large parts of the financial industry still run on mainframes. The institutional barriers will delay the rollout many years after the technology becomes viable.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Why do so many tech companies struggle to make a proft?
Answer: First of all, no one needs another app. Whether you're a consumer or a business, you have too many of them already. To be able to sell software, you need to solve a specific problem better than your competitors, and you also need to convince your customers that you will solve their problem, and that their problem is even worth solving. That's product-market fit, and that's just step one. Second, you need a scalable, repeatable and profitable business model. Even many companies that find product-market fit end up dying. Either because they fail to find a scalable, repeatable and profitable business model or simply because they run out of cash before they get to break-even. While software has very good margins once you get to scale, it also has high up-front development costs. The only way to turn a profit is to sell many licenses. And the company will go through a valley of death (or “trough of despair”) before breaking even. Identifying a scalable go-to-market strategy, and executing it, is even harder than developing the product. And it's a race against time.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Do you think Apple will end up using Google Gemini AI? Why or why not?
Answer: In a surprise move, Apple announced its own family of multimodal LLMs dubbed MM1 yesterday. The MM1 family includes models with up to 30 billion parameters, both dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. Apple even published a paper on it: MM1: Methods, Analysis & Insights from Multimodal LLM Pre-training At the moment, Apple, infamous for its walled gardens, is more open about its AI models than another well-known company with “Open” in its name. This looks like a strategic move to avoid having to use 3rd party services for apps like Siri. The AI itself is not an end product for Apple. The company rarely uses the term “AI” at all in presentations and marketing content. That's probably why they're so open about this.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is it true that it’s practically impossible to get hired as a software engineer in the current job market? Should I still pursue it, I’m very passionate for it, but the fact that people say such things make my thoughts clouded with uncertainty.
Answer: There are close to 30 million software developers in the world. More than there’s ever been. Even more than there were prior to the tech layoffs in 2022–2023. So no, it’s most definitely not impossible to get hired as a software engineer. There is a growing nervousness about the future of software engineering as an occupation due to the advancements of AI. However, AI is not replacing software engineers just yet. And even if AI were to make software engineers in their current form obsolete, chances are that whatever new role pops up instead will suit you well. If you are passionate about something, pursue it and good things will happen. Don’t overthink it too much.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is it true that senior developer candidates who do not succeed in interviews are typically seen as lacking in problem-solving skills? And how many of you are skilled developers but struggle during interviews?
Answer: It's well known that the typical whiteboarding tests are bad measures of on-the-job skill level. They don't capture what the actual job looks like. These tests can even select against the best candidates, because they favor the developers who are so desperate to get a new job that they are willing to study algorithms and data structures specifically to prepare for the interview. So why are they still so prevalent in the industry? Well, if you're recruiting for a huge company employing literally thousands of developers, what's the alternative? You want to know the best way to filter senior developer candidates? The very best way by far? Ok, here it is: Hire someone you know. That's it.
