Find someone you or one of your colleagues have worked with in the past, or someone that you trust very well has worked with. Then the candidate is already pre-vetted. It works like a charm! Of course, that approach doesn't scale. Once you hit a few hundred employees, you need a process. You start running out of people you know. Because of that, large companies resort to whiteboard interviews, even though it's a broken process. At least it's a process. So no, you will not be seen as lacking in problem-solving skills if you fail an interview as a senior developer. And yes, many skilled developers do poorly in interviews.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: As a software engineering manager, how do you balance tech debt vs feature development work for your team?
Answer: Most software engineering managers are middle managers. They're in that famous squeeze between their team and higher-level management. The squeeze is primarily a people problem and not so much a tech problem. You have to answer to sales who wants to please their prospects to meet quotas. Then you have executive management who wants to show off innovation when presenting the company outward. And finally you have your engineers, who usually have the product's best interests at heart, but are also often naive to the harsh realities of running a business. Balancing all of that is an impossible task, so you try to be practical and give a little in every direction to keep everyone somewhat pleased. A well-run tech company will have a VP of Engineering that shields their engineering managers from outside pressures so that the engineering managers in turn can shield their engineers and deliver the best possible product.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Regarding the AI hype, do you think people have too high expectations?
Answer: I used to think that. When I worked as a data scientist in the mid-2010s, there was so much hype surrounding machine learning that my clients expected me to come in and magically solve all their problems even when they had no data. This often caused unrealistic expectations and failed projects. Back then, all we had was supervised learning, and most of my projects started with setting up data collection pipelines from scratch. With the rise of self-supervised learning and generative AI in the 2020s, all of that has changed. Now, it's actually possible to solve advanced problems even without any training data. If anything, I'd say that people have too low expectations these days. The disconnect I'm seeing now is a different one. While many people are aware of the capabilities of current models, they underestimate the fact that the state-of-the-art is moving at a rapid pace. I'll hear things like “LLMs are cool, but they can't do X”, where X is some capability that is undoubtedly coming in the next generation of models.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Why are Europeans not as fat as Americans are when Europeans eat white bread and pasta and butter all the time?
Answer: It’s a simple matter of calories in, calories out. Whether you eat white bread, wholewheat bread or rye bread is not going to make a significant difference. Whether you have pasta, potatoes or rice on your dinner plate doesn’t matter much either. It’s the amount that matters. When I went to the movies in New York and ordered a large coke, they gave me the largest cup of coke I have ever seen. My popcorn serving was humongous too. You don’t see that in Europe. So that’s the calories in part. As for calories out, it mostly comes down to how much walking you do. Sure, you can exercise, but unless you’re a professional athlete, you’re not really burning that many calories through exercise. It’s the walking that matters. Americans drive everywhere. American cities are literally designed to be unwalkable.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Which algorithms are the most difficult for programmers to program, and why?
Answer: Let me make an analogy. Mathematics at the undergraduate level is not that hard if you have the knack for it, because it’s pure logic. Economics can be quite complex because it combines math with subject matter. However, the math in economics is very simple. Overall, that makes the study of economics non-trivial, but not too hard either. Physics, on the other hand, can be very hard. It combines advanced math with complex subject matter. Algorithms in computer science are like math. Just pure logic. It’s when you apply them to real-world problems that things become difficult. The programming equivalent of physics is something like a large distributed system that operates within a complex domain. Not only does it involve advanced algorithmic problems, but one also has to deal with how these algorithms interact with the specific quirks of the domain.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What makes Devin different from other coding AI tools?
Answer: The difference between Devin and existing tools is that they're all copilots. This is the first real attempt at full automation. Copilot tools give you code snippets, but they won't solve tasks end to end. With a tool like Devin, you can give it a high-level task, and it runs off and does everything it needs to do to deploy the final deliverable, such as reading documentation, compiling and debugging the solution and finally deploying it. With copilots, you’re essentially a senior developer pair programming with a junior one. You're holding its hand more than it’s holding yours. With an automated AI assistant, you're a project manager creating tickets. Copilots can enhance developers, automation can replace them. From a business perspective, that is night and day. As a disclaimer, I don't think the technology is quite there yet from what I've seen. An AI programmer that can only solve 14% of GitHub issues is not someone I would want on my team. But we're getting a lot closer to something that's commercially viable. It's only a matter of time now.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How is AI killing software engineers? What can we do to stop it?
Answer: There is nothing we can do to stop the progress. Consider the following: In conclusion, AI programming is inevitably going to be rolled out pretty soon, and we can't stop it even if we wanted to. Will this “kill” software engineering as a profession? I don't know, but I think that's going to take a while. For those of us who have been around in the AI scene for some time, you might remember this meme: As it turns out, this was all wrong. The intelligence delta between the village idiot and Albert Einstein is much greater than we thought. Yes, we have AI agents that are approaching the level of a mediocre junior developer (the village idiot, if you will). However, that's a far cry from an experienced 10x developer. I think we're about to enter an extremely weird interregnum where human and AI programmers co-exist. The software engineers who succeed in this era will all have to rely on AI tools to a certain extent. How long this period is going to last before we go to full-blown automation is very hard to predict.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: With the release of Devin (software engineering AI), how will that impact the market?
Answer: Devin at its current state is more of a proof of concept. While developing an AI that solves ~14% of open GitHub issues is an impressive feat, it needs to improve before it starts disrupting the job market. Cognition Labs, the company that develops Devin, also has the disadvantage of being first to market. First movers rarely win in the end. That being said, the implications of what is happening these days cannot be understated. Most people have a normalcy bias and fail to recognize the disruptive changes that AI will bring about in the next few years. It’s simply hard to imagine a near future with a job market that’s suddenly radically different. Once we have an AI that can solve most coding tasks in a run-of-the-mill software project based on simple ticket descriptions, there will be huge incentives for employers to replace their junior engineers with AI. I believe we’ll probably see that within five years. I don’t claim to know what the future holds for software engineering or how this will all play out, but I’m pretty sure it will cause massively disruptive changes to software engineering teams.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Which developer should I hire, the one who will write a messy program in three hours, or the ones who will make a well-structured program in twelve? Which is more important, speed or quality?
Answer: I have written an in-depth analysis of this dilemma here: I call them cowboys and turtles. Ideally you want the unicorn who can deliver high quality quickly, but those developers are so rare that you can't expect to be able to hire one. When faced with the choice of a fast but reckless cowboy or a reliable but slow turtle, I would usually lean towards hiring the turtle. However, there are situations when you simply want something quickly out in the market to test it, and then the cowboy is your friend.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is the role of an AI prompt engineer already dead, given that LLMs are better at it?
Answer: Prompt engineering is very much alive and kicking, but someone who can only write prompts has limited use. Now, combine prompting skills with programming skills and you have a powerful skillset that can solve a wide variety of problems in novel ways. That kind of software engineer is going to be in high demand.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What is the chance that the entry market for software engineering will be better in 4 years from now?
Answer: Probably quite low to be honest. Today, a startup called Cognition Labs launched a product they call Devin, the “world's first AI software engineer”. Devin can solve ~14% of GitHub issues that's thrown at it. Not that impressive compared to an experienced software engineer, but it's starting to approach the level of a mediocre junior. In 4 years time, I suspect these agents will outperform most professional software engineers in coding abilities. What that means for software roles and the job market is unclear as of yet, but it could potentially be very bad news for those who graduate with computer science degrees in the next few years. The good news is that the tech industry will generate more value than ever before. The bad news is that it might end up in the hands of the few rather than the many. The development of software engineering AI agents will undoubtedly have a profound effect on the industry, transforming existing job roles and creating new ones. The traditional role of software engineer is certainly under threat.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Where's the best place to read a book that's particularly special to you?
Answer: Once a year, when my birch pollen allergy kicks in, I escape up in the Norwegian mountains for a week where the birch blooms later in the summer. As a bonus, I get a break from the daily hustle and bustle of life in the city. My days are filled with solitary work, walks in the woods and lots of reading. Last year when I went up, I had an entire valley to myself. With clean air, no distractions and the only sounds coming from birds chirping and the humming of nearby rivers, it's the perfect climate for immersing myself in a heavy novel.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Why is Microsoft only a 49% stockholder owner of OpenAI? Who owns the other 51%?
Answer: The original nonprofit OpenAI owns 51% of the for-profit entity. The significance of 51% is that the nonprofit maintains control of the company and has the majority vote. It's a really weird dynamic having a nonprofit with the primary goal of owning a large for-profit enterprise though. We saw the result of that when the board fired CEO Sam Altman only to have him return a week later. The entire situation was a circus.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Why should I pay for Rider IDE if the Visual Studio Community is free?
Answer: Rider is faster and has a more complete feature set. It's just a better IDE, even when compared to Visual Studio Professional or Enterprise editions. Another reason to pay for a .NET IDE is that VS Community is not available for professional developers unless they're working in a small company. That being said, I have used VS Community in the past when I was working on my own and cost was an issue. While Rider is great, I'm not sure it's worth the steep price, since Visual Studio is also really solid.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How is the salary progression in software engineering?
Answer: It's pretty steep in the first few years. As a software engineer, you can already be considered senior after ~5 years if you're decent. At that point, you could be earning twice that of a junior engineer. After that, it tends to plateau quite a bit though. The market doesn't tend to pay that much more for a software engineer with, say, 15 years of experience than one with 5-10. Some large companies have technical ladders where software engineers can continue a steep salary progression, but it usually involves taking on managerial responsibilities of some sort.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is engineering management a good major for job prospects and salary?
Answer: By the time someone is ready to be an engineering manager, they don't need a degree to land the job. It requires experience as an engineer more than anything else. Engineering management is one of those degrees that should only exist as an executive degree in my opinion.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Who has a better chance at climbing high in an organization (director, VP, C-Suite, etc.), a software engineering manager or a product manager? Why?
Answer: Product managers very often have better people skills, so that would be your answer. On the other hand, a technologist such as a former software engineer with strong people skills would be pretty high on the wishlist for many organizations to have in their leadership group. Since most organizations are technology-centric these days, there are ample opportunities for engineers to climb ladders.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: As a software engineering manager, what do you expect from your new hire during the first month at the job?
Answer: That depends on the maturity of the company and seniority of the hire. Case in point, I just hired a software engineer that I expect to transform our product so that we can 100x our revenue in the next few years. No pressure. Now, this is a very senior engineer that I've worked with in the past, and we're a startup that's been severely understaffed. So it's an extreme case of high expectations. I expect them to be the main contributor to the codebase from day one. Conversely, if I were to hire a junior engineer for a large corporation, I would expect them to show up and learn in the first few months.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Who is earning more, an engineering manager or a solution architect?
Answer: Whoever has the higher market(*) value and/or higher willingness to move around to cash in on that market value earns more. * Market value, here meaning the minimum amount that employers in the geographical region think they have to pay to sign that person with a decent likelihood that they'll stay for a few years.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is it correct for a single team to own multiple microservices?
Answer: There is no “correct” way to design software systems. That's the beauty of it. It's more art than science. I've been involved in a small (3–4 devs) team that owned 14 microservices. I've also been the sole developer on a codebase that spanned multiple microservices. Currently, my team is running a complex multi-tenant B2B SaaS solution as a monolith. So everything is possible. One microservice per team can be a good organizational architecture, since physical separation of concerns can reduce friction between teams. However, that's not to only reason split a system into microservices. Perhaps different parts of the solution has different scaling requirements. Perhaps you want to use different programming languages. Perhaps you need stronger fault isolation to improve reliability. And so on. There is no catch-all architecture that works in every case. You need to consider the unique requirements of each system.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Will reading "Garry Kasparov on Garry Kasparov" be a good decision if my goal is to improve my chess skills (1500 USCF), or is it more of an enjoyment book?
Answer: Here is my experience: Enjoyment is a crucially important and underrated aspect of improving your performance, whether we’re talking about chess or other types of skills. If you read a chess book and enjoy it, chances are it’s going to improve your playing strength. My first chess book was The Life and Games of Mikhail Tal, which is an autobiography and not really an educational book. I read it three times cover to cover, and it definitely made me a better player. Among other things, I learned how to play blindfold chess, because I couldn’t be bothered to set up a board to play through hundreds of games.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Has microservice architecture proved itself to be overrated over the years?
Answer: Yes, by many. Microservices vs. monoliths is one of those divisive topics that cause developers to lose their minds and engage in pointless flame wars. Kind of like tabs vs. spaces. Or Vim vs. Emacs. Or PC vs. Mac. As we all know, only a Sith deals in absolutes. There is nothing holy in software engineering. Only tools and techniques that may or may not be useful to your specific problem. Microservices is an architectural style. Sometimes it’s the right one and other times it’s not. Monolithic architectures have been declared dead many times. So have microservices. In reality, they are both very much alive and kicking.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What makes working for FAANG companies seen as a gold standard? Why do some FAANG developers view those who haven't worked for such companies as tier 2 talent?
Answer: Both your questions contain incorrect assumptions. FAANG is no longer the gold standard The FAANG acronym is outdated. It was coined back in 2013 when web 2.0 and social were the main drivers of stock value in big tech. Back then, the Netflix stock was experiencing 300%+ YoY growth, while Microsoft was seen as a slowly dying company. Fast-forward to 2024, and Microsoft has 10x’ed to become the most valuable company in the world, while Netflix is “only” 38th. AI is now the main driver of stock value in big tech, as can be seen with the meteoric rise of NVIDIA and the effect of Microsoft’s partnership with OpenAI. We now talk about the “Magnificent Seven”: Microsoft, Apple, NVIDIA, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Tesla. Developers without big tech experience are not viewed as tier 2 I don’t know of anyone who thinks of you as a lesser developer just because you haven’t worked at a big tech company. Yes, some will be pretty impressed if you have a prestigious logo on your CV and assume you’re pretty smart. They might even lose their objectivity and hire someone just based on their experience at a certain company even when it’s not the right move. On the flip side, big company experience can sometimes be seen as a slight negative in the startup world, where you need to be very agile.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is AI too hyped since this field hardly gets people rich?
Answer: Have you heard about Jensen Huang? The CEO of NVIDIA? He added $10 billion to his net worth last Friday. It was a pretty good day for Jensen. All those billions are thanks to the increased demand for GPUs used to train and serve AI models. But not everyone can be the CEO of NVIDIA, you might say. And you would be right. Then what the about the good people at OpenAI? The total compensation for an entry-level engineering position at OpenAI is upwards of $500k. Enough to make you rich after a few years. Then again, not everyone can get a job at OpenAI either. Again, true. But you can easily make six figures, and then some, in a run-of-the-mill ML Engineer or Data Scientist job at lesser-known companies. AI is simply driving a ton of value these days with the success of generative AI, and it’s not just the founders and CEOs that are flourishing.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How important is AI diversity in technology, as highlighted by Google CEO's comments on Gemini AI diversity errors? What steps should tech companies take to address diversity issues in AI?
Answer: It’s important, but unfortunately managing bias in Large Language Models (LLMs) is an almost impossible task. These models have hundreds of billions of parameters and will take on a life of their own. You can try to micromanage an LLM through techniques like Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), but it will never be enough. There will always be an opportunity to jailbreak them with clever prompts. You can’t go into every little parameter and remove every ounce of bias. LLMs are trained on vast repositories of real-world data generated by people on the internet. Human society has a ton of biases, and those are reflected in the training data and ultimately in the LLMs.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Why are major tech companies like Alphabet, Microsoft, and Amazon announcing significant layoffs despite reporting robust profits, and how does this relate to their strategic shift towards generative artificial intelligence (AI)?
Answer: The mass layoffs in big tech are primarily a consequence of the 2022-2023 downturn in the tech industry. These things go in cycles. Do the layoffs have anything to do with the strategic shift towards generative AI? Not directly. Then again, large tech companies are notorious for using these downturns to get rid of engineers with outdated skillsets only to staff up with new talent a year or two later. I'm sure the shifting technology trends and the generative AI wave were in the back of these companys’ hive minds when they were downsizing.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Can you speak up if a team member gives incorrect information during a daily standup meeting?
Answer: Of course you can. That's sort of the point of having standups. To clear up misunderstandings. A team that lacks the psychological safety to allow everyone to speak their mind will not be a high-performing team.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Hikaru Nakamura’s IQ is 102, does this mean you don’t need to be intelligent to be a world-class chess player or IQ is not a good measure of intelligence?
Answer: I have met and talked to Nakamura. I have played chess against him, and I have followed his games online for two decades. Naka's personality is controversial, but make no mistake, he is a highly intelligent guy. He's not just good at chess. He excels at pretty much anything he applies himself to. Just look at the way he has created a social media empire by forging an online persona despite being socially awkward in real life. I don't buy the 102 IQ result for a second. Naka's true IQ is almost certainly a couple of standard deviations above the mean at least. You don't get to 2800 in chess without having a very high general intelligence. You just don't.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Do you think Alireza will pass Carlsen's peak rating?
Answer: It's not looking very likely at the moment. To get to 2882+, Alireza needs to have a good win rate against other 2800s and completely dominate the 2750-2800 cohort. Right now, only Magnus Carlsen and Fabiano Caruana are above 2800, and just barely. In addition, there are only 7 other players, apart from Alireza himself, above 2750. Back in 2014 when Magnus first reached 2882, there were more 2750s, more 2700s and Aronian was at 2830. There has been rating deflation at the top since then. The second time Magnus reached 2882, in 2019, there were four players above 2800. Alireza surpassed 2800 two years ago, but since then his rating has dropped and he seems less focused on classical chess. Finally, Magnus is still very dominant. In conclusion, a few things need to happen: I figure Alireza won't see 2882+ unless at least three of these things happen.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Why do most experienced programmers prefer to use dark themes for their IDE?
Answer: Cargo cult. There is no inherent advantage to dark themes. Programmers use them to appease the programming gods. It also gives them a feeling of superiority. Programmers hope that some project manager is going to walk past their screen and think they're working on something difficult and important.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Why is there no Nobel Prize for chess?
Answer: There used to be a chess “Oscar” awarded every year to the consensus best player in the world that year, but there has never been a lifetime achievment award in chess as far as I'm aware. Chess is a competition where the results usually (in the words of Hans Niemann) speak for themselves.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Could Mikhail Tal have been the GOAT of chess if it wasn't for his poor health/addictions?
Answer: I'll preface this answer by acknowledging that I'm a huge fan of Mikhail Tal. His autobiography was the first chess book I ever read and it shaped the way I play chess more than anything else. It left a major impression. Could Tal have been a greater chess player if it weren't for his drug abuse and health problems? Yes! I have no doubt that his poor health had a negative impact on his results during his adult years. Maybe he would have defended his title against Botvinnik in 1961. Maybe he even would have been the dominant player in the 1960s. Could Tal have been the greatest player ever if not for these problems? No. Tal was a huge talent for sure, but you know who was an even bigger talent? Garry Kasparov and Magnus Carlsen. And unlike Tal, those guys stayed healthy and maximized their potentials.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What do you think about The World Rapid Chess Championship? Who is the world's best chess player over the past ten years?
Answer: What do you think about The World Rapid Chess Championship? As a friend and fan of Magnus Carlsen, I think it's great that he won it again. It means a lot to him now that he no longer is playing for the classical title. Who is the world's best chess player over the past ten years? Hmm, let me think about that. Tough one… Well, first of all, Magnus has now won 5 of the 11 official world rapid championships FIDE has arranged since 2012. He's the only player to win it more than once. Magnus has also won 5 of the 10 world blitz championships. Grischuk is the only other player to have won it twice. Of the 6 classical world championship matches played in the last decade, Magnus won 5 and withdrew from the last. He has been the highest rated classical player on every rating list for the last 13 years or so. I'll go out on a limb and say it's Magnus.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Should a software engineering interview be geared towards ensuring that a poor developer isn’t hired even if it means losing 10 good developers?
Answer: It depends on the company that's hiring. Are we talking about Google, that gets 3 million applicants yearly and only hires 0.2% of them? In that case, yes. Google can afford a lot of false negatives to limit the number of false positives to the absolute minimum. Naturally, their hiring process is extremely risk-adverse. Or, are we talking about the early-stage startup that no one's heard about that is struggling to get even a single relevant application? In that case, the best bet is to headhunt someone that the hiring team has worked with directly in the past, or who has been recommended by someone they know. The technical interview is usually redundant in that case. Most companies fall somewhere in between. A typical job post at a medium-sized company will get a handful of relevant applicants, and perhaps only one or two of them are strong candidates. A technical interview can be conducted, but at the end of the day, it usually comes down to judging the candidate's character. Do they seem to have integrity? Will they be a good cultural fit in the team? And so on. A company like that can’t afford to reject too many good developers.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Why most of the great programmers can not become rich like Bill Gates or Elon Musk?
Answer: Bill Gates and Elon Musk are both extremely hard-working geniuses. Forces of nature. These are guys who can do pretty much anything they set their mind to. To have the ability to create something out of nothing, raise money and rally smart and determined people to join your case. That's an exceedingly rare skillset. There are millions of good programmers out there, but there is only one Elon Musk.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Computational Biologist vs Data Science? Which pays more in terms of salary? Which has more impactful meaning? Which has more future?
Answer: Data science pays more on average. Computational biologists typically work in research institutes funded by public grants. When the work is not tied to some kind of commercial entity, the salaries tend to be good but not great, at best. On the flip side, computational biology research can be very intellectually stimulating for someone who is interested in data science. Both have a good future, but there are probably 100 data science jobs for every computational biology job, so job security is a lot better as a data scientist.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What do the top 1% of software engineers do that the other 99% do not?
Answer: To be a bit pedantic, there is only a marginal difference between a 99th-percentile software engineer and 98th-percentile one. In my view, the path to mastery of software craftsmanship consists of several levels. Level 1: Writing simple code A surprising number of salaried software engineers actually struggle to write working code for anything but the simplest features. It requires a baseline of talent and motivation to progress beyond this. Level 2: Solving advanced problems At this level, a software engineer is able to tackle basically any problem coming their way. The solution won't always be pretty, and it will probably include a few hacks along the way, but it will get the job done. These guys can be good to have on your team to get new features quickly out the door. The drawback is that the technical debt will pile up. Level 3: Writing elegant code With some experience, the more talented software engineers will eventually be able to write elegant code that is maintainable, testable and production-worthy. Sometimes they run the risk of over-engineering and taking too long to finish relatively simple task. These types of engineers are good to have on your team when you have a mature, mission-critical system. Level 4: Writing simple code At this point, we come full circle. The best software engineers know how to reduce complex problems to something simple. When you read their code, you'd think “I could have written that”. That only comes from years of experience and an uncanny ability to see the forest for the trees. If you're familiar with the “midwit meme”, it illustrates things nicely: The levels beyond that are about being able to leverage other people, but that has more to do with leadership and less with software engineering itself.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is it correct that salaries in industry quantum computing top out way less than in AI, even if quantum AI or quantum ML? (People are making a million a year in AI, but I think at Google Quantum AI Lab they top out below 300k., right?)
Answer: Quantum isn't really a field yet, apart from the odd research lab here and there, while AI is very much an established field in tech at this point. Software engineers may make 300k at Google, or 1M if they're at a very high level (like L7 or above). That's true for any type of SWE. It's more about the career ladder and less ablut the field they're working in. Also, keep in mind that these salaries are not representative for normal SWE salaries in the vast majority of companies.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Tech companies think most senior developers who fail interviews lack problem-solving skills. About 99% of developers are in this category. Why don't these incompetent developers focus on improving their skills instead of blaming the entire system?
Answer: I disagree with several parts of your problem, so let me break it down. Tech companies think most senior developers who fail interviews lack problem-solving skills. No, they don’t. Big tech companies are well aware that their interview processes filter out many strong candidates. However, they enjoy the luxury of having so many candidates to choose from that they can enforce extremely demanding interview processes and still meet their recruitment targets. About 99% of developers are in this category. Perhaps if you count everyone who considers themselves a developer that would be the case. But among strongly qualified developers, I think the percentage who fails outright on the coding problems is much lower. Why don't these incompetent developers focus on improving their skills instead of blaming the entire system? First of all, just because someone fails big tech interview problems doesn't mean they're incompetent. These problems typically have very little to do with the actual job of being a developer. Among those who would fail, I find that most simply don't care. They can find great jobs elsewhere, so why bother studying undergraduate-level computer science again just for the possibility that some big corporation might hire them?

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Does Quora have a future in the age of AI?
Answer: Quora is like any other technology company. It needs to innovate to stay alive. In my opinion, Quora has failed to innovate in recent years. Its product feels stale, and the enthusiasm from its users has clearly dropped. There are some brilliant people working at Quora, but the company is underfunded and underemployed. Possibly this is due to the leadership not being proactice enough in monetizing the platform's large userbase. It's not too late for Quora to become a significant player, but I feel like something needs to change. And I don't think generic AI-generated answers is the solution.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Does Magnus Carlsen has some IT background? I'm asking this question, because most of the very good chess players (2000+ ELO) that I know have a decent knowledge of IT or mathematics and I wonder if being good at chess correlates with any of these.
Answer: No, he does not. He barely finished high school. That being said, Magnus could easily have become an expert in computer science and/or mathematics had he chosen to go down that path. It's just that his interests were elsewhere. Also, thanks for calling me very good!

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is it worthwhile to go for an MS degree in CS for transition from DevOps to Data Science after 14 years of experience?
Answer: Not really. With all that experience, you already have the practical CS knowledge you need for a data science role. What you're lacking is knowledge of statistics and machine learning. A more effective way of acquiring that would be to attend a few MOOCs, go through some YouTube videos, maybe participate in a Kaggle competition, try out some experiments and read up on relevant research. It's much easier to transition into another role when you're already a seasoned veteran. Pursuing an entire master's degree would be overkill.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is it possible to build muscle well by putting in minimal effort and time?
Answer: The minimal effort would probably be to inject testosterone every other week without any training whatsoever. That would still increase your muscle mass. Not recommending that, by the way.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: After a Greek Gift Sacrifice (Bxh7+, Kxh7, Ng5+) what happens if the King comes forward (g6/h6) preventing Qh5?
Answer: Every position is a little different, but in a typical Greek gift sacrifice situation there is usually a bishop on c1. In those cases, Kh6 just walks into a discovered attack. In this example position, Kh6 loses the queen on the spot to Nxf7+ or Nxe6+. Qd3 also happens to be a forced mate. Kg6 is usually met with either Qg4, h4 or a combination of both. In the example position, if black plays Kg6, both those moves win. For instance Kg6 Qg4 f5 then simply Qg3 and the black king has nowhere to hide.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: At 13 years of age, I'm rated 1400 on Chess.com and I have lessons twice a week. Will I get to IM or GM level if I play consistently?
Answer: Nobody knows. Getting to IM, let alone GM, is not for everyone. Most people simply never get there, no matter how hard they try. There is such a thing as innate talent. A 1400 rating on chess.com is nothing out of the ordinary. It doesn’t really tell me much. I have a friend who was rated 2700 on ICC at age 13, and he became an IM. But I also know of someone who only picked up the pieces at age 15 and became a GM. So you never know. If you’re 1400, becoming a titled player is not a realistic goal yet. Instead, you could focus on more immediate goals, like improving your game and getting to 1500.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What is the best way to train and eat in order to become strong without gaining bulky muscles (for example like Bruce Lee)?
Answer: Believe me, getting muscles that are too big is never a thing you have to worry about, ever, unless you do steroids. To get big muscles, you have to train specifically for it. They don't just happen by accident. The best way to train for pure strength is to lift heavy compound weights (think squats, deadlifts, bench press) with few repetitions. Most of your working sets should be in the 1–5 rep range. Progressively overload those lifts 2 times a week each, and you will become a lot stronger. Your muscles will still grow bigger, of course. Just not as big as if you ran a bodybuilding program with higher volume, more isolation exercises and higher rep ranges. As for eating, the best way to avoid bulky muscles is to stay in a calorie deficit long enough to get to a low bodyfat percentage and stay there. Kind of like Bruce Lee did. As a side note, supposedly Bruce Lee bulked up to 75 kg at some point, which is actually quite heavy for a man of his stature. He definitely had bigger muscles than the vast majority of men. But I digress. A smaller body means less water to fill out your muscles. Of course, this will limit your strength potential as well. But you can still become very strong without increasing your size much. I’ve seen guys with average-looking physiques squat 200+ kg and benchpress 130+ kg. That’s plenty strong. To get strong, you should eat plenty of proteins and lean food. That’s the same as for building volume. You just need to avoid staying in a calorie surplus if you don’t want to grow bigger.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What's up with the sudden attention surrounding chess, which is a really nerdy, obscure hobby revolving around a board game that quickly becomes rather boring?
Answer: When the last glacial period subsided, humans started domesticating plants and animals, sparking an agricultural revolution. Suddenly, food could be harvested instead of hunted and gathered, freeing up time for frivolous activities like building civilizations, pursuing science, going to brothels, ingesting dangerous chemical compounds and playing board games. Among those games, chess-like variants quickly became the most popular. The Royal Game of Ur, ca. 2600-2400 BCE. Nerd Queen Nefertari playing Senet against herself, or perhaps analyzing a game, 13th century BCE. The modern game of chess was played with minor rule differences in the Gupta empire in the 5th century CE and was known as Chaturanga. However, it seems likely that the precursor to this game originated in the Harappan civilization. Board game closely resembling chess, found in Lothal in modern-day Gujarat, dating to 2400 BCE. So it seems that this sudden interest in chess in the last 5000 years is simply a result of people having more time for nerdy hobbies now that we have agriculture.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Do you think a rating of 2600 Elo in classical chess is enough to live from pricemoney exclusively?
Answer: Pretty much, yeah. A 2600 can win weaker Swiss tournaments outright a good portion of the time and consistently finish in the money. In addition, there are appearance fees, league play in the Bundesliga and other big leagues, weekend tournaments and so on. There are many opportunities for a 2600 to earn some bucks here and there. It's not going to be a breeze, and it won't make anyone rich, but it's possible for a 2600 to grind it out as a pro purely on tournaments. Most players at that level will have extra income by doing coaching, commentating, writing, streaming or similar activities, though. It's fairly easy for a strong GM to pursue chess full-time by combining several of these things. 2700+ is the level where chess players can make very good money from tournaments alone. And a small handful of the top players are genuinely rich.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Would it be okay to play the Sicilian if I’m about 1800-1850 on lichess and 1700-1770 on chess.com?
Answer: It's always okay to play the Sicilian. It's a great opening. I wanted to play the Sicilian Najdorf for a long time because it's such a dynamic and aggressive opening, but I refrained from it because I thought I needed to learn a lot of theory. During a tournament in Czechia in 2006 I decided screw it. Let's just play it and see what happens. Turns out, it's not really a big problem if you don't know all the theory, because your opponents don't know it either. In my debut tournament as a Sicilian player I ended up winning several miniatures against 2100s (I was rated around 2000 myself at the time) with surprising ease. Since then, it's been a mainstay in my opening repertoire. The great thing about the Sicilian is you can play for the win as black from move 1 and it's completely sound.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Elon Musk says we may reach AGI within 3-6 years. Is it realistic? I am pretty skeptical, given his track record with Tesla, SpaceX, Neuralink, Twitter, and so on and so forth. I'm still waiting for the Cybertruck to come.
Answer: When software developers estimate how long something is going to take, you can usually multiply their estimates by π . Elon is a former software developer, but he is also an entrepreneur, so you get the worst of both worlds. Not only does he underestimate complexity, but he also adds his marketing agenda to it. Any Muskian estimate should be taken with bucketloads of salt. As for the question of AGI, it's basically a question of definitions. Under some definitions, you could say that GPT-4 is AGI already. It certainly has general capabilities. However, the traditional definition of AGI is something that's closer to superintelligence. An AI that can do any task at least as well as humans. Obviously, we're not there yet, and I doubt we'll get anywhere close in this decade. The prediction markets at Metaculus are currently trending at 2026 for weak AGI and 2032 for strong AGI, down from 2059 just last year. Again, take those predictions with some salt, as the people who hang out in those prediction markets aren't necessarily representative for the general population, nor do they know the future, as the wildly fluctuating predictions clearly demonstrate. But I'm pretty sure we'll have something in 3–6 years that blows current technology out of the water. And that says a lot. The near future is shaping up to be pretty wild.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: AI will inevitably surpass human intelligence and eliminate humanity, but can any country stop pursuing AI, when doing so will put them at a military disadvantage? Already too late? Was this unpreventable?
Answer: I guess Andorra and Liechtenstein can, since they don't have armed forces anyway. For any serious country though, AI is here to stay. With any new advanced technology, the military powers will be all over it unless they think it's too inhumane (and even then they will probably use it). Moreover, the military industry doesn't view AI as a potential doomsday machine like the hydrogen bomb. To them it's just a shiny new toy. Kind of like stealth technology or drones. I think it's too late to stop this, and I don't think it could have been prevented. But the main threat with AI is not what it can do in the hands of a military superpower in my opinion. AI could potentially threaten the very fabric of society on a global scale. I'm frankly more concerned about AI generating YouTube videos than I am about AI targeting soldiers in a war.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Can I realistically reach the IM level in 4-5 years if I am currently 2000 fide and 16 years old (no more than 2-3 hours of effort a day due to school and college)?
Answer: I think it's definitely possible. If you study smart for those 2–3 hours, you're going to improve a lot, and you're still at an age where you have great potential for improving over the next few years. It might end up taking a little longer than 5 years to get the actual title. Because even after you get to IM playing strength, your rating will not have caught up and it will take time to climb to 2400. Getting three IM norms is also pretty hard. Some players get to 2400 and never achieve the norms, while others have more than enough norms but never get to 2400. You should also be realistic about your expectations. There is no guarantee that you will make IM even if you put in the hours. Most players don't. If you focus on steady improvement rather than reaching some arbitrary goal, I think you'll have a better peace of mind. Keep in mind that getting the IM title will not make you rich or famous. It's far from pro level. It just means that you're a little better than the players at 2300 and a little worse than the players at 2500. At the end of the day, you're still a hobby player like everyone else. Keep that in mind when deciding on how much of your life you want to commit to the game.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What is Quora's policy on answers that are obviously AI-generated? For example, answers that match ChatGPT output 90-100%. Since AI-generated answers are not copyrighted, is this even a problem?
Answer: I don't believe there are any restrictions on using AI to write answers. In fact, AI-generated content fits well with Quora's business objectives of increasing the sheer amount of content so they get more clicks and ad views. It does not fit so well with Quora's original mission of sharing and growing the world's knowledge, but that seems to have taken a backseat anyway. In any case, it's getting harder and harder to tell what's AI-generated by the day. Models like ChatGPT are non-deterministic, so you never know for sure what they might produce.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How do you feel about people who post AI-generated answers without attribution? Especially those who get paid on Quora? Since AI-generated answers are not copyrighted, do you think it should be banned? Is it even unethical?
Answer: The way things are now, I think it's inevitable that AI-generated content will soon eclipse human-generated in total volume on the Internet. Is this a good thing? In my opinion, no. It will lead to confusion about what is true, weaken our democracies and lead to a hollower society. But I have mixed feelings about it, because I also know that generative AI has many useful practical applications. I think the only way forward is transparency. We need to be able to say with a good degree of certainty where the source material originated from. However, that introduces some serious engineering challenges. We basically need to rewrite the Internet. At present, it's simply not practically achievable for Quora to ban AI-generated content. They could do it, but they wouldn't be able to enforce it. I think cryptography will play a central role going forward. There needs to be a chain of trust where all content is signed, so that it's possible to trace it back to its original author, whether that's a person or an AI. This fits nicely with existing ideas about Web 3.0, or the decentralized Internet. But I think we need to double down on those ideas and accelerate their development.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is the "full head of black hair" an important factor for excelling in chess (top 100)? At the "top 100" level there aren't many blond or bald players
Answer: If you ask Vishy Anand, then probably yes? His pitch black toupée seems to be working for him, as he is still in the top 10 at the age of 53. Veselin Topalov has gone for a more natural style, yet he is also a very strong player despite approaching 50. Vasily Ivanchuk, also a top 100 player, has gone for a silver grey approach, but he is lower rated, so that sort of fits with the narrative. Richard Rapport is (at least occasionally) the blondest top player I can think of. But that color is about as real as Anand's hair. By the way, I love these questions that are so ridiculous that they're clearly not AI generated.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Will Magnus Carlsen be talked about in the future like Bobby Fischer, as a player who could have been defeated?
Answer: Magnus may still be defeated in matches or in the FIDE ranking in his 30s. Eventually he will be anyway. But at least so far in his career he has been nearly flawless. Every time Magnus tried to win or defend the world championship, he successfully did so. He has held on to the top spot on the world ranking for over 12 years straight. And he has won way more tournaments than anyone else in this century. He only lost the world championship title by giving it up voluntarily to a player who is clearly inferior to him. There is simply no one in the current generation of players that could have defeated Magnus in the long run. If Magnus retires early from chess like Fischer did, and a new super strong player comes along, we can wonder what would have happened had he not retired. But so far there are no indications that he's retiring.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is Interstellar a must-see movie?
Answer: The IMDb top 250 list is a pretty good reference for movies you should see at some point if you have an above average interest in movies. These are films that have been rated very highly by a large number of people. You'll probably enjoy most of them. You definitely won't like all of them. Some are universally liked while others are controversial. But they all have something interesting about them. Interstellar is one of those polarizing movie. Many people love it and many people hate it. But it's 26th on the list. So there are definitely more people who love it than hate it. Interstellar is not an all-time classic like Citizen Kane or The Godfather. But it's almost required viewing if you're a movie buff. It's a visually striking science fiction blockbuster that's well directed and acted, with a unique plot that combines elements of speculative physics in interesting ways.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What could have happened if Korchnoi had won against Karpov in Baguio? (Alternate chess history)
Answer: First of all, it’s not an unlikely scenario. The Baguio match was played as first to 6 wins. Although Karpov was leading 5–2, Korchnoi made a comeback to 5-5, winning 3 out of 4 games in rounds 28 to 31. Karpov struck back immediately with a win in round 32, clinching the title, but it feels like it could have gone either way. If Karpov had lost the title, he would have been seeded directly into the 1980/1981 candidates tournament, which was a knockout tournament with 8 players. There, he would have faced Tigran Petrosian in the quarterfinals. Petrosian was even older than Korchnoi, and would have been 50 by the time the candidates tournament started in 1980. He would have been no match for Karpov at the peak of his powers. In the semifinals, Korchnoi would have faced either Minhail Tal or Lev Polugaevsky, who were both in their mid-40s. Again, Karpov would have been the overwhelming favorite. In the actual 1981 candidates final, Korchnoi faced Robert Hübner. The German was actually leading by one point after 6 games, but then he lost two games in a row and just… resigned the match, even though he was only down by a point with several rounds left. That kind of weak mentality would not have fared well against Karpov, who was infamous for his killer instinct over the board. The most likely scenario in this alternate version of chess history is that Karpov would have qualified for the 1981 world championship rematch against Korchnoi, and that he would have won it easily, just like he did in actual history. Anatoly Karpov was just way ahead of everyone else by the turn of the 1980s. It was a period of generation shift and relatively weak competition at the top, but Karpov was one of the best players in history in his absolute prime.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Why aren’t there any African American GMs competing in Norway Chess, Tara Steel, etc?
Answer: Norway Chess and Tata Steel are pretty strict about who they invite. Norway Chess only invites the very best players in the world (top 20), in addition to Norwegian top players such as Aryan Tari, Jon Ludvig Hammer and Simen Agdestein. Tata Steel only invites 2700+ players in addition to Dutch top players like Jorden van Foreest and a few up-and-coming youngsters who are right below 2700 as well as the winner of the previous year’s Challenger tournament. Right now, there are no African-American players who satisfy any of these requirements. Chess was traditionally a pastime for the wealthy elite of Western Europe. In the 20th century, it became extremely popular in Eastern Europe. But in the 21st century, it’s becoming a global phenomenon. We’ve now had world champions from India and China. I don’t think it will be long before we see African-American players in the strongest tournaments as well.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is the microservices architecture always better than monolithic? Or are there cases where you should prefer monolithic?
Answer: A monolithic architecture should be the default choice when designing a new system. They’re simpler and avoid the latency overhead of RPCs between your modules. Microservices significantly increase the complexity. You should not introduce them unless there is a valid reason to. Valid reasons: Non-valid reasons:

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What is the role of software architecture in large-scale projects?
Answer: Software architecture is just a fancy word for any part of the design of a software system that is on a higher abstraction layer than the code itself. If your software system has several modules split up by logical or technical boundaries, the way you compose these modules and enable them to interact is called architecture. Choice of technical infrastructure, programming languages and frameworks can also be considered architecture. The way your system interacts with other systems, or even the way it's embedded in an organization, can be considered architecture. The role of a software architect, then, is to design the software system at a high level such that it meets the requirements efficiently. A well-functioning software development team doesn't really need to appoint an architect. The natural leaders and architects will emerge by merit.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: When there is very little time left in a chess match, how do the players have time to write down their moves?
Answer: When you have less than 5 minutes left on your clock in a game with no increments, you are no longer obliged to write down your moves. Some still do, but it can get hectic. Most classical games are played with increments today. With 30 seconds per move, you have plenty of time to write down the moves.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Why do chess players around 2500 rating don't improve much anymore? Is it because they memorized most of the best move in the game? What I don't like about chess is that there's a lot of draws in the top league.
Answer: The higher you climb up the rating ladder, the harder it becomes to improve. The early gains are easy. Anyone who is a club player rated 1400–1600 can improve their rating by a few hundred points if they just dedicate time to it and make a consistent effort. The players who get all the way to 2500 are exceptionally talented, have played chess practically their entire lives and have worked extremely hard to get to where they are. The Elo rating follows an approximate normal distribution. The players rated 2500 are already in the 99.99th percentile of competitive chess players. Statistically speaking, most who get there, will never get to 2600, let alone 2700 or 2800. Needless to say, that's much harder.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How did Hikaru Nakamura manage to become 2nd of the world in chess again despite being a full-time streamer?
Answer: The assumption here is that being a streamer has a negative effect on your chess development. I tend to think it's the other way around. One of the reasons why Vladimir Kramnik was such a great player was that he was able to work on chess 10-12 hours every single day. Most top players can't do that. I know from my personal experience with Magnus Carlsen that he will frequently take days off and focus on other things for long stretches of time. The incentive program at Twitch almost forces Hikaru to stream 8 hours a day. The opportunity cost if he doesn't is pretty high. During all those hours, he is playing, analyzing and discussing chess. That's it. That's all he does. It's only natural that all that chess exposure sharpens his game, even if it's not “serious” studying. If it's one thing the current generation of top players have shown us, it's that the classical Soviet approach to chess is overrated. It doesn't have to be so serious and disciplined all the time. Having fun actually leads to better learning. I think that streaming has revitalized Hikaru's love for chess. He's clearly having fun, and he has a casual attitude when playing in classical tournaments. Besides, Naka has always spent a great deal of time playing online blitz. Only difference now is that he's doing it professionally. The financial freedom that provides him means that he only plays in classical tournaments when he feels like it and is motivated.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Chessgames.com has a huge database of games and is very useful. Why has it not evolved over time?
Answer: I can see from my user profile that I joined Chessgames 20 years ago. It looked almost exactly the same back then. The only difference is more ads and a few new minor features. You'd think that there would be more potential in the site. It has 3 million monthly visitors, and could have been so much more than it is. Tragically, both the site's co-founders died young in their 50s. That has probably played a part. Currently it's being maintained by volunteers in the community. What it needs is for a professional company to acquire it and revamp the design.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is Magnus starting to decline as a great chess player and who is next, Alireza, Naka or Fabi in strength of play?
Answer: Magnus just had a bad tournament result in Norway Chess with a -1 score. It happens. In fact, it's not even his worst showing in the tournament. He scored -2 in the 2015 edition and -1 in the 2017 edition. It's a tough tournament. He can't win it every time. Even after shedding 18 rating points in this tournament, Magnus is still the highest rated player in the world by an almost 50-point margin. His rating is a bit lower now at 2835 than it has typically been in the past, but that also has to do with the fact that his closest competitors are rated lower as well. Nakamura is currently second with 2787. Keep in mind, Magnus was down to 2822 in 2017, but climbed back to tie his own rating record in 2019. He is still only 33 years old, so I think it's too early to conclude that he is declining just based on one tournament. Nakamura and Caruana are both of the same generation as Magnus. They have been unable to overtake him for the past decade, so I see no reason why they should suddenly do so now. I think it will take a younger player. Firouzja has been promised as the next big thing for some time noe, but his tournament results have been uneven. We'll see. He's still very young at 19, and will have many more chances to prove himself.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Do good software engineers always think about user experience when they build software?
Answer: For user-facing applications, yes, good software engineers always have user experience in mind when developing software. However, good software engineers also realize that simply thinking about it is not enough. User experience is a craft in its own right, and one that most software engineers are not very good at. It requires right-brain thinking and very different traits than being a good programmer. There are some developers who can do both UX and UI design while also writing frontend code. But I've seen very few, if any, examples of full-blown fullstack developers who were also good at UX. They're just completely different skillsets.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What is difference between a Principal Software Architect and a Senior Software Engineer?
Answer: Senior Software Engineer usually means: A competent software engineer with a minimum of 3–5 years of experience. However, there is no upper limit when it comes to experience and skill level. Principal Software Architect usually means: Exceptional software engineer/architect with 10+ years of experience and strong leadership skills.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: 98% of software developers work at small and midscale companies that don't solve novel engineering problems and are paid less. Do these developers have the right to call themselves engineers? Give valid counter arguments?
Answer: 98% of software developers work at small and midscale companies No. Large enterprises account for over 30% of all employees in Europe and almost 40% in the United States. The numbers for software developers are in the same ballpark. that don't solve novel engineering problems Engineers at smaller companies are more likely to be working on novel problems in my experience. Large enterprises are by definition already successful. Most of their engineers will be assigned to optimizing the company's existing product offering, while only a select few of the top engineers are working on novel problems. In small companies, everyone has to contribute to everything. Startups will generally look to solve problems in novel ways to disrupt the status quo. are paid less Not necessarily the case. Some of the largest and most well-known tech companies pay very well, but so do a number of smaller companies. Most large enterprises pay average. Do these developers have the right to call themselves engineers? Yes. Give valid counter arguments? Engineering is not about solving novel problems anyway. When you're coming up with something truly novel, you're really doing R&D. Engineering is about applying existing knowledge to solve problems efficiently.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: As a software engineer do you feel there is a strong argument to go back from micro services to monolithic architecture given that Amazon prime was able to save cost and be more performant by doing the same?
Answer: The Amazon Prime blog post has been widely misinterpreted. The article describes how one of the software teams at Prime were able to reduce infrastructure costs with 90% by going from a microservice to a monolith architecture. Actually, if you read it carefully, that's not even what they did. They took one service and moved it from a serverless compute model to running on reserved instances. Serverless and microservices are two completely different things. Serverless is essentially a cost and scaling model. Microservices are about separating different parts of your software system with logical boundaries, regardless of how the different microservices are deployed. So does this mean that reserved instances are 90% cheaper than serverless? Of course not. If your application has bursty and unpredictable traffic, serverless can be a highly cost-efficient deployment model that is much cheaper than paying for a server that is always on. On the other hand, if you have a constant and predictable load, and you know that's going to continue a few years into the future, nothing is cheaper than reserved instances. What the team at Prime essentially did was to refactor their architecture because its requirements had changed. This happens all the time. That does not mean that “microservices are dead” or “serverless sucks” or any of the silly clickbait takes I've seen are true. There has been a trend in recent years to move away from microservices and serverless because they were so overused for a period of time by developers who tried to shoehorn in these patterns everywhere. That does not mean they have become any less useful when applied appropriately. Real software architects apply patterns and deployment models according to the specific requirements of their solution.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is it possible to create a software that is unbeatable at chess?
Answer: All the top chess engines in 2023 are unbeatable, and they have been for a while. The last time a human being beat a top-level engine was back in 2005, when GM Ruslan Ponomariov beat the program known as Fritz. Since then, no one has been able to win even a single game of chess against the silicon monsters without odds play or some sort of unfair advantage. Humans are gradually improving at chess, but software is improving much faster. We'll never catch up. At least not without artificially modifying our brains. That being said, it's not theoretically impossible to beat even the best chess engines. They don't play perfect. The game tree complexity of chess is so vast that it hasn't been solved and probably never will be. But their level of play is so many levels beyond us that it makes no practical difference.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How important is a software engineer’s ability to adapt in the world of generative AI?
Answer: It's imperative. Generative AI is the defining technology of our generation. The software engineers who fail to realize that or refuse to acknowledge it will be left in the dust. When the GitHub Copilot X vision is realized, it will drop like a bomb. It will be like having an exoskeleton while others are still running around in jogging pants. And even that is just scratching the surface of what's possible. The current state-of-the-art (GPT-4) could enable even greater levels of automation. Its ability to write high-quality code is already there. Meanwhile, the state-of-the-art is also moving forward at a rapid pace. The next generation of LLMs will be even better at writing code. Combine that with more mature Copilot-like tools, and we’ll have something that is simply too good to be ignored by professional software engineers. That future is not far away, and we will all have to adapt. Technologies come and go, but the ability to adapt is the one thing that never gets old.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: I have seen many people hate the Python indentation style. Why, and what syntax style do you like?
Answer: Syntax is mostly a matter of taste. People tend to prefer what they’re used to. I love the Python syntax, but I started out with Python as my first programming language. I didn’t have the baggage of being used to other syntax styles. The forced indentation style quickly became second nature to me. The beginner-friendly syntax was one of the reasons I picked it up in the first place. Throughout several years of developing production code in Python professionally, I’ve never had any issues whatsoever with whitespace or indentation. However, I can see why developers who have years of experience programming in C-style language would find it annoying to adapt to whitespace being a part of the syntax. I like C-style languages too. Especially C#, which I think is just a beautiful language. But again, it’s what I’m used to. I picked up that language early in my career too. If I had only been developing in Python for years, I’m sure I would have been annoyed by the curly brackets. I personally think the Lisp syntax is hideous with all its parentheses, but those who’ve used it for a while generally seem to like it.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is it worth it to get into the IT/Tech industry considering the AI boom and its rapid developing and its "human replacing" stage? Is there any room left for newbies?
Answer: The AI boom is a reason to enter the tech industry, not to shun away for it. We've had an AI boom ever since I started dabbling in deep learning ten years ago. Many people felt like we were overdue for another AI winter, since the hypetrain had come and gone in cycles in the past. Well, guess what. The deep learning revolution of the 2010s was just a tiny teaser to the massive AI tsunami that's washing over us in the 2020s. The new generative AI technologies we see now will undoubtedly have a profound influence on the tech sector. Jobs will change. There will be a need for different skillsets. But what they will not do is make the tech industry any less relevant. Quite on the contrary. The industry will become larger and more powerful than ever before. The subset of the industry that concerns itself with AI will become dominant. In many ways, this is the perfect time to enter tech as a newbie. I was just watching a documentary about the legendary visual effects company Industrial Light & Magic the other day. During the making of Jurassic Park, it suddenly became clear that computer graphics (CG) would change movies forever. A bunch of young new talents with strong software skills emerged during this time and made their mark on the development of special effects. Some of the old-timers decided to re-educate themselves and move to digital. Many of them went on to have great careers for years to come. Others were too stuck in the past, and insisted that this new technology could never make the model shop and traditional techniques obsolete. They became less relevant. The tech industry in 2023 is like the visual effects industry in 1993. The release of GPT-4 marks an inflection point, where a new generation of talent will come in with more powerful tools and make their mark.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What are your thoughts regarding Elon Musk’s prediction of when humans will land on the planet Mars?
Answer: Elon Musk's predictions about emerging technologies generally follow a linear relationship y = x + c where y is the predicted year, x is the current year and c is some constant. For humans on Mars, c m = 7 ± 1 For self-driving cars, c s = 1 Coincidentally, the stock prices of Elon's two main companies, SpaceX and Tesla, benefit from c m and c s being the lowest numbers that Elon can say with a straight face.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is Interstellar (2014) the best science fiction movie, or is there a better one?
Answer: Interstellar is a cool movie, and one of very few examples of hard science fiction in a movie done right. For instance, the physics are much more realistic than what you’ll see in most other science fiction movies. The acting, special effects, musical score, directing and cinematography are all great as well. But to me, it’s not the best science fiction movie ever made. I wouldn’t even put it in the top 10. Here are movies I would personally put ahead of it: 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) Stanley Kubrick’s masterpiece is more art than entertainment. Not only was the story and imagery evocative and thought-provoking. It was a landmark in special effects and film-making in general. It influenced everything that came after it. Star Wars (1977) Star Wars is approaching its 50-year anniversary, and it may be hard for kids today to imagine just how groundbreaking it was back then. The movie revolutionized the art of science fiction film-making and probably advanced special effects and the development of CGI by close to a decade. It broke the box office record and launched one of the most successful movie franchises of all time. And it was just damn good entertainment. Alien (1979) One of the best films in both the science fiction and horror genres. In an age of over-the-top space operas, Ridley Scott made something that was gritty, terrifying and truly alien. Star Wars: Episode V - The Empire Strikes Back (1980) Empire did the impossible by topping the original Star Wars. The script was better, the special effects were better, the directing was better and the story was darker with more adult themes. It was so far ahead of its time. I recently watched the Disney documentary Light & Magic, and it just reinforced my respect for George Lucas and the amazing people that made the original trilogy happen. Blade Runner (1982) Blade Runner, with its original tech noir setting, basically invented the cyberpunk genre. It was well ahead of its time and mostly misunderstood when it came out. It was an early exploration of what it means to be human in a world of AI and robotics. Ridley Scott nailed the visuals as always. And of course, there is Rutger Hauer’s iconic Tears in rain monologue. Jurassic Park (1993) A near perfect movie. The story is amazing, the directing is amazing, the acting is great, the score is iconic and everything else is pretty awesome too. And come on, it’s a dinosaur park, what’s not to like. It’s easy to forget that this was essentially the first movie that made CGI blend into the surrounding scenery in a realistic way. It looks good even today, 30 years later. Starship Troopers (1997) A controversial one. The novel is one of the all-time classics, but the film is very different. While the book glorifies violence, the movie puts a satirical spin on it and flips everything on its head. The dark humor has often been misunderstood, but I love it. Inception (2010) Yes, I don’t even think Interstellar is the best sci-fi that Christopher Nolan has made. While Interstellar has style and cool space settings, Inception is an extremely creative story and that explores some truly unique concepts. Inception also manages to do something else that Interestellar doesn’t. It takes a mindblowing sci-fi story and gives it a perfect and satisfying ending. The Martian (2015) The novel is a modern-day classic, and the movie stays true to the book. It’s just very well made and highly entertaining. Arrival (2016) An intelligent story about a meeting with something alien and terrifying. My favorite genre. Denis Villeneuve’s masterpiece has spectacular visuals, yet manages to stay human and intimate in the face of the otherwordly. It had me on the edge of my seat. Dune (2022) Villeneuve did the impossible and made a faithful adaptation of Dune, something I thought we’d never see. To tackle such a huge project and succeed just shows virtuosa skills in science fiction film-making. The visuals are next-level and the score is amazing.
