Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Why hasn't an asteroid wiped out mankind?
Answer: Humans haven’t been around for that long on an astrogeological (yes, that’s a thing) timescale. Humans in the broader sense evolved a little more than 2 million years. Planet killer asteroids are exceedingly rare. There is an inverse cubic relationship between the diameter of asteroids and the frequency of Earth impacts. As they get bigger, they become much less common. (Source) An asteroid the size of the one that caused the Chicxulub impact crater 66 million years ago will occur every 100 million years or so according to the limited data we have. Its diameter was about 10 km and it wiped out 75% of life on the planet. If an asteroid like that had hit Earth in the last couple of million years, no more humans. Maybe a smaller one would have sufficed, but probably not that much smaller. But like I said, there is only a one in a hundred millionth chance of a new Chicxulub in any given year. That gives us about a 98% likelihood that we go through 2 million years of human evolution without any planet killers, and you'll have to excuse my handwaving with the estimates here. Of course, if an asteroid like that comes towards us in the future, we'll probably just deflect it and go about our day.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How do software engineering teams manage their cognitive load?
Answer: Software engineers use a very simple but effective trick known as “breaking down large task into more manageable pieces”. A software project often starts with a very high-level goal like “develop a web application that does X”. X could be quite complex, like a data collection and reporting platform with custom dashboards, user administration and a bunch of other features, just to name a made-up example. To attack a problem like that, the developers will start sketching a high-level architecture. To develop a web application, you need a backend system, a frontend UI, a database and so on. Then you can break down each component further. The backend will have data access repositories, domain logic, interfaces, an API and so on. In turn, the API will have a user controller, company controller and so on. Which endpoints should the user controller expose? Probably “Create User“, “Get Users by ID” and so on. How does the GetUsersById method work? Well, you probably call on an interface to a UserService that calls on a UserRepository for data access and so on. Only when they have drilled down to that level of detail will the developers start writing the actual code. That's at least 5 levels of cognitive abstraction. Software engineers are very good at this, but it really works for any type of job. If you need to plan a wedding, which may seem like a daunting task, you can break that down into components like finding a venue, writing the guest list, choosing a menu and so on. And so on.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: As generative AIs are getting popular, I think the market demand for software engineers are gradually going down. Is it a good time to go back to do hardware?
Answer: That's a strong assumption. Since the dawn of the computer age, higher-level software abstractions have always meant that software engineers became more productive and useful, leading to an increase in demand. There is an estimated 28 million software engineers in the world, up from 23 million in 2018[1]. When we get to superintelligent AGI, things will perhaps become a bit weird. But until then, the world will still need millions of software engineers. Foundational AI models like ChatGPT are already useful for laypeople. But you know what's even more useful? A skilled software engineer who builds on top of those models to create even more powerful tools. As for computer hardware, that's commoditized and standardized for the most part. It's become a niche field that only employs a small fraction of what software does. On the other hand, it might be a good time to get into robotics. That's a field that's ripe for disruption and ready to explode.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is AI an existential threat to humanity?
Answer: This has always been a hot topic of discussion, but with the recent release of GPT-4 it has become one of the most important questions of our time. The way I see it, there are three main threats that need to be discussed: Social manipulation We’ve already seen to some extent how the Internet and social media can fuel political extremism and make people go down the rabbit hole of conspiracy theories. With the Internet, all of human knowledge is just a few Google searches away, which incentivizes people to not absorb knowledge in long-term memory. Source criticism has already been severely compromized, especially in the younger generation that has grown up with the Internet. Generative AI will amplify this to the extreme. It will become harder and harder to tell what’s real and what’s AI-generated or fake. And Large Language Models like ChatGPT have a tendency to represent common misconceptions and half-truths as fact. At the very minimum, I think we’ll see more unrest and extremism. In the worst scenarios, we’ll end up in an Idiocracy-like Brave New World type of future. Transhumanism Transhumanism, or posthumanism, involves enhancing ourselves with technology. In the long-term, we’ll artificially evolve into a new species through the use of emerging technologies like genetic engineering, neural implants and mind uploading. Perhaps we’ll dispose of our physical bodies altogether. AI plays a central role in enabling this future. To transhumanists, this is a desirable development. Some AI philosophers like Eliezer Yudkowsky think that this is the only way to offset the risk of AI killing us all. But to most people, a transhumanist future will seem like a scary proposition, because it represents a departure from what we think of as human and a journey into the unknown. I think we’ll see more of this, but I also think there will greater pushback and stronger regulation. Human cloning and germline editing is already outlawed in many countries. The paperclip maximizer This is the sort of stuff we know from movies like The Terminator. AI one day wakes up and decides that humans are no longer required and proceeds to kill us all. An alternative version of this is that they keep us alive with our heads in proverbial glass jars, like in The Matrix. The more sophisticated version, proposed by Nick Bostrom, is that a superintelligent AI pursues some seemingly harmless goal, like manufacturing paperclips, and inadvertently kills all humans in the process, because it won’t stop until the entire Universe is made of paperclips. In Yudkowsky’s version, the paperclip is some arbitrary nanostructure that the super-AI has found to be the optimal building block, and it ends up using self-replicating nanobots to turn everything into goo. His argument is that in the space of possible AI loss functions, very few of them include humans. Furthermore, he thinks that it’s borderline impossible to align strong AI with human goals, or even to align our own goals with what’s best for us. To him, everyone dying is an inevitable scenario given the current trajectory. I find it implausible. While philosophers are engaging in hypotheticals and thought experiments, deep learning researchers are struggling with real-life problems such as the curse of dimensionality and scaling AI systems. At present, these seem like much greater challenges than dealing with a super-AI spinning out of control. While I can follow the logic of Yudkowsky’s arguments, it all seems unscientific to me. I have yet to see any evidence that we’re heading towards an impending doom, or that we will create AI that is as severly unaligned as has been suggested. So I’m still in the camp that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence on that one.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Do you agree with Goldman Sachs prediction that AI could replace 300 million jobs?
Answer: I read the 20-page Goldman Sachs report[1]. With all due respect, the economists who wrote that report have no fucking clue about AI or its impact on society. Look at this shit: They describe GANs here. But it’s transformers and diffusion models - not GANs - that have sparked the current generative AI revolution. Not mentioned anywhere. This section of the report reeks of a 30-minute Google search by someone who has no idea what to look for. Now look at this: Here we’re looking at the ridiculous relationship between mentions of AI in earnings calls and change in corporate capex. And it’s showing a regression line with an R squared value of 0.12? Seriously? Spurious relations, anyone? Actually, this is not even spurious. Just a non-correlation really. I’m not sure what such a relationship would prove anyway. And then we come to the assumptions that they’re basing the predictions on. Based on our review of existing literature on the probable use cases of generative AI, we classify 13 work activities as exposed to AI automation. By “existing literature”, they mean papers that were published before the current breed of generative AI even existed. Sure enough, the 13 work activities listed in the appendix are essentially all tasks that could have been automated by a previous generation of machine learning models, or in many cases by deterministic algorithms. And again, the authors base the estimated productivity growth by adoption of generative AI on yesterday’s technology. All of these results predate GPT-3.5. “Much More Powerful AI” would apparently represent a 1.4 percentage point increase in productivity over the baseline. I don’t think the authors can even begin to comprehend what a “much more powerful AI” would look like. That’s essentially a superintelligence. I think you get my point by now. The report is a steaming pile of hot garbage and should not be given any weight. Yet, this is the sort of weak ass shit that gets quoted by the media. Not too long ago, analysts would routinely claim that unskilled and manual repetitive labor would be the first to be automated. Creative and tech workers were the least likely to have their work automated by AI. How wrong they were. In 2022, generative AI came along and flipped everything on its head. Just goes to show that you should never trust economists that are making predictions about the future of AI. Especially when they represent a conservative corporation in a slow-moving industry like Goldman Sachs. But do I agree with the prediction? I think it’s basically impossible to tell how AI will affect employment in the future. Even if we froze all development of AI at this point, GPT-4 would have an incalculable effect on the global workforce. But of course, we’re not going to do that. There will be a GPT-5, and there will be other breakthroughs in AI that we haven’t even thought of yet. I’ll make one prediction. By the early 2030s, I think at least one purely AI company will be among the 10 most valuable companies in the world. It could be OpenAI or someone else. Or multiple companies. If anything, I think that Goldman Sachs’s predictions are too conservative (shocker, I know). But nobody really knows.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Why does the big tech want to replace programmers by AI so badly?
Answer: The incentives are obvious. Software developers are expensive, hard to recruit, hard to retain, hard to manage and frequently not very good at their job. Because their job is difficult. But they also form the backbone of the most valuable companies in the world. If you had a technology that could replace all software developers, it would be the most valuable technology in the history of mankind. Now, even the most optimistic AI enthusiasts would probably agree that replacing all developers is not viable in the foreseeable future. Here is my rough guesstimate of the near future: An experienced developer in 2024 who is exploiting AI to the max will be about as efficient as a team of one senior and four junior developers in 2021. In fact, a software developer who is not using GPT models to boost their work output today is not being as efficient as they could be. Once you start to work out the numbers for tech companies, they are staggering. Example: Google employs about 27,000 software engineers as of 2023[1]. The average total compensation is $265,000 according to one source[2]. Let's assume the total cost of an employee for Google is around 1.5 the total compensation. This means the company spends $10 billion yearly on its software engineers. And that's not even counting the cost of recruitment and management. If they could cut the number of software engineers in half while retaining the same output, that's billions of dollars saved every year. For larger companies like Google, the process of shifting towards AI-driven development will be slow and painful. For small, agile companies, the change can be effectuated today. EDIT: As pointed out in the comments, an increase in productivity wouldn’t necessarily lead to a reduction in workforce. It can also be used to achieve more with the same staff. In either case, the incentives are obvious.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What are your thoughts on Elon Musk calling for a temporary pause on artificial intelligence development?
Answer: 1. I would question his incentives to do so. Elon co-founded OpenAI, but left the board after he unsuccessfully tried to take full control over the company. As he has shown time and again, Elon very much adheres to the credo of “you're either with me or against me”. 2. I think it's a terrible idea. It's better to allow a good-intentioned company like OpenAI deploy the technology in the open and allow the world to experiment with the technology when it's still benign, rather than to try to hold it back until a more powerful AI is inevitably unleashed on society. Eventually, some bad actor will get access to AGI in the future, and we need to be prepared for that. There were people who tried to hold back color television and the Internet, but you can't stop progress. AGI is going to be here relatively soon whether we want to or not.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Will companies use an AI API like chatgpt? I don't mean that they will take over the machine learning jobs, but I do mean that companies will use the API instead of bringing in machine learning engineers?
Answer: Absolutely. At my company (sklls.ai), we develop conversational AI for call centers. In the past, we trained our own intent recognition models based on recurrent neural networks such as LSTMs, and I had highly-paid machine learning engineers helping me with that. The challenge there, as has always been the main challenge in my career as a machine learning engineer, is to collect enough data. We had tens of thousands of samples and a good model architecture, but it just wasn’t enough for a data-hungry deep neural network. In fact, very simple similarity-matching algorithms like the Sørensen-Dice coefficient would routinely outperform our deep learning models. As an early-stage startup, it takes time to gain a large enough user base to collect the volume of data needed for high performance. In October 2022, when the GPT-3.5 version of InstructGPT was launched, we started using this model through OpenAI’s Completions API as an integral part of our core AI. This revolutionized the conversations we could provide through our platform. The main win there is that the GPT models are pretrained and don’t need training data. The GPT-3 paper was literally called Large Language Models are Few-Shot Learners. By complementing our existing intent-based solution with GPT-3.5 the AI became much more robust. It could give reasonable answers even when the users went outside the scope of our intents. Last month, when the ChatGPT API was launched, we upgraded to that. The feedback from users is amazing. This model knocks it out of the park even when compared to GPT-3.5 model we were using up until now. This doesn’t mean it will replace our machine learning efforts entirely. We are still training in-house models for speech recognition, speech synthesis and intent recognition. But it definitely helps to magnify the results provided by our AI team. I think we’ll quickly see a new breed of AI engineers that don’t necessarily have the theoretical foundation of a data scientist. You don’t need that to use the ChatGPT API.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Why do software developers age over 40 leave the industry?
Answer: People over the age of 40 are old and boring. Unlike us youngsters (I’m turning 39 this year) they’re not interested in having fun or being intellectually challenged anymore. They simply want to collect a paycheck and go home to watch Netflix. Software development is a bad fit for people over 40 because it’s too much fun. The IDEs have dark backgrounds and weird font colors. It just doesn’t seem serious enough. Plus, everyone knows that after the age of 40, your brain stops working. And let's not forget clothing. Software developers are known for their stylish wardrobes of hoodies, jeans, and quirky t-shirts. Once developers reach the big 4–0, they’ll want to wear more serious clothes, like suits and ties. We can't have that kind of outdated fashion sense in the workplace. The truth is, these old geezers should bid farewell to the tech industry and make room for the next generation of baby-faced geniuses. It's time for the older generation to embrace their true calling: playing bingo, yelling at kids to get off their lawn, and reminiscing about the good ol' days when the internet made that weird dial-up noise.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Will Norway turn poor once they run out of resources? What backup plan do they have?
Answer: You’re probably thinking of oil and gas, which is what we’re known for. But Norway has plenty of other natural resources. Marine resources Norway has one of the world's largest exclusive economic zones (EEZ), and it’s rich in marine resources. We’re the world’s second largest exporter of seafood after China. Metals and minerals Norway has large deposits of minerals, metals and rare earths. Probably more than any other European country. A recent study found a substantial amount of metals and minerals on the seabed of the Norwegian continental shelf. Water With all the mountains, valleys and fjords, Norway is a hydropower paradise. We have more 800+ meter waterfalls than any other country in the world. We’re the only country in the world that produces more hydroelectricity than the total electricity consumption of the entire country. Apart from that, Norway has forests and arable land. It’s a windy country with one of the highest productions of wind power per capita in the world. If it ever gets to a point where Norway has no natural resources left, humanity is most likely extinct already. I don't think we have a backup plan for that scenario. As mentioned in other answers, we also have the world’s largest sovereign wealth fund (it’s about the same size as China’s), which is our insurance for the future.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Why did Anand not participate in the 2004 FIDE World Championship tournament?
Answer: This seems like a random question to ask 19 years after the fact, but I’m a sucker for chess history and I remember this tournament very well, so here goes. Only two of the top ten players in the world at the time played in the 2004 FIDE World Championship. There were two main contributing factors: The Israel situation The tournament was controversially held in Tripoli, Libya, under the auspices of the Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, who was friends with fellow dictator and FIDE president Kirsan Ilyumzhinov. While this choice of venue was already highly controversial, it was exacerbated by Libya’s poor relations with Israel. Libya denied Israelis entry to country at the time. There were several world-class Israeli players. World #13 Boris Gelfand would have been among the top contenders had he played. At first, FIDE sought to mitiage this situation by having a parallel event in Malta. However, that event was cancelled when the Libyans issued a press release stating that all players would be allowed to play. Additional confusion arose when Muhammad Gaddafi (the dictator’s son, and president of the Libyan Olympic Committee) categorically denied that the “Zionist enemy” would be allowed to play. In the end, none of the Israeli players participated in the event. The unification situation After Garry Kasparov and Nigel Short broke with FIDE in 1993 to form the Professional Chess Association (PCA), the world championship title had been in a state of constant turmoil. The PCA experiment had been a failure, and by the early 2000s, the chess world sought to unify the lineal world championship title, then held by Vladimir Kramnik, and the FIDE world championship. FIDE had arranged a series of knockout tournaments that had the status of official world championships. However, the knockout format and the short time control introduced so much randomness that the title lost much of its legitimacy. Especially when it was won by lesser-known players such as Alexander Khalifman and Ruslan Ponomariov. The plan was to have a unfication match to unify the title once and for all. The match were to be played between the winner of a match between Kasparov (world #1) and Ponomariov (the latest world cup winner) on the FIDE side and Kramnik (lineal champion) and Peter Leko (winner of Dortmund 2002) on the PCA side. For these reasons, the 2004 FIDE World Championship, which was not part of the unification process, had lost much of its prestige and importance. Viswanathan Anand declined to play in the tournament because of ethical considerations relating to the Israel situation. But he also (correctly) assumed that he would be a part of the unification process anyway, being a perennial top 3 player. And he had already won FIDE’s knockout tournament in 2000. These years were transformative for top-level chess, as many of the top players either retired or stopped competing at the highest level as a result of the world championship mess, while others were catapulted to new levels of fame. What happened to our main cast of characters? Garry Kasparov (World #1, 2817, Russia) declined to play in the 2004 tournament. The match with Ponomariov never materialized after the latter refused to sign what he felt was an unfair contract. Kasparov retired from classical chess the next year, having been the world’s strongest player for 20 years straight. Viswanathan Anand (World #2, 2774, India) declined to play in the tournament, citing the Israel situation. He played in the 2005 world championship tournament in Argentina, finishing second. He then won the 2007 world championship tournament in Mexico, before beating Kramnik in a match in 2008 and finally being crowned the undisputed champion of the world. He held the title until 2013. He is still a top 10 player at the age of 53. Vladimir Kramnik (World #3, 2764, Russia) declined to play in the tournament, since he was part of the unification process and was preparing for the match with Leko later that year. He won that match in dramatic fashion, and went on to win the unification match against Topalov in 2006, the infamous “Toiletgate” match. Kramnik lost the title to Anand in 2008 and retired from classical chess in 2019. Peter Leko (World #4, 2741, Hungary) declined to play in the tournament, since he was part of the unfication process and was preparing for the aforementioned match against Kramnik. He was leading the match until Kramnik struck back in the final game. He played in the world championship tournaments in 2005 and 2007, finishing 5th and 4th. After that he fell out of the top 10 and never played world championship chess again. Veselin Topalov (World #5, 2737, Bulgaria) played in the 2004 tournament as the top seed and was completely dominant until he was knocked out by eventual winner Rustam Kasimdzhanov in a shocking upset in the semi-final. He qualified for the 2005 world championship tournament by rating and won it by a wide margin in one of the greatest tournament results ever. He was the world number one for a brief period in 2006, but lost the unification match against Kramnik in 2006. He qualified for another WC match against Anand that he also lost. Peter Svidler (World #6, 2733, Russia) declined to play in the tournament due to the Israel situation. He later finished joint second in the 2005 world championship tournament and 5th in the 2007 tournament. He also played in the candidates tournament in 2013, 2014 and 2016. These days he focuses mostly on commentary. Alexander Morozevich (World #7, 2732, Russia) accepted the invitation to the tournament in Libya, but in one of his many unpredictable moves he never showed up. He would later play in the 2005 and 2007 tournaments, finishing 4th and 6th. He was the unofficial world number one for one day in 2008, but mostly retired from classical chess in the 2010s. Michael Adams (World #8, 2731, England) played in the tournament in 2004 and reached the final for the first time, having been a semi-finalist in three events prior. He was the favorite going into the final, but he too fell to Kasimdzhanov. He played in the 2005 tournament and came 7th. Adams never played at WC level again but remains a strong player in his early 50s. Judit Polgar (World #9, 2728, Hungary) declined to play in the tournament. She was pregnant and gave birth to her first child that year. Following the birth of her children, Polgar stepped down from top-level chess. But she played in the 2005 tournament as the first and only woman ever to play at the world championship level, finishing 8th and last. Rusland Ponomariov (World #10, 2722, Ukraine) declined to play in the tournament. He had opted out of the world championship unification process when he failed to come to agreements with Kasparov over a match. He still plays chess as a top 100 player, but never lived up to his early promise. He has never eclipsed his peak since when he was 19 and won the 2002 world championship tournament. Boris Gelfand (World #13, 2714, Israel) declined to play in the tournament despite getting a last-minute invitation from the Gaddafi regime. He would enjoy a late spring in his early 40s, and qualified for a world championship match against Anand in 2012. He was even leading that match at one point, but eventually lost in the rapid tie breaks. At the age of 54, he is still rated in the high 2600s. Rustam Kasimdzhanov (World #44, 2652, Uzbekistan) was virtually unknown going into the 2004 tournament but won it in one of the most surprising upsets in chess history. His win gave him a spot in the 2005 world championship tournament, where he finished in a respectable 6th place alongside fellow finalist Adams. He also played in the 2007 candidates tournament, where he was knocked out by Gelfand. He became well known as an opening theoretician and was on Anand’s team as his second in his subsequent world championship matches. Magnus Carlsen (World #275, 2552, Norway) played in the tournament and got a really tough pairing against Levon Aronian in the first round. He impressed everyone by taking the match to tie-breaks, but was knocked out by the much older opponent. Magnus later went on to win the world championship title from Anand in 2013 and held it for 10 years before voluntarily giving it up. He still remains the world number one for 13 years straight. Kirsan Ilyumzhinov (Russia) sat as FIDE president from 1995 until he was forced out in 2018 due to his long history of corruption. He reigned as the president of the Russian republic of Kalmykia from 1993 until 2010. He still contends that he was abducted by aliens in 1997. Muammar Gaddafi (Libya) reigned as dictator in Libya until the Arab spring of 2011, when he was dragged out in the streets, tortured and murdered by his own people.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is it possible to become a FM at the age of 45, if I am 40 now playing at a 1800?
Answer: I’m going to be realistic and say no. For reference, I’m 38 years old and rated in the high 2100s. I think that if I dedicated myself to chess again like I did in my early 20s, studying for hours every day and playing in multiple tournaments, I might get to 2300 in the next five years, but I’m honestly not sure. I think 2400 is too late for me no matter how hard I study. And I have a much better starting point than you. By far the best time for a chess player to learn is when you’re young. To continue improving when you’re middle-aged is extremely difficult for various reasons. Especially if we’re talking about going from club level through expert level to strong master level in just a few years. The difference between 1800 and 2300 is vast, as I’m sure you know. I’ve known hundreds of chess players, and I’ve never heard of anyone who came even remotely close to that kind of improvement in their adult years. If you were 15 years old I would have said of course it’s possible. 25 years, maybe. 45 years, no. Now someone is going to comment that anything is possible, but that’s not a very useful statement in my opinion. In practice, this is not happening.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: You ought to be familiar with Mira Murati if you enjoy using ChatGPT and OpenAI. She serves as the CTO for the business that developed these incredible technology. Has she received the proper credit?
Answer: I think the executives at tech companies generally get too much credit, and I say that as a CTO myself. Not that Murati's contribution isn't valuable. The CTO at a tech company like OpenAI is second only to the CEO in terms of importance for the company. If the two of them don't perform, the company goes nowhere. And I'm sure Murati is brilliant to be in the position she is in. That being said, it's not the CTO that developed ChatGPT. OpenAI has strong leadership, but so has many other companies. The brilliance of the company lies in its ability to come up with breakthroughs in AI. And the technology that enables those breakthroughs is developed by the engineers on the floor. The real stars of ChatGPT are people you've never heard about, because they're not the public-facing part of the organization. Meanwhile, Murati and Sam Altman are declared as geniuses even though they didn't implement the technology themselves. They merely ran the company in a way that allowed amazing engineers to do groundbreaking work.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How should programs manage API and SDK credentials when acting as clients?
Answer: If a bad actor gains access to your API keys to 3rd party services, they can start spending your money if it’s a paid API. That’s not as bad as say exposing the connection string to a database, which would be a lot worse, especially if it contains personal data. But it’s still bad enough that we should definitely protect our API keys. This is how OpenAI provisions API keys: This is an excellent flow that encourages the developer to think about security best practices. If I go back to my API keys, I can’t see the full key, I can only revoke it. This allows me to generate temporary keys like this one for experimentation, and I can easily set up a key for production that I can recycle whenever I want. The general guiding principle about secrets is this: Secrets should be seen by human eyes as few times as possible. Once I’ve generated my production key, I will store it in an encrypted vault like Azure Key Vault or AWS Key Management Service. My application will authenticate with that service through Role-based access control (RBAC) and only access the key from there. This means my key will never be checked into version control, stored in some unsecure location or sent to someone by message or email. I’m the only person who has ever accessed it, and it only existed in my clipboard history for a brief while.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Can the movie Prometheus be considered an underrated sci-fi movie?
Answer: Hell no. It's overrated. Prometheus had a lot going for it. A large budget, amazing visuals, great actors, one of the all-time great directors. The concept of an Alien prequel was interesting too. There was just one problem. The story never went anywhere. You can't have a good movie with a meaningless plot. Ridley Scott is a great director who makes visually outstanding movies. But he has one big flaw. He can't tell a good script from a bad one. That makes his movies totally hit and miss. He's the director behind amazing movies like Alien, Blade Runner, Gladiator and The Martian. But then he makes crap like 1492, Exodus: Gods and Kings and Alien: Covenant. Prometheus is not his worst movie, but I’d say it's in the bottom half.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is it wise to DEVOUR all data in the world for our ChatGPT, or could it be more efficient to curate the data?
Answer: The first thing you have to realize is that ChatGPT is trained on hundreds of billions of words of text. We can’t really curate that amount of data in any sort of detailed manner. We can only make high-level decisions, like “should we use the Wikipedia corpus”. We can’t go through every Wikipedia page and decide whether to use it or not. The amount of training data has a huge effect on performance of GPT models. A model trained on 500 billion essentially uncurated tokens like ChatGPT is going to vastly outperform a model trained on a dataset of 5 billion carefully curated tokens. The process of curation is anything but efficient. Whenever we need to involve human input, it's painstakingly slow, and expensive. ChatGPT has also been finetuned through reinforcement learning with human labeling. But what OpenAI did next is quite telling. They trained a neural network that imitates the human labelers, so that they could continue the reinforcement learning without human input. That's the breakthrough that made the last generation of GPT models, including ChatGPT, possible. Is it wise to train models on essentially the entire internet? That's a complex ethical question. But from an engineering standpoint it's the only way to achieve state-of-the-art language AI.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Has any human player been able to consistently beat the level 25 bot on chess.com?
Answer: I’m guessing the engine behind the level 25 (3200 Elo) engine is actually Stockfish 11, which is used at chess.com to analyze games. If my assumption is correct, that bot is basically unbeatable for humans. It’s an older version of Stockfish, but not that old. From the release notes: This version 11 of Stockfish is 50 Elo stronger than the last version, and 150 Elo stronger than the version which famously lost a match to AlphaZero two years ago. This makes Stockfish the strongest chess engine running on your smartphone or normal desktop PC, and we estimate that on a modern four cores CPU, Stockfish 11 could give 1:1000 time odds to the human chess champion having classical time control, and be on par with him. [1] There was previously a bug in the web version that allowed you to appear as if you were playing against the bot on level 25 when you were actually playing it on level 1. It looks like they removed the engine level bots entirely from the web version. It’s still available in the mobile app. By the way, the estimated ratings at the other levels are definitely inflated. I was able to beat the level 22 (2600) engine with some consistency. That one’s supposed to be grandmaster level, but as you can see from my credentials, that’s far from my actual playing strength. EDIT: The engine used for the bots is actually Komodo, not Stockfish, but the same applied. It should essentially be unplayable at the strongest setting.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Isn't it interesting that when you talk about famous Norwegians, people will probably think about Ole Gunnar Solskjær, an ex-football player who wasn't his team first-choice and not about the reigning five-time chess world champion Magnus Carlsen?
Answer: Most will probably first think of Erling Braut Haaland, who's breaking all kinds of scoring records in the Premier League and was recently ranked as the most valuable football player in the world. I assume Martin Ødegaard is also more famous than Solskjær, being the current captain of the team leading the Premier League (Arsenal). But worldwide, I'm not even sure those guys are more famous than Magnus. Few people care about football over in the US, and in India chess is a huge sport while football is not. World chess champions also tend to leave a more lasting legacy than top footballers, since there are so few of them. And Magnus is one of the greatest, if not the greatest, player chess has ever seen. His name will be well known a hundred years from now but I'm not so sure about the other guys.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What do you think would probably prevent humans from potentially surviving any timescale longer than the time since we bonked Neanderthals, let alone a billion years, like with other animals and plants and especially bacteria?
Answer: About the duration of species Animals as we generally think of them only arrived with the Cambrian explosion some 530 million years ago (mya). Plants a little later. Not quite a billion years, but still a fairly long time ago. It’s important to note that no extant species have existed for that long. The horseshoe crab is often called a “living fossil” because we have found 445 million year old fossils that look almost exactly like them. The horseshoe crab and its 400 million year old great-great-great… (I’m not going to write that all out) grandparent. However, despite the similar body type, they have evolved so much over the years that it’s not the same species anymore. The four extant species of horseshoe crabs belong to a family that evolved 250 mya, and the oldest of those four species only evolved around 25 mya. Similarly, the tadpole shrimp was thought to be over 200 million years old, but a recent study found the extant species to be much younger. According to Africa Gómez[1], one of the senior authors of that study: I don't think there is evidence that any single species has been around for more than a few million years We can infer from the fossil record that individual species generally last between 500,000 and 3 million years[2] before going extinct or evolving to a descendant species. About human evolution Anatomically modern humans (Homo sapiens) have existed for some 300,000 years. And our archaic ancestors who looked very similar to us existed for 2 million years. That’s already a significant amount of time when considering the above quote. A reconstruction of a female Homo erectus. Like all others animals, humans are constantly evolving. And it’s happening ever faster. In the last 5000 years, we evolved 100 times faster than in the past[3]. This has the surprising consequence that the first pyramid builders were genetically closer to Neanderthals than to us. There are now 8 billion of us, and the majority of us are living in urban areas, leading drastically different lifestyles than our nomadic ancestors. At the current rate, we’ll evolve to a different species in a relatively short period of time. Humans as we know ourselves almost certainly won't survive for much longer. We will be different. How much different is hard to tell. But will the Homo genus survive? Will there still be humanoids walking Earth? Doomsday scenarios When we talk about the possible extinction of humans, it’s usually the same doomsday scenarios that pop up. Climate change This is the most pressing matter. We talk about saving the environment and the conservation of wildlife, but it’s really ourselves we need to save. The world is going to become a really crappy place for humans if we don’t do something about it, and it’s already become quite bad for many. The good news about climate change is that it’s not a sudden event, like some of the others on my list. We still have time to reverse the trend. Personally, I don’t believe humanity will be wiped out by climate change. I think the worst case is some sort of Mad Max scenario where a few survivors are eking out a meagre existence. But the most likely scenario in my opinion is that we eventually manage to reverse things and only end up in a slightly worse place. Giant asteroids Large asteroid impacts are inevitable and can be quite devastating. Planet killers on the size of the one that nearly wiped out the dinosaurs are fortunately very rare, striking only every 100 million years or so. And we’re not that far off from having a really solid planetary defense system in place. We’re still missing some potentially dangerous asteroids, but the automated monitoring systems are getting better and better. With the success of the DART mission[4], we already have the technology to deflect large asteroids and change their trajectory enough to prevent a collision event. An illustration of the DART mission that altered the trajectory of an asteroid. Supervolcano eruption Supervolcano eruptions inevitably happen, but still only once every 50,000 years or so. These events are pretty bad, but we know that humans will likely survive one, since we have done so in the past. There is some genetic evidence that the human population was greatly decreased following the last major eruption 74,000 years ago[5], and that we went through a genetic bottleneck of only a few thousand individuals. However, there is no physical evidence supporting this, so the theory is disputed. Gamma-ray bursts A gamma-ray burst could potentially wreak havoc on our planet, and would be near impossible to prevent. Fortunately, it is an extremely unlikely event. Not only does the burst need to happen in our galactic neighborhood (within a few hundred light-years) to be deadly, but it also needs to point directly at Earth. A theory has been proposed that a gamma-ray burst caused the Ordovician-Silurian extinction event 440 mya[6]. This would have stripped the Earth of half its ozone layer and led to global cooling, which is consistent with some observations, but there is no unequivocal evidence that this is what happens. Before it happens again, humanity might even develop technology to predict and defend against the effects of a burst. We’re already seeing hints that it may be possible to predict certain gamma-ray bursts ,[7] and who knows what might be possible in the future. That’s highly hypothetical though. For now, a deadly gamma-ray burst remains a scary but exceedinlgy unlikely scenario. Nuclear holocaust The threat of an apocalyptic nuclear winter has been greatly exaggerated in the public discourse and in popular culture, often by people with a political agenda. More recent attempts at modelling the effects a nuclear World War III have suggested that the planet would remain habitable even in the worst of scenarios. For instance, the Toba eruption was far more explosive than all global stockpiles of nuclear weapons combined. While nuclear fallout would lead to increased levels of cancer, it would not kill off everyone. It’s also a question of how likely it is, considering there hasn’t been a single atomic bomb used in warfare for almost 80 years and countries have been actively disarming their stockpiles. AI-powered killer robots This is the one I would personally worry the least about. Again, we’re affected by Hollywood narratives that greatly exaggerate the risk. A killer robot from the Black Mirror episode “Metalhead”. The proposal that an artificial superintelligence would suddenly run amok killing everything in its path (the paperclip scenario[8]) still lingers in the realm of science fiction. As the makers of robots and AI technology, we still have the power to control it, and I don’t believe we’ll lose that power any time soon. The much more realistic scenario is that corrupt powers use this technology to inflict death on their enemies. Pandemic We have just gone through a major pandemic that has killed almost 7 million people and counting. Because of its relatively high R number it spread quite quickly. However, Covid-19 has a low mortality rate well below 1% in young people, although it’s higher in elders. A high-mortality disease like Ebola hasn’t spread globally yet because the infected get very sick very quickly and tend to die off before they infect too many people. The worst scenario is a disease with a high mortality rate, long incubation period and high R number. For instance, the H5N1 strain of influenza has been estimated by WHO to have a mortality rate of 60% in humans. It does not transmit between humans yet, but it’s killing tens of millions of bird, and could easily mutate to a strain capable of human-to-human transmission. Fortunately, we were able to respond very quickly to Covid-19, and hopefully we learned something from it and are better equipped for the next major pandemic. A pandemic could still be very bad, but it almost certainly won’t wipe out humanity altogether. Conclusion I strongly believe humans will survive in the foreseeable future. But we’ll change. Rapid evolution due to our urban living environment and advanced technology such as AI and cybernetic implants will alter us in ways we probably can’t imagine yet. We bonked the Neanderthals 40,000 years ago. Who knows who we will bonk 40,000 years from now. All I know is the bonking must go on.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Given that there are less than 2000 GMs in chess, yet there are over hundreds of millions of doctors, is it safe to say that becoming a GM is exponentially harder than medical school?
Answer: Well, it’s certainly not exponentially harder, because that would mean it becomes increasingly harder over time at an ever faster rate. Becoming a GM has actually become easier in recent decades. Partly due to rating inflation and partly because there are so many more learning resources readily available these days. But it’s still extremely hard to become a GM, and way harder than becoming a doctor. Graduating from medical school is more about going throuth the hoops. There are certain classes you need to attend and exams you need to complete over a number of years. But as long as you work hard and do what you’re supposed to, you will become a doctor. Hard work is not enough to become a GM. You actually need to perform at a world-class level in competition. You need to consistently beat other players who have also worked very hard to get to where they are. That requires not only hard work, but talent. It’s also a prerequisite that you start when you are very young.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How hard would it be for an improving player rated 2200-2400 FIDE to get the IM and GM titles if they were suddenly diagnosed with early onset dementia?
Answer: Obtaining the IM title, let alone the GM title, is already incredibly difficult for players in that rating range. Unless we're talking about a rare child prodigy who is already at 2200+ in their preteens, getting the GM title is far from given. With Alzheimer, it would be near impossible. I once met a man who had previously been rated above 2000 before being diagnosed with early-onset dementia. His rating had dropped to 1300. You could still see glimpses of his chess understanding and pattern recognition, but he couldn't calculate variations anymore.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How does Magnus Carlsen, the world's best chess player, calculate moves ahead?
Answer: In principle he calculates the same way as everyone else, with some caveats that I will explain. Let’s imagine the following position between two complete beginners. Level 0 thinking is: A young kid who is learning the game for the first time is likely to take one of these pawns, not realizing they will lose their queen. Level 1 thinking is: Now let’s imagine the game continues like this: If I take the pawn on f7, the queen can take back, then I can take the queen with my bishop, but then the king can take my bishop. I give away a queen and a bishop for a queen and a pawn, so I shouldn’t do that. This is still just level 1 thinking. The concept is still the same, except you have to calculate 4 ply (half-moves) ahead instead of 2 as in the first example. Of course, a grandmaster like Magnus Carlsen will frequently calculate many more moves ahead than a beginner, but it’s the same type of thinking. Once you get it for the first time, you can apply the same thinking and train yourself to be able to look further and further ahead. The principle is still the same. “I do this, you do that, I do that” and so on. Then you count the material in the end. Level 2 thinking involves an assessment of strategic factors in the position. These can sometimes even outweigh material imbalances when you knowingly enter a variation where you lose material, also known as a sacrifice. Usually when someone sacrifices material it’s because they’re able to calculate that they will regain the material or deliver checkmate. That’s not really a sacrifice. It’s called a sham sacrifice or a pseudo sacrifice. That’s still level 1 thinking. Example: In this game from 2005, Magnus Carlsen played Bxe6, sacrificing his queen. But after Rd1+ Qxd1 Nxd1 Bb3 black knight’s was trapped, and after Nxb2 Kxb2 the players arrived at this position where white has a rook and two pieces for a queen and a pawn. A classic sham sacrifice. A real sacrifice involves giving up material for positional compensation. In this game against Sergey Karjakin from 2019, Magnus castled, giving up his pawn on h5. He relied on his domination over the light squares on the kingside to give him strong attacking chances, and felt that it was more important to get his king to safety and to connect the rooks than to hold on to the pawn. And indeed, he won the game. This type of level 2 thinking is something you start seeing in games at expert (2000+) level, and it’s what really separates the men from the boys. Obviously, both Karjakin and Magnus had seen that the pawn on h5 could be captured if black castled. That only required a calculation of 2 ply. But Magnus had a greater understanding of the positional factors. Finally, there is the meta thinking. Sticking to the same example game, Magnus knows that Karjakin is an excellent technical player who is extremely hard to beat in dry positions. By going for a more complex double-edged position he gave himself a greater chance to beat that specific player. Magnus excels at all these types of thinking including raw calculation, but it’s his strategic assessment of positions that really sets him apart from the rest of the world elite.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How do you know if you are related to Vikings?
Answer: Simple. I'm European. The Human Genome Project has revealed a number of surprising and counter-intuitive facts about our heritage. One of those facts is that the last common ancestor of all Europeans lived just 600 years ago. There was a person who lived in the 15th century who is the direct ancestor of every European alive today. If we go back to the Viking Age, the number of common ancestors increases drastically. At around 1000 CE, we reach what is called a genetic isotope. That means that all the Europeans who lived at that time either have no living descendants or are ancestors of every European alive. Around 80% of all Europeans who lived 1000 years ago are the direct ancestors of all Europeans today. If you're European, or an American or Australian of European descent, then you're directly related to most of the vikings who ever lived. If you're Afro-American, Afro-Caribbean or Afro-Brazilian, you're most likely related to Vikings too. Now, someone like me who lives in the viking heartland on the west coast of Norway probably has more viking DNA than you. But the Norsemen were travellers, and their genes quickly spread far and wide. It's quite possible that all living Native Americans are related to Norse settlers who lived in Newfoundland a thousand years ago. It has already been shown that the majority of the Icelandic population are descendants of a Native American woman who was most likely brought back to Iceland in the Middle Ages, probably in the 11th century. Oh, and there is even a global genetic isotope as recently as 1400 BCE. Without knowing who you are, I can tell you that you're related to most people who lived back then, whether they lived in Eurasia, Africa, the Americas or the Pacific.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What's the highest rating you've ever beaten in a speed chess match?
Answer: Back in the mid-2000s, the Internet Chess Club (ICC) used to host a prize-money tournament called Dos Hermanas. Prize money in online tournaments was quite unusual back then, so this attracted many Grandmasters and amateurs. The nice thing was that anyone could play, regardless of rating and title. It was a unique chance for players like me to play against a caliber of players I normally didn’t get to play against. By far the biggest scalp I ever took in the tournament was blitz specialist GM Rauf Mamedov, who played under the screenname MLRAKA. His peak blitz rating was 3690, which is the fourth highest rating ever achieved on the server according to this list. He was rated around 3300 when I beat him, and my rating would have been around 2300. I remember the game not only because of who I beat, but because he nearly flagged me at the end. The games were played with 3 minutes and no increment. This was before the main ICC client BlitzIn even had premoving as a feature, and servers were generally a bit slower back then, so losing on time was always a real danger. I had king and queen against king, but only a couple of seconds left. I finally checkmated him with 0.1 seconds left on the clock.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Who is stronger: Max Deutsch or Magnus Carlsen?
Answer: Max Deutsch is an “obsessive learner” and “genius” who set himself goals of mastering different skills in one month each. Whether it was doing backflips, painting self-portraits or solving the Rubik’s cube in 20 seconds, he was able to conquer these challenges one by one. His final challenge was to beat the world number one chess players Magnus Carlsen at a game of chess. After only a month of practice, Max Deutsch played Magnus Carlsen and did the unthinkable… He played a game that was even worse than I had imagined. After 13 moves, Max was already dead lost with the white pieces. But instead of recapturing with the pawn in the diagram position, he played 14.Qxe3?? giving away a free piece. A few moves later, Magnus Carlsen was threatening an epic fork with Bc3. Ignoring that completely, Max played 18.Bd3?? Interestingly, in this position, Max played 26.Re4, which tells me he probably didn’t know about the en passant rule. So the guy studied the game for an entire month and still didn’t know the rules. Brilliant. His play was so abysmal that players with the minimum FIDE rating of 1000 could probably give the guy piece odds and still win. My 4 year old daughter plays better. Magnus Carlsen has a rating of 2852 and is the greatest player in the history of chess. My overall conclusion is that Magnus is a stronger player than Max Deutsch.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How good is a 1400 rating on Lichess? I've casually played for 1-2 years.
Answer: If you go to your profile page and click on blitz, it will say “You are better than xx.x% of Blitz players”. If you click on the percentage, you can even get a complete distribution diagram of all the active blitz players on Lichess. There will be a dashed line with your rating. 1400 is pretty much smack in the middle. That means you are average among 800,000 people who play blitz on Lichess, many of whom are active tournament players and have played for years. It also means you are better than ~400,000 other players who regularly play online chess. Not too shabby for someone who’s relatively new at the game. Keep in mind that the 2000+ crowd are generally very serious about the game and have for the most part studied it far longer than you have.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Why was King Harold II more popular than King Harald Hardrada in England, even though they were both foreigners invading from Scandinavia? Did people prefer Normans over Danes at that time?
Answer: Harold II was not a Norman nor a foreigner. He was an Anglo-Saxon born and raised in Wessex. The Anglo-Saxons had already been a dominating presence in Great Britain for 600 years at that time. They were the founders of England. Obviously Harold would be preferred by the local population to a Norwegian outsider who just invaded the country on a whim. Perhaps you meant William the Conqueror? Keep in mind that William had also just arrived in England, and the subsequent history was written by the victors, i.e. the Normans.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Are there other earths somewhere in space?
Answer: If we take “other earths” to mean rocky planets orbiting Sun-like stars that could host liquid water on the surface, there are plenty of them. According to the most conservative estimate of a recent study[1], there is at least a ratio of 0.07 rocky planets in the Goldilocks zone per Sun-like star. Their best estimate was 0.58. In terms of sheer numbers that adds up to around 2 billion Earth-like planets in the Milky Way alone, with a lower bound of 300 million. Now consider that there are trillions of galaxies in the Universe, and we're looking at an order of 10 20 − 10 22 Earth-like planets out there. An unimaginably large number. Silly things start to happen with numbers that large. We can say with near 100% certainty there is at least one other star out there that's almost exactly like our Sun, with a rocky planet with a diameter of 12,000 km orbiting at a distance of 1 AU. The most similar planet will be so much like our Earth that the differences are like rounding errors. The implications of this are quite fascinating.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What would you say to the CEO of a company who belittles your work?
Answer: I've been a consultant for several years, specifically in the field of machine learning and AI, so I'm used to people belittling my work all the time. Case 1: “I don’t believe you” I once pitched an automated planning algorithm to the billionaire CEO of a large oil service company. I made a presentation to the entire board. The CTO and tech advisors had already read my whitepaper on the algorithm and were really excited about it. We had even tested the algorithm on live production data and showed that it would save the company millions of dollars annually. All we needed was buy-in from the CEO. He rejected the proposal out of hand. And I quote: “I don’t believe this machine learning stuff works. I watch the weather forecast every day, and they never get it right. You can’t predict the future.” What could I say? This guy had built the company from the ground up using his own two hands. I wanted to go on a rant about how weather forecasts are actually highly accurate and that I had empirical data to back up my claims. But I already knew my project was dead in the water. I’m not a salesman and I’m not very good at convincing people who don’t want to be convinced. Case 2: “It’s simple” If I had a dollar for every time some CEO or business person has told me to do some task and added “it should be simple”, I would have a lot of dollars. As a tech person you just hate hearing this. Unless you work hands-on with technology, you have no idea how hard it is to implement something. Like, no clue. It’s very often counter-intuitive. Tasks that are hard will appear simple, and vice versa. I’m so used to it now that it doesn’t really bother me anymore. And to be fair, there is no ill intent on the part of the business person. It’s simply ignorance. As a CTO, it’s my job to say “wait a minute, not so fast” and “it’s actually not that simple”. I may come off as an eternal pessimist, but it’s much better to be a realistic party pooper sometimes than overpromising and not being able to stick to your word. Because business people are always optimistic, and that’s their job.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How accurate is the out of Africa theory? Some say Europeans have different origins
Answer: There are multiple “Out of Africa” theories. The traditional view was that archaic humans, namely Homo erectus, migrated out of Africa around 1.8 million years and settled throughout Southern Asia stretching as far east as Indonesia. This has been known as “Out of Africa I”. Then modern humans (Homo sapiens) supposedly left Africa in a single event known as “Out of Africa II” around 60,000 years ago. As we uncover more archeological evidence, those dates are being pushed further and further back. It’s also becoming increasingly clear that there have been many independent migrations that happened over long time periods. Obviously, prehistoric humans didn’t care about what continent they were in. There is a strait in the Red Sea between Ethiopia and Yemen that’s less than 30 kilometers across. There has been a land bridge here several times during human prehistory. The Bab-el-Mandeb strait. It’s also entirely possible to walk across the Sinai desert, which was a fertile landscape in the relatively recent past. There is evidence that Homo sapiens may have reached Greece as far back as 210,000 years ago[1]. We also have more solid evidence that modern humans were present in the Levant around 185,000 years ago, far earlier than previously thought. And of course, we know that Neanderthals and Denisovans lived in Eurasia even earlier than that, having descended from Homo heidelbergensis, which left Africa half a million years ago. The modern humans in Eurasia mixed more with these now extinct species than humans in Africa and we have more of their DNA, around 2%. But as recent studies have shown, even native Africans carry a non-negligible amount of Neanderthal DNA[2]. So how is that possible? Well, migrations went both ways. There were several waves of migrations from the Near East to Northern Africa and the Horn of Africa during the Paleolithic and Neolithic. Human evolution is incredibly complex, and new archeological evidence is constantly making the story more fragmented. While modern humans from different geographical regions have slightly different origins, we’re still one species with a common ancestry.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Can investors take over your startup and replace its founders with their own choice of CEO, CTO, etc.?
Answer: No one can really take over your startup as long as you have majority ownership. If you issue enough shares to investors so that you and your co-founders own less than 50%, you no longer have control, and the new majority can appoint whoever they want in executive positions. But it’s your own conscious decision to do so. No one is forcing you. A so-called “hostile takeover” can occur if an outside investor offers to buy the company for a price that’s so good you can’t refuse it, even if you don’t really want that person in charge. This sort of stuff usually happens to big publicly traded that have lots of owners. It’s basically what happened when Elon Musk bought Twitter. Most startup owners would be thrilled to sell the company if someone offered a ridiculous price. It means a big payday. That being said, controlling the cap table so that you can take investor money while still remaining in control is something startup founders should be prudent about. Some inexperienced founders are so excited about the prospect of raising money that they give up more than half of the company even before raising a series A. For experienced investors this is a red flag since it can limit the startup’s ability to attract talent later down the road.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How important was Nidaros in the viking age? How much power and respect did the Jarls of Lade have, were they know all across the Norse world (perhaps even as far away as Jorvik, Holmgard and Miklagard)?
Answer: The foundation of Nidaros The city of Nidaros (now known as Trondheim) wasn’t founded until 997, and as such didn’t even exist throughout most of the Viking Age. The Lade estate, while only 4 kilometers from the city center, was never a part of the medieval city of Nidaros. In fact, the entire concept of having cities was relatively new in Norway at the time. A monument in Trondheim of king Olav Tryggvason, who founded the city in 997. The importance of Nidaros grew with the sainthood of Olav Haraldsson in 1164, after which the Nidaros Cathedral where he was buried became a popular European pilgrimage site. By that time, the Lade dynasty had already ended. Construction of the Nidaros Cathedral began in 1070. That being said, the area surrounding modern-day Trondheim was an important power center already from the onset of the Viking Age. Øretinget and the hailing of kings When Harald Finehair was crowned the first king of Norway after the battle of Hafrsfjord in 872 (the exact year is disputed), he was officially hailed at the Øreting at Lade. This tradition may even have older roots, but at least we know that Norwegian kings were hailed here from the 10th century. The house of Lade The founders of Lade were traders who controlled the trade of goods like fur, seal skin and walrus teeth from the far North to Southern Norway and the European continent. During the 9th century, Lade had unified 8 distinct counties under one banner, and reigned over a much larger region than the petty kingdoms in the South. This is how Harald Finehair divided the country after he came to power. Norway in the early 10th century CE. The land area granted to Lade was huge. Larger than all of Denmark and comparable to Sweden at the time. The part of Norway ruled directly by Harald Finehair (the Southwestern coastline) was substantially smaller, albeit more populous. As a result, the Lade Jarls enjoyed immense power and respect, and often commanded large armies. They were certainly more powerful than the petty kings of Southeast Norway. A note about the title of Jarl The English title of Earl was a rebranding of the Anglo-Saxon title of Ealdorman. While the word itself was borrowed from the Scandinavian Jarl, it had a slightly different meaning. After the unification of England, the ealdormen (and later earls) were landowners who were appointed by the king to lead individual shires. In Scandinavian countries, and in particular in Norway, the jarls ruled more independently. In later medieval times, there was usually only one (or sometimes no) jarls in mainland Norway. This person was a sort of viceroy that would rule in case the king was incapacitated or if there was no recognized legitimate king. As such, the Scandinavian jarls had more relative power in their respective countries than any noblemen had in England. At least this was the case towards the end of the Viking Age when England had been unified. The Jarls of Lade At the height of the Lade dynasty, the Jarl had power to rival kings. The most powerful of them all was probably Jarl Håkon Sigurdsson, sometimes given the epithet The Powerful. Formally, he was a vassal of the Danish king Harald Bluetooth. In reality, he was the de facto ruler of Norway between 970 and 995. He arguably ruled directly over a greater part of Norway than any of the kings of the Finehair dynasty that came before him. He was the last pagan ruler of Norway. An illustration of Håkon Sigurdsson from a 19th-century edition of Snorre Sturlason’s Heimskringla. Håkon helped his relative Vladimir the Great of Kiev reconquer Holmgard (Novgorod) in the 970s. He also defeated the Holy Roman Emperor Otto II in battle in Denmark around 974, which speaks volumes about the military power he wielded. His name would have been known throughout the lands where vikings roamed, which extended all the way to Kievan Rus and Miklagard (the Old Norse name for Constantinople). Keep in mind that Europe had gotten smaller in the High Middle Ages. During the late antiquity, Norway was known in the Roman world as the mythical land of Thule, hardly more than a legend. But in the Viking Age, thousands of Scandinavians would traverse the rivers of Eastern Europe to serve in the Varangian Guard in Constantinople. Håkon Sigurdsson must have been well known there, even though he probably never ventured that far south himself. His son and later Jarl of Lade Eirik Håkonsson was also the Earl of Northumbria between 1016 and 1024, where Jorvik (York) was capital at the time. In conclusion, the Jarls of Lade were extremely powerful and must have been known throughout the Norse world and by extension most of Europe.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Who would win? Norway or Sweden (Military comparison)?
Answer: I’ll answer this question in two parts. First, I’ll go through the pointless, but fun, exercise of comparing the military strength of both countries. After that, I’ll give you the real answer. Pointless comparison The armed forces of Norway and Sweden are relatively evenly matched in terms of numbers. Global Firepower ranks Norway 35th and Sweden 37th in the world in overall military strength[1]. Manpower Both Norway and Sweden have been steadily decreasing the number of active military personnel in the last few decades. At this point, it’s around 20,000 for both countries. But Sweden has twice the population of Norway, and could muster a larger force if push comes to shove. Swedish soldiers participating in a NATO exercise on Swedish soil in 2022. Winner: Sweden Financials Norway has a slightly larger military budget, but of course that could change in a war. Sweden has a slightly larger GDP than Norway. Winner: Sweden Airforce Norway has a fleet of fifth-generation F-35s, which might be the most advanced fighter jet in the world. The Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II. Then again, Sweden has more aircraft in total than Norway. And importantly, they produce their own craft, the JAS 39 Gripen, which is considered generation 4.5. The Saab JAS 39 Gripen. Winner: Sweden Navy Norway has four large frigates that are really more like destroyers. Sweden doesn’t have comparable ships, although nominally the Swedish fleet is larger. Winner: Norway Army Sweden has more tanks than Norway, but Norway has more armored vehicles, and unlike Sweden has mobile rocket launchers. The M270 Multiple Launch Rocket System. Winner: Norway Natural resources Norway is one of the world’s largest producers of oil and gas, which is an important advantage in a war. The Norwegian petroleum industry is one of the world’s largest. Winner: Norway Allies Norway was one of the founding members of NATO in 1949, and has strong ties to the United States Armed Forces. Sweden is actively trying to become a NATO member, but is currently being blocked by Turkey. Winner: Norway The real answer Sweden and Norway have fought more wars against each other than any other two countries in the world, perhaps with the exception of Sweden and Denmark. However, the last time was over 200 years ago. Today, it is exceedingly unlikely that any of the Scandinavian countries will end up in wars on opposite sides. We have essentially no conflicting interests and are very similar culturally and politically. In theory, a Swedish attack on Norway would mean an attack on all NATO members. In practice, NATO would do their utmost to resolve a conflict diplomatically, since Sweden is an ally in all but name. Even if we disregard the extreme unlikelihood that an armed conflict would occur, it’s still a pointless discussion. We can compare military strength all we want, but as we’ve seen time and again, wars are not decided by simple arithmetic. We need look no further than the ongoing war in Ukraine. On paper, Russia should win easily, but it doesn’t work like that in practice. Modern wars generally end up being a huge loss for all parties involved. A full-scale war between two evenly matched, modern armies, would be a complete mess with no winners.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Why did Greece not become an empire like Rome or China?
Answer: The canonical answer is that Greece remained a collection of city states because of its isolating geography of mountains, valleys and islands. But the city states did have extensive contact with each other and there were definitely times when they united into larger constellations. The Delian League, founded in 478 BCE, was an alliance of city states led by Athens with the aim of fending off Persian attacks. During its height of power in the second half of the 5th century it could be considered an empire. The member states of this alliance, with a few exceptions, paid tribute to Athens. However, there was one instance in which Greece definitely became an empire. Of course, I’m talking about the Macedonian Empire forged by Alexander the Great in the late fourth century BCE. It was the second largest the world had ever seen at that point, eclipsed only by the Achaemenid Empire and overlapping most of its territory. Macedonia was a Greek kingdom and very much a part of the Hellenistic world. The Macedonians spoke classical Greek and worshipped Greek gods. Macedonia is a region of modern Greece even today, where Thessaloniki is the largest city.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Can you share the first sentence of your favorite novel? What hooked you to this work of fiction?
Answer: The opening line of the prologue in Dan Simmons’ Hyperion: The Hegemony Consul sat on the balcony of his ebony spaceship and played Rachmaninoff's Prelude in C-Sharp Minor on an ancient but well-maintained Steinway while great, green, saurian things surged and bellowed in the swamps below. It’s a great opener. It instantly draws you in by showcasing the worldbuilding with a vivid alien landscape, and leaving you with a bunch of questions. Why is a spaceship made out of ebony? Why is there a swamp with great, green, saurian things inside it? From that sentence alone you immediately realize that this is not going to be some understated, gritty hard science fiction story. This is extravagant and over the top. A space opera. At the same time, you can sense some of the literary quality inherent in the work. The expression “surged and bellowed” is probably not one you’d find in a pulp novel. Hyperion is a great novel primarily because of the stories and the unique science fiction concepts. But what really sets it apart from other good sci-fi novels is the excellent writing and imaginative worldbuilding. And this is what hooked me to the book at first.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Did the English ever try to attack the home bases of the Vikings in Denmark and Norway?
Answer: No, for various reasons. The peoples of Great Britain were too busy warring against themselves Prior to the Viking age, the English world consisted of the seven kingdoms of Wessex, Essex, Sussex, Kent, East Anglia, Mercia and Northumbria. Britain ca. 8th century. The rulers were North-Germanic people like Saxons, Anglians, Frisians and Jutes, who had immigrated from present-day Germany and Denmark to Britain after the collapse of the Roman Empire. There were various Britonnic kingdoms to the West and North, consisting of Cornishmen, Welshmen, Picts and Scots. The native Celtic Britons had invited the Anglo-Saxons over to defend their lands against invasions from the Picts and Scots of modern-day Scotland and Ireland. But they eventually turned against the Britons. By the time the first Vikings arrived at Lindisfarne in 793, Great Britain was truly a multi-cultural melting pot of numerous ethnic groups who were fighting for control over the island. The seven kingdoms had been consolidated into the four major kingdoms of Wessex, Mercia, East Anglia and Northumbria. And by the 9th century, the rulers of Wessex had increasing ambitions to merge the kingdoms to a unified England. In this context, the Viking raids were a distraction that couldn’t have come at a worse time. The initial Viking raids took the English by surprise The first Viking raids attacked unarmed monasteries, and the English were shocked by the viciousness of the attacks. The kneejerk reaction was to pay the Vikings to go away. Of course, that wasn’t very sustainable, as the Vikings simply kept coming in greater numbers, lured by the promise of silver. It was only during Alfred the Great of Wessex’s reign at the end of the 9th century that the English started changing their tactics. Alfred implemented fortified burhs and local mercenary armies known as fyrds to meet the Viking threat. The Vikings were too mobile in their longships and too unpredictable with their guerilla raids for traditional military tactics to work. The Vikings were always on the move The Scandinavians were the best seafarers in Europe in the Early Middle Ages. They had incredible range, and roamed the seas and rivers from North America to Russia to the Near East. The Oseberg ship, an early example of a Viking longship. When the Norwegian king Harold Hardrada invaded Northern England in 1066, he had experience from military campaigns in Kievan Rus, Byzantium, Anatolia, Palestine, Mesopotamia, Bulgaria, Italy and of course in Scandinavia. Imagine trying to track down a guy like that 1000 years ago if he didn't want to be found. Scandinavia was vast and sparsely inhabitated. Scandinavia is sparsely populated even today, but during the Viking age, Norway may have had as few as 100,000-200,000 people spread across an area twice the size of Great Britain. Denmark had a larger population over a smaller area, but it was still a far cry from the relatively heavily populated England. There were no central power bases There were no Londons or Winchesters or Yorks to attack in Viking age Scandinavia. Even the kings lived in relatively modest farmsteads consisting of a few longhouses when they weren't out on military campaigns or Viking raids. And power was constantly shifting. There were always usurpers and pretenders to the throne even during the times when Norway and/or Denmark was unified in one kingdom. The only guaranteed outcome the English would accomplish by assassinating an important Viking king is that any brothers and sons of the king would come after them for blood revenge.
