Question: Will Elon Musk and the Twitter debacle jeopardise his dream of colonizing Mars in 2026?
Answer: First of all, we will not colonize Mars by 2026 or anywhere near it. We might see the first manned mission to Mars and a permanent research station on the Moon by the 2030s, but definitely not as early as 2026. Of those two, I'll put my bet on the Moon base to happen first. Elon operates on a different time scale, but I think we've all learned by now to take his projections with more than a grain of salt. As for the Twitter debacle, I think Elon is starting to put it behind him. Most of his recent tweets are actually about SpaceX. I think he's come to terms with the fact that his incessant micromanagement of Twitter wasn't doing his reputation or net worth any good. His focus now seems to be back on his pet companies SpaceX and Tesla. And I wouldn't be surprised if SpaceX plays a major role in humanity's exploration of the red planet over the next few decades.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Why has it been difficult to properly scale ChatGTP? What are the limitations?
Answer: It's not that difficult. It's just extremely expensive. GPT-3 is a huge model with 175 billion parameters that requires substantial GPU capacity even for inference. At the moment, ChatGPT is a free service. Until OpenAI monetizes it, they will try to keep server costs as low as possible. Some downtime will be tolerated until the product starts generating revenue. Another thing to add is that the popularity of ChatGPT caught OpenAI off guard. The company had quietly launched the equally capable davinci-003 based on the same model the week before ChatGPT, and only nerds like me were hyped about it. Turns out, when they added a simple chat interface to it, suddenly everyone and their mother got excited, even if the previous models already had a simple enough playground interface. Within a week, the service had 1 million users, which is unprecedented growth even when compared to the most popular internet services. I don't think anyone saw that coming. It might even be the case that Microsoft is struggling to allocate enough GPU servers in Azure. The servers running GPT-3 is not your average cluster. I believe any scaling issues will be handled with ease once the service is commercialized. The engineering team at OpenAI is highly capable and tends to deliver on its goals.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What are the top 10 positional-style chess players, considering the period from the 1948 FIDE Tournament for the World Championship (but excluding "classical" players from the Alekhine/Capablanca generation) to present?
Answer: I'll define a positional player as someone who prefers clarity over complications. A player like Bobby Fischer falls just short of being included under this definition. While his play was mostly straightforward, he was always trying to make the best move according to what the position demanded. Magnus Carlsen is included because he will knowingly make sub-optimal moves to keep the position simplified. Arguably, you could consider both of them “universal” players. Others, like Karpov and Petrosian are more clear-cut positional players. 10.Michael Adams One of few positional players who sticks to 1.e4 as his first move, Adams has a unique ability to turn aggressive openings like the Najdorf English Attack into quiet positional affairs. He is one of the strongest, if not the strongest, British players ever. He has been a mainstay in elite chess for three decades. 9.Sergey Karjakin Karjakin is a practical player who excels in all types of positions. But if given the choice, he prefers clarity and simplification. He is an excellent technical player. He held the record of being the youngest Grandmaster ever for a period of almost 20 years, and has won numerous big events, like the Candidates Tournament, World Cup, Rapid and Blitz World Championship and Norway Chess. 8.Lajos Portisch Portisch was an eight-time World Championship Candidate, reaching as far as the semi-finals in 1977 and 1980. Like Smyslov, he was a baritone singer who favored harmony of the pieces. Perhaps the least well-known player on this list, he was nevertheless a top player for three decades. His positional style earned him the nickname “The Hungarian Botvinnik”. 7.Péter Lékó Lékó was sometimes nicknamed “Drawko” during his heyday in the early 2000s because of the tendency of his games to “Peter out” into draws. He was one of the most archetypical positional players of the era. At the same time, he was a very strong player who dominated the strongest tournaments in the world and was one game away from dethroning Vladimir Kramnik in their 2004 World Championship match. 6.Tigran Petrosian There is a great Botvinnik quote: “If Tal sacrifices a piece, take then think. If I sacrifice a piece, think then take. If Petrosian sacrifices a piece, resign”. Indeed, prophylaxis was the order of the day for the Armenian, who became known as “The First Defender”. The ninth World Champion was arguably the greatest defensive player in the history of the game. 5.Vasily Smyslov Smyslov was a musician who would compare the beauty of chess to the harmony of music. His play was all about harmonic piece placement, perhaps the most tell-tale sign of a positional player. Not only did he he play in three World Championships, winning one and drawing one. He also continued to be a top player well into his sixties. 4.Vladimir Kramnik Kramnik was in many ways the successor to Karpov as Kasparov’s positional archnemesis. Although he was tactically inclined in his younger days, he is most well known for grinding out technical wins with his beloved Catalan as white and defending the black side of the infamous Berlin Wall. Kramnik is a three-time world champion and was among the three best players in the world throughout the 90s and 2000s. 3.Mikhail Botvinnik Botvinnik was the scientist of chess. He laid the foundations for modern opening preparation. He played few tournaments, but whenever he did, he was always a top contender. Botvinnik is the only player to have dominated top-level chess both before and after WWII. He would outwork his opponents with better preparation and better concentration at the board. His play always had a deep sense of positional logic. 2.Anatoly Karpov The quintessential positional player, Karpov was known as the “boa constrictor” in his heyday. He used passive and unassuming positional play to strangle his contemporaries. Until Kasparov came along, the chess world was starting to believe this was the only correct way to play. Had it not been for his younger adversary, Karpov might have stayed on top for 20 years. 1.Magnus Carlsen The world number one is very much a pragmatic player who will play anything required to win the game. When he feels like it, he can be a swashbuckling attacking player. But his main tendency is to steer his games into quiet technical positions, where he relies on his unmatched endgame skills and ability to squeeze water from a stone. Magnus is by many, if not most, experts regarded as the greatest chess player ever. And certainly among positional players, there is no contest.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How many hours does it take to reach the Candidate Master (CM) title in chess?
Answer: The CM title is often scoffed at in the chess community. Having been introduced much later (in 2002) than the stronger title of FM (1978) and the traditional titles of GM and IM, for a long time it wasn't really considered a proper title. Most players who reached 2200 back in the early 2000s didn't even pay the fee to attain it. But you clearly need to be a strong player to get your FIDE rating above the required 2200 to be eligible for CM. Most players will never reach this level, even if they play chess for tens of thousands of hours. I have personally spent over 10,000 hours on chess, which is often cited as the magic number to become an expert at something, and I still haven't been able to get above 2200, which frustrates me to this day. At one point, I was rated 2192 and had a winning +5 advantage in a rook endgame against a GM. Had I won that game, I would have become a CM. Since I haven't been active on the tournament circuit for a few years now, it will probably never happen, regardless of how many hours I try. Number of hours doesn't translate to rating. Innate talent and your age when you start playing also matter a lot.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Will ChatGPT replace Google Search?
Answer: ChatGPT is designed to not do internet search. GPT models can do that, it’s just that OpenAI has purposely restricted the model. Compare a search output from ChatGPT… …with that of its sibling GPT-3 model InstructGPT: As I’ve already stressed in this answer… …large language models are unlikely to replace Google Search, since they’re already a central component of the search engine. You can already search for specific information, and if the AI is confident enough in the answer, it will feature prominently at the top of the results page. That’s possible because it’s using the BERT language model. Unlike GPT-3, Google will not spit out an answer to any question regardless of confidence. That could easily lead to misinformation. Google Search is used by billions of people, and the company needs to be wary of its responsibility to provide reliable information. However, BERT is four years old now, and Google has access to much more powerful models that will eventually be incorporated into Search. They won’t replace the product, but they will gradually transform it into something different. In the future, it’s likely that we will primarily converse with an AGI when searching for information instead of browsing through links. But I think the AI still needs to improve by quite a bit first. And Google is very much a central player in developing the technology that will get us there.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Do you think that expanded 48-team format for the 2022 FIFA World Cup is a good idea?
Answer: I like the general idea. Football has spread to all corners of the world, and there are now way more national teams that have a fighting chance. That’s what I love about the World Cup. Suddenly you’ll see teams like Japan and Morocco, that normally aren’t considered top teams, take down giants like Germany, Spain and Portugal. Japan beat both Germany and Spain in the group stage. In this year’s World Cup, all six continents were represented in the round of 16. You have the disciplined European teams, the technical South American teams, the talent-stacked African teams and outsiders from North America, Asia and Oceania. It’s a beautiful clash of cultures. I’m not so sure about the distribution of slots, though. I do like that the South American federation of CONMEBOL gets 6 1/3 slots instead of 4 1/2. There are only 10 countries in CONMEBOL, but all of them have good football teams. The African federation of CAF gets its quota increased from 5 to 9 1/3, which is also great. There are easily 9–10 strong teams in Africa. The federation of OFC, which includes Oceania but not Australia, is increased from half a slot to 1 1/3. In practice, this means that New Zealand gets a free spot. Not so sure about that one. The team is not great, and I don’t think they deserve an automatic ticket to the World Cup. CONCACAF, which is North America including the Caribbean, is increased from 3 1/2 slots to 6 2/3. This is just ridiculous if you ask me. It means we’ll see teams like Panama, Jamaica, El Salvador and Honduras fight it out for those spots. Those teams just aren’t very good. AFC in Asia is increased from 6 1/2 to 8 1/3 and will also see some mediocre teams qualify. Iraq, UAE and Oman will be among the favorites to join this year’s qualifiers, alongside China and Syria. Finally, UEFA in Europe gets 16 slots instead of the previous 13. This could easily have been increased a lot more. There are 24 European teams in the top 50 of the FIFA ranking. Perhaps I’ll finally see my beloved Norway with Erling Haaland qualify for the first time since 1998, but it’s far from guaranteed. The reigning European champions Italy failed to qualify for this year’s World Cup, which should tell you how tough the UEFA qualification is. Will this guy get to play in the 2026 World Cup? Who knows. Having recently seen the Netflix documentary about FIFA, it kind of seems suspicious that Africa and the Caribbean get that many slots. The FIFA delegates in those federations have been corrupt to say the least.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Gmail creator Paul Buchheit predicts new chatbot ChatGPT will challenge Google's monopoly on internet searches. Will AI eliminate the search engine result page?
Answer: I see a lot of misunderstanding surrounding this and I think Buccheit is misquoted in this question. Here is what he tweeted: He says AI, not ChatGPT specifically. To be clear, ChatGPT is optimized to have conversations, not to retrieve information. In fact, it’s purposely designed to avoid giving definitive answers to information queries. OpenAI may design other models for search, but it’s not going to be exactly like that one. The other misunderstanding is that AI is a Google killer and that the company is somehow losing the AI arms race. Google is arguably the largest beneficiary of AI in the world. Google search runs on BERT, another large transformer model. That technology is 4 years old now, and that’s why we see newer language models yield more impressive results. But Google owns DeepMind, which is the only entity that consistently delivers even more impressive AI results than OpenAI. And that’s all proprietary Google tech. If Google wanted to, it could deploy any of its own large language models, like Gopher or Chinchilla, to search. And that will surely happen eventually. It just takes a bit of time when you’re running the world’s largest internet service. I think what Buchheit is trying to say is that search will become so efficient that it becomes harder to monetize. When people browse through search results and try different links, Google makes a lot of ad revenue. If you can consistently get the information you’re looking for straight away, that’s bad for business. So even if Google is on top of the AI game, the technology itself can be disruptive, unless the company is able to innovate on its product.

Question: Maybe Elon Musk is as nuts as I think he is, while being brilliant at many creative things, but what will he do about the Tesla stock falling to 50% as it has?
Answer: Tesla has been valued as a tech company, not a car company. It has a 10x value-to-revenue multiplier that’s relatively normal for a growing tech company but unheard of in the car industry. It’s valued like that based on the notion that the self-driving software, Autopilot, is going to give it a competive advantage over all other car companies. Since Tesla is bound to the tech market, its stock fell this year along with all other major tech stocks. It will likely bounce back up when the tech industry recovers from the current downswing. Valuation aside, Tesla is actually doing extremely well with its fundamentals. Revenue and profits are increasing exponentially. Debt is low. So even if you think the valuation is all wrong, there is no denying that the company is prospering. There is no need for drastic, kneejerk reactions just because the market is down.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Would it be possible to completely automate Quora and eliminate all question and answer writers by combining the Quora Prompt Generator with ChatGPT?
Answer: Not only would it be possible. It would be very easy. Give a GPT model a prompt, and it will happily answer any question. ChatGPT is also quite verbose, which fits the semi-long-form style of Quora well. Of course, it would defeat the entire purpose of Quora, which is to share knowledge that isn't already found on the internet. ChatGPT is trained solely on data from the internet. That's all it knows. And it's not intelligent enough to connect previously unconnected dots based on its knowledge. At least not yet.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Why are valuations so difficult to calculate for start-ups?
Answer: Because it’s often not a calculation at all. Valuating a publicly traded company is one thing. The market has already established a valuation. There are hard numbers to go by. Revenue, profits, costs and so on. You can put the fundamentals into simple formulas, compare that to the market value and make an assessment. I’m not saying that’s simple, but it’s relatively simpler. A startup may not even have revenue at all. They’re usually not profitable. The costs could swing wildly. The valuation is a negotiation between the founders and investors. The investors have to make a qualitative assessment based on the team and their vision. Essentially a judgment call. Startups are weird assets. They typically end up being worth either a lot more or, more commonly, a lot less than what they’re valued at initially. For VC investors it’s a numbers game. They invest in a bunch of startups, hoping that 10% of them will make exits that yield at least 10x ROI.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Will ChatGPT replace programmers?
Answer: ChatGPT isn’t even made with programming as its primary use case. It’s optimized for conversation. It just happens to be pretty good at programming because its base model is trained on a huge corpus that also includes code. OpenAI does have a model that is optimized for writing code that is called Codex. However, that one is built on the iteration of GPT-3 that was available last year. The new and updated GPT-3.5, which has been finetuned with reinforcement learning, is so much better than last year’s model that its derivate models, ChatGPT and the sibling InstructGPT model called davinci-003, are probably better at writing code than Codex itself at the moment. However, there will surely be new iterations of Codex that are even better. And it’s likely that Google will launch a competing product. In the not-too-distant future we will see programming tools built on top of these models that will make the current iteration of ChatGPT look primitive in comparison. At that point, you can probably start to replace mediocre web developers with AI. And in 10–20 years… who knows? The rate of improvement in AI is accelerating, and it’s almost impossible to predict what will be possible just a few years into the future.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Correct me if I'm wrong but, is a PhD in ML worth it when it comes to money? I am going for my Master's but a professor told me that a PhD would provide a leverage moneywise. I thought a Master's degree was more appropriate in that regard.
Answer: That’s misleading advice from the professor, whether intentional or not. While it’s true that people with PhDs on average earn more than people with master’s degrees, that doesn’t account for the cost of getting the PhD. One thing is tuition, but by far the biggest cost is the opportunity cost. If you spend three years getting a PhD, your career will be shorter. You’ll essentially lose three of your best-earning years at the tail end of your career. You’ll also be older when you start earning, which means you’ll lose out on investment opportunities. And you’ll have less money in the phase of your life when you need it the most. Another thing we have to remember that correlation is not the same as causation. Sometimes the PhDs earn high salaries not because of the degree they have, but because they’re exceptional individuals who would have earned a lot of money regardless of education. Finally, there is more money to be earned in industry than in academia. A PhD program is meant to prepare you for a career in academia. It might not always be relevant in industry. I’ve even seen job seekers omitting the PhD from their CV because they were afraid of being seen as over-qualified. All things considered, you should not do a PhD if your only motivation is to make more money. In that case, you might find that doing the PhD is excruciatingly hard, and you might not even be able to finish. You should do it because you want a career in academia and/or because you’re obsessed about the research topic and intrinsically motivated to do the research.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: As the CTO of a fledgling tech startup, how do you balance new 'critical' feature requests from sales with maintaining a consistent, maintainable, cost-effective product?
Answer: As a fledgling startup CTO, you don't have an abundance of resources. A large company may have the luxury of working on many things at once, not all of which are essential. If you do that as a startup CTO, the company will die. As simple as that. That means you have to prioritize whatever moves the needle the most at any given time. If you're still searching for product/market fit, which is the case with most startups, moving the needle means removing the pains that are stopping sales leads from becoming paying customers. On that note, I think it's really bad advice to stop listening to sales, which was suggested in another answer. Your sales team is talking to potential customers daily, and will have real insights into some of the pain points. At the same time, every feature request coming from sales needs to go through your technical bullshit filter. You need to educate the non-technical team members on what’s possible, how difficult it is and why some of the features they want aren’t such a great idea from a technical standpoint. A lack of product/market fit usually means that the very core feature of your product is not good enough. So focus on that, and don’t be tempted into working on low-hanging fruits or cosmetic changes. Go for the big-impact problems that can realistically be solved within weeks or a few months and go all-in on solving those, one at a time. If you’ve previously worked as an engineer in a more mature company, you need to unlearn some things about technical debt and architectural improvements. There is a time and place for those things, and it’s usually after product/market fit is established.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Should we be scared of ChatGPT?
Answer: ChatGPT is not a revolution in and of itself. It's another incremental improvement in the GPT-3 series from OpenAI. ChatGPT is basically a fine-tuned version of InstructGPT, which has been the best version of GPT-3 until now. In fact, the latest version of InstructGPT, called davinci-003, was also announced last week. That model is about as good as ChatGPT, but it has been fine-tuned to take instructions, while ChatGPT has been fine-tuned for conversations. However, no one is talking about that model (well, no one except me), since it's not freely available and doesn't have a simple chat window interface. But despite being incremental improvements, these latest models (coined GPT3.5) are clearly much better than what we had just a year ago. If you sum up everything that's happened in 2022, especially with generative language and image models, this has probably been the most transformative year in AI ever. The GPT3.5 models have mindblowing capabilities, especially when it comes to generating code. They can develop working programs in pretty much any programming language. Just look at the example in this blog post where someone makes ChatGPT act as the terminal of a virtual machine and makes it call ChatGPT and instruct it to make a virtual machine inside the virtual machine. Truly a mindfuck of a blog post and a brilliant exploit of the model. So should we be scared? I think it's too early yet. We are still in control and will hopefully continue to be. However, we should also recognize that AI models like these will transform our society in ways that we probably can't even imagine yet. We have barely scratched the surface. In the next few years, we'll see a mad rush to build tools on top of these models that will change society as we know it. There will be tools that do your homework. In all the subjects. There will be no-code tools that can create entire websites with only human language instruction. In another 10 years, you probably can't survive as a programmer if you're not utilizing AI. That's how big of a deal it is. The future of AI is both mindblowing and terrifying. But I'm mostly optimistic that we will harness this new power for good.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What commands in a chatbot or GPT3 could be used to predict the likelihood of future events?
Answer: Ironically, this is one of the worst use cases for a large language model like GPT-3. I say ironic, because a Generative Pretrained Transformer is still a predictive machine learning model. However, what it’s trying to predict is the next word in a sentence. It’s not trying to predict the future. GPT-3 is excellent at a wide variety of NLP tasks, like text generation, text summarization, text classification, information retrieval, question and answering, translation, named entity recognition, sentiment analysis and so on. It can even perform more high-level tasks like writing computer programs or solving math puzzles. But it does all of these by predicting what word comes next in the document at hand.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What do you want to criticize about Quora?
Answer: Quora hasn’t been able to effectively monetize its user base. Why should we care, you might ask. The thing is, a social network is only as good as the content produced by its users. If it can monetize those users, it can also provide incentive programs for creators to produce engaing, high-quality content. This has worked very well for YouTube and Twitch, where the content quality has actually increased over time, with the rise of professional content creators. Quora doesn’t really have such an incentive structure. Yes, it has the Quora+ revenue sharing program, but the payments are so laughable that no one really bothers with it. As a result, there are no professional content creators, and Quora’s content quality has actually decreased instead. The problem is that Quora’s yearly revenue was only around $20 million in 2018 and probably not drastically higher now (see my reply to one of the comments), which is not enough to provide proper writer incentives. YouTube’s revenue is $28 billion. Perhaps YouTube is not a fair comparison. But even Medium, which is more of a direct competitor, has a larger revenue than Quora with a much smaller user base. Medium is able to reward its writers with meaningful monetization, and it shows in the quality. In the early days of Quora, it was a great place where intellectuals gathered to share interesting insights. But the natural tendency of social networks is to degenerate as they grow. Unless the users are incentivized to provide quality content.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How powerful is Elon Musk?
Answer: My gut feeling says he is the third most powerful person in the world after Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. There is immense power in his net worth alone. With Tesla and SpaceX, he is already a dominant player in both automotive and space, with the potential to increase his dominance in the years to come. While his net worth has taken a hit following the recession in the tech industry, he is still the richest person in the world, and his overall influence has increased after he acquired Twitter.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Why hasn't the problem of self-driving cars been solved yet? Is it because like most of math, it has no analytical solutions?
Answer: I'll answer this from a computational AI perspective. First of all, self-driving can't be solved with an expert system. For that, the problem space is just too great. When you think you've solved 90% of the edge cases, there is a mountain of edge cases you haven't thought about just waiting to blow up in your face. It never ends. Deep learning is currently the most promising approach to reach level 5 self-driving. Tesla is all-in on this. They use active learning to collect more training data by relying on a set of cleverly constructed triggers that detect problematic situations in their live fleet. However, that training data still needs human labeling. Tesla has ~1000 human labelers and they're still not remotely close to level 5, which tells me that this approach probably doesn't scale. The challenge with deep learning is that it requires extremely dense sampling of the problem space. You can employ 100,000 labelers and collect data from 100 million cars, but will it be enough? Nobody knows. There have been lofty promises that self-driving would be solved within a few years, but that was basically just marketing. Perhaps we need to mass-deploy car-to-car communication for self-driving to work. That will take a looong time.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How important do you think the SOLID principles are?
Answer: I think they’re somewhere between totally unimportant and interesting from a historical perspective. The SOLID principles were written down when dinosaurs roamed the Earth. One of those dinosaurs was named Uncle Bob. This was back when Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) was the next big thing, and the good uncle had a rather dogmatic approach to OOP. He felt very strongly that everyone should write squeaky Clean Code™. According to Uncle Bob, this is what an optimal function should look like: Paraphrasing based on my memory of examples from Clean Code. Any function that was longer than one line should be refactored into multiple functions, and any variable name that was shorter than 20 characters should be refactored into a novel. Half of the SOLID principles could be summed up as “use interfaces”, which is fairly obvious once you have more than one month of experience as a software developer. The Single-Responsibility Principle is kind of useful as a general guideline, but in practice we end up breaking it all the time. Besides, no one seems to agree on what it actually means. Responsibility for what? Then there's the Liskov Substitution Principle. No one knows what the hell that means unless they read the Wikipedia page 5 minutes ago. Personally, I believe in a different principle called GSD: Get Shit Done. Software development is very much a practical endeavour. We use our real-world experience to make constant tradeoffs. It’s a good idea to aim for readable, maintainable code, but at the end of the day the goal is to ship products. If you try to make your code perfect, you will end up in refactoring hell.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: This question is for the people who work in the tech industry, What are your thoughts on Elon Musk Twitter layoffs?
Answer: It's a fascinating experiment on a massive scale. What happens if you abruptly remove 90% of the workforce at a huge tech company with thousands of employees? As far as I'm aware, this has never been done before. According to popular belief, an internet company of that scale needs thousands of employees to function properly. Personally, I don't believe a one-product company like Twitter needs more than a few hundred, as long as there is a no-nonsense culture that emphasizes getting shit done. But that remains to be seen. I agree with the widely held opinion that Musk executed this restructuring in a clumsy and haphazard manner. The selection process for who to lay off seemed random and nonsensical. But it just might work.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What did Elon Musk do right with Paypal, SpaceX, and Tesla that he hasn't done with Twitter so far? Or are the situations so different that anything he would have learned with those companies wouldn't translate to Twitter?
Answer: Elon is running Twitter according to his beloved First Principles Thinking, just like he has done with Tesla and SpaceX. In the words of the man himself: First principles is a physics way of looking at the world. You boil things down to the most fundamental truths and then reason up from there. With this philosophy, you strip away all the non-essential features and make the core thing work as efficiently as possible by optimizing and automating the hell out of it. This is why the Tesla interior has no buttons and knobs and why Starship is over a hundred times cheaper than competing launch systems. This is exactly what he's planning to do with Twitter. When Elon took over the company, it had 7500 employees, out of which around 3000 were software engineers. Tesla has 300 software and hardware engineers on its Autopilot system. So it's definitely possible to run a much tighter ship. He has already reduced the workforce by something like 80%, a combination of layoffs and people who resigned because they didn't want to be a part of Elon's hardcore work demands (or perhaps disagreed with his vision for the company). He's also planning to strip down the technical architecture, which is totally in line with his philosophy. It's too early to tell if any of this will actually work. Elon has never taken over a company as mature as Twitter before. And a social network is quite different from the companies he's run before. It's unclear if the radical changes he's introducing in such a short time will benefit the company in the long run. Things seem out of control at the moment, but I honestly wouldn't be surprised if Twitter comes stronger out of this and turns profitable in 2023. So far, the people betting against Elon Musk haven't been doing too well.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Will Node.js replace many backend technologies?
Answer: Node.js was all the rage around 2015, when the MEAN stack (MongoDB, Express.js, Angular.js and Node.js) was the latest hotness. The idea of using JavaScript and JSON across the entire stack was compelling. Node runs on the V8 engine, which is also what Chrome runs on. So now you only needed to learn one language to be a fullstack developer. Of course, the problem with that strategy is that JavaScript is an awful language, especially on the backend, with its lack of type safety and numerous design quirks. As many development teams learned the hard way, shoehorning MongoDB into every application wasn't the best of ideas either. It can be a good fit for storing independent collections of documents, but most applications are dominated by relational data, and Mongo is just not a good fit for that. In addition, React took over from Angular as the most popular frontend framework. Due to all of this, the MEAN stack quickly fell out of fashion. Node is still used along with its package manager npm in most frontend projects. In many ways, npm turned out to be more important than Node itself. Node as a backend language is far from dead. But it was never able to challenge the dominance of Java and C#.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: A host of tech companies, like Twitter, Meta, Lyft and Stripe, have recently announced hiring freezes or job cuts. Why are we seeing this sudden wave of tech layoffs?
Answer: The market for tech stocks has crashed. We haven't seen a recession in tech this bad since the financial crisis of 2008, or perhaps even since the dot-com bubble burst at the turn of the century. Why has this happened? That's too complicated to explain in a single sentence. Some of the dynamics involved are so complicated that we don't fully understand them. The stock market is a complex beast. But it's probably not wrong to say that it has to do with macroeconomic effects resulting from the Covid-19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine. In any case, trillions of dollars in value has been shaved off. The inevitable consequence of such a dramatic downswing is that companies need to lay off large numbers of employees in order to manage costs and avoid bankruptcies. I can tell you from first-hand experience that the downswing is also affecting unlisted startups seeking investors. During a recession like this, VC funding dries up. As a result, we've had to lay off a number of people too.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Why would White play 2.a3 as their 2nd move in the Sicilian Defense? It's not an accepted opening and I see no benefits. How would you go about strategizing a reply, as black?
Answer: The 2.a3 Sicilian is a more sound version of the Wing Gambit (2.b4). White still inteds to gambit the pawn with b4, but on more favorable terms. It leads to fun positions that aren’t well known. Perfect for blitz games or even classical games if you want to surprise your opponent. Here is one sample line: 1.e4 c5 2.a3 Nc6 3.b4 cxb4 4.axb4 Nxb4 Accepting the gambit. This is very risky. 5.d4 d5 6.c3 Nc6 7.exd5 Qxd5 8.Na3! Now Nb5 is coming whatever black does. Nf6? Already losing. 9.Nb5 Qd8 10.d5! The pawn is poisoned. 10…Nxd5 11.Qxd5 Qxd5 12.Nc7+ wins a piece. Ne5 11.Bf4 Nfd7 12.Nf3 f6 13.Nfd4 Nb6 14.Bxe5 fxe5 15.Qh5+ g6 16.Qxe5 1–0 I’m not exaggerating when I say I’ve reached this position in blitz games hundreds of times. I even beat former world number four GM Ulf Andersson in this line in a prize money tournament. And I reached it in a classical game once. Here is a fun classical game I played in Gibraltar in 2007. My opponent was rated around 2000. 1.e4 c5 2.a3 3.b4 cxb4 4.axb4 Bxb4 This is another way of accepting the gambit. Also risky. 5.Bb2 Nf6 6.e5 Nd5 7.c4 Nb6 8.Ra3!? A shocking move! White sacrifices an exchange to keep the white king stuck in the center. If the sacrifice is not accepted, white will swing the rook over to g3. Bxa3 9.Bxa3 Qh4? After this, white is already winning. The king and queen are too exposed. 10.Nc3 Nc6 11.Nf3 Qh5 12.d4 f6 13.Nb5! Kf7 14.exf6 Kxf6 15.g4! Opening even more lines. Qxg4 Black is up the exchange and two pawns, but his queen will be trapped. 16.Nd6! a5 17.Rg1 Qf4 18.c5 Nd5 19.Bc1 And there goes the queen! Trapped in the middle of the board. Nc3 20.Bxf4 Nxd1 21.Bg5+ Kg6 22.Nh4+ Kh5 23.Be2# A picturesque checkmate. Games like these is the reason I play chess. The best way to counter 2.a3 with black is simply to play sensible developing moves instead of accepting the gambit. It becomes a normal Sicilian where white will try to claim that the inclusion of a3 is useful, while black will try to claim that it’s not. It’s when black players try to punish this provocative move that they go astray.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: In the Sicilian opening, after 4. Nxd4, why is there no standard line 4… Nxd4? I’d think forcing white’s queen to the center would give black good opportunities.
Answer: 4…Nxd4 is a loss of tempo.. Before that capture, white and black have developed one piece each. After the capture, white has developed the queen while black has not developed a single piece. The disadvantage of developing the queen too early is that it can usually be chased around by minor pieces. For each developing move black can make that attacks the queen so that it needs to move, black gains a tempo. However, that is not easily possible here. Black could play e6, Ne7 and Nc6, or e6, Qc7, Nf6 and Bc5. But both those plans are very slow.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: When AI becomes super intelligent which millennium prize problem will it work on the most seeing a potential solution?
Answer: In all likelihood, we will still be in control of the AI even after it becomes superintelligent. So obviously, once we have AI capable of tackling unsolved problems in mathematics, we will try to make it solve all the millennium problems. They're all important, so why limit ourselves? The question is rather, which problems are the most likely to be solved by AI first? I would think a problem like Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness would lend itself better to computational methods and might be easier to solve using AI than let's say P vs. NP, which seems to require some sort of paradigm shift. But I'm not really a mathematician, so I'm shooting from the hip here. In any case, I think this will happen much sooner than people expect. I don't even think we need general intelligence to make it happen. I mean, look at what DeepMind did with AlphaFold. It practically solved the protein folding problem. Of course, there is still a leap from that to a formal mathematical proof, but I don't think it's as large as people tend to assume.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Why was Twitter worth $44 billion to Elon Musk when he says it is losing $4 million a day?
Answer: Twitter is making north of a billion dollars in revenue per quarter. For a large social network, that’s not best in class, but not terrible either. Considering the company only has one product to deal with, it can obviously turn profitable if it wants to with that kind of revenue. However, running a large technology company is usually a balancing act between optimizing for profit and optimizing for growth. Twitter has mostly optimized for growth throughout its 16-year history. It was only profitable for a brief period of time in 2018–2019. Overall, it has been operating at a net loss of over a billion dollars. However, Twitter’s growth has been stale for the last decade. The strategy to invest heavily in the product hasn’t been working. Musk clearly disagrees with that strategy and has a plan to turn the company profitable. That plan is textbook corporate restructuring: Using layoffs to cut costs. Personally, I believe that’s the right move. It’s almost certainly going to work unless Musk manages to piss off all his advertisers and users in the process. So, to the question. Is Twitter worth $44 billion? Not even close. There is wide agreement among analysts that Musk overpaid by a long shot. Twitter’s shareholders didn’t want to sell to him, but his mind was set. It became a question of personal prestige. So he made them an offer they couldn’t refuse. As gross as it sounds, overpaying by a few billion will hardly make a dent in Elon Musk’s net worth.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What's faster, or easier, get 10,000 people pay $100 or get one investor put $1 million?
Answer: If you get 10,000 people to pay you $100, it means you have a repeatable, scalable business model. That means you have struck gold. Certainly not easy at all. If you get money from an investor, well, you just have an investor. In most cases, your startup will fail and the money will run out. Not saying it's easy to get $1 million from an investor, but it's a hell of a lot easier than getting 10,000 customers.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Mr. Musk will fire all those employees who don't meet the required deadline. As a senior engineer, what is your opinion about it?
Answer: Jack Dorsey who founded Twitter is a highly capable engineer and entrepreneur, but not the right person to run a large business. He cared more about idealism and politics than about turning the company profitable. In his own words: As a result of his mismanagement, Twitter has only been able to turn a profit in two of its fiscal years (2018 and 2019). That is simply inexcusable for a company that has been around for 16 years and has hundreds of millions of users. Prior to the Musk takeover, Twitter had 7500 employees. You don't strictly need 7500 people to run a relatively simple social network like Twitter. Not even close. At this point, laying off large portions of staff was the only sensible business decision. Of course, in typical Musk fashion, the world's richest man hasn't exactly gone about this in the most delicate way. Empathy isn’t his strong suit, and he doesn't care if he hurts thousands of people in the process. He has basically ordered the workforce to work 80+ hour weeks, or else they'll be fired. A large number of people will undoubtedly suffer from burnout and incredible stress as a result of this high-pressure situation. I personally think this way of handling the situation is way too harsh on the employees, even if layoffs were inevitable. I also think there must have been much better ways to filter out the high performers.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: If everyone had a chess coach from the start, would there be more chess prodigies (almost all chess "prodigies" have had a coach which helped them develop)?
Answer: I believe the role of coaches in the development of chess prodigies is highly exaggerated. I coached a genuine child prodigy, Aryan Tari, who later went on to become world junior champion. When I tried to teach Aryan how to checkmate with bishop and knight, he saw the moves faster than I could show them to him. He was six years old at the time. His brain learned at a faster pace than anything I've ever seen. Our sessions were more like me stimulating his brain by having him sit in front of a chess board than me actually teaching him something. I could probably have shown him anything and he would have learned from it. His brain was a sponge that soaked up patterns. I believe Aryan improved the most by simply playing a ton of online blitz. My impact as a coach was minimal. Magnus Carlsen was also mostly self-taught. He had a few coaches, but would usually surpass them within very short time. Probably the most impactful thing anyone ever did to Magnus’ learning trajectory was to give him unlimited access to the chess library of GM Simen Agdestein. He basically read all the books there and remembered every position of every game he read about. When you have a memory like that, you don't need a coach. You just need more books. Bobby Fischer was another child prodigy that was mostly self-taught. Sure, he had a few coaches here and there, but like Magnus, he would routinely surpass them. Fischer actually learned a lot by playing against himself, when he was at home and had no one to play against. For mere mortals, this training technique simply wouldn't work. But again, his brain just soaked up the patterns. It didn't matter how he was exposed to them. The truth is that while it can certainly be beneficial to have a chess coach, the top prodigies are just extremely intelligent outliers that learn in ways that the rest of us can't.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Does AlphaZero use an opening book?
Answer: No. The Zero in AlphaZero comes from the fact that the model was given no prior knowledge on how to play the game. That is, the rules were encoded into the model. In principle it could have learned to play without even knowing the rules, but they were implemented for simplicity's sake. The AlphaZero research project showed that a reinforcement learning agent trained without prior knowledge yielded superior results to the one that was bootstrapped with human games.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: If Evariste Galois understood that his chances at the duel were not high, why couldn't he simply not show up?
Answer: Evariste Galois was 20 years old when he died. A mere child. Boys that age, no matter how intelligent, are incredibly immature. It's only when approaching 30 that their brain matures to the point that we can consider them grown up men. If I think back at all the stupid stuff I did myself at the age of 20, it's a wonder I survived at all. Of course, the contradiction with Galois is that his contributions to mathematics at that age was already greater than what the vast majority of mathematicians are able to achieve within a lifetime. Galois was clearly a genius, but he was also a troubled mind. His father had committed suicide when he was 17, and this affected Evariste deeply. Some time later, he attempted to take his own life by stabbing himself. He had lost his beloved father, his mathematical ideas were being rejected, he was being (at least in his own mind) politically persecuted and he had few real friends. That's the place he was coming when showing up to that fateful duel. Unlike the extremely lethal rapier duels of the 17th and 18th century, the pistol duels of Galois’ time actually had a fairly good chance of survival, with as few as 5% or less of them resulting in a lethal outcome. Most ended in misses from both sides. Duels were mostly a way to gain “satisfaction”. Galois had entered a love affair with the fiancée of his opponent, and this was a way to resolve the offense. If he had not shown up for the duel, it's likely that something bad would have happened to him in any case. At the same time, Galois clearly realized there was some risk, considering the famous notes he hastily wrote down the night before. In the lower left of this page, we can see the words “Une femme”, referring to his lover.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Has Stockfish or any other top chess program performed an analysis of the Karpov-Kasparov matches? For me, that was the pinnacle of chess, though probably Carlsen would beat either; (i.e. was Muhammed Ali better than Joe Louis, etc.)
Answer: Yes, Lichess did this with Stockfish 14 NNUE last year. The results are summarized in this box plot. It looks like the five Kasparov-Karpov matches played between 1984 and 1990 were the most accurate world championship matches up until that point. An outlier is Capablanca - Lasker in 1921 which surprisingly had a similiar centipawn loss to the K-K matches. As you can see, the playing quality in world championship matches has improved drastically in the 21st century with the advent of strong computer engines. The 2014 return match between Carlsen and Anand was an outlier that had several huge blunders. But the last three matches have been the strongest in history, with last year’s match between Carlsen and Nepomniachtchi being the strongest ever in terms of centipawn loss. The slight caveat is that centipawn loss is somewhat sensitive to playing style, and Carlsen’s style is better suited to produce very accurate play than Kasparov’s.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What is your prediction for the Hans Niemann lawsuit against Magnus Carlsen, Hikaru Nakamura, Chess.com, et al.?
Answer: The entire thing seems so amateurish that you'd think it was a joke. First of all, he's suing for $400 million, which is a ridiculous amount. He's including Magnus Carlsen, Play Magnus, chess.com, Danny Rensch personally, and he threw in Hikaru Nakamura for good measure. The lawsuit contains emotional color commentary such as this passage: Notorious for his inability to cope with defeat, Carlsen snapped. Enraged that the young Niemann, fully 12 years his junior, dared to disrespect the “King of Chess”, and fearful the young prodigy would further blemish his multi-million dollar brand by beating him again, Carlsen vicously and maliciously retaliated against Niemann by falsely accusing Niemann, without any evidence, of somehow cheating during their in-person game and demanding that the organizers of the Sinquefield Cup immediately disqualify Niemann from the tournament. It’s hard to take this stuff seriously. I'd be surprised if Niemann can successfully sue for damages from Carlsen or any of the other defendants. Even if he can, it would be for a much, much smaller amount. And if he wants to have any hopes of winning the case, he needs to up his game substantially from the sort of argumentation he's provided here.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What keeps back-end developers from calling themselves full stack developers? Don't most of them know some front-end techniques?
Answer: I learned the basics of HTML and developed my first websites with Java applets and JavaScript 1.0 back in the mid-90s. When I started pursuing software development as a career much later, I touched on jQuery and Backbone briefly, before learning Angular and TypeScript. In my previous job, we used Vue, and now I’m using React. I’ve been around the block, but I still wouldn’t call myself a full stack developer, for a few reasons: All in all, I'd rather just call myself a software engineer and try to highlight the things I'm good at and that I enjoy.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: In chess, to win by flagging is the strategy of trying to win by making the opponent run out of time. For classical time controls it is not viable. Opposite for bullet. What is the threshold of time controls where forcing a flag starts to make sense?
Answer: To pressure your opponent on the clock is a viable strategy in any time control. In the 2013 Candidates Tournament, Vassily Ivanchuk lost four games on time. The time control in that tournament was 2 hours for the first 40 moves, followed by 1 hour for the next 20 moves and finally 15 minutes with 30-second increments for the remainder of the game. He got himself into huge time trouble in complicated positions and couldn’t make 40 moves within 2 hours. This is rare at the top level, but it can happen even there. With a 30-second increment for the entire game, you can’t really flag someone, but you can still put a lot of pressure on them if they’re playing only on increments. What doesn’t work is to play speculative, or outright bad, moves in an attempt to flag an opponent. That will backfire even in 1-minute games. The smart way to use the clock as a weapon is to play sound, aggressive moves relatively quickly.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Will India get another chess player as good as Vishy Anand?
Answer: Anand is a hard act to follow for sure, but let me say this: I would be very surprised if we don't see another world champion from India within this century. The Indian chess scene is booming out of control. It's just getting stronger and stronger. When Anand became a GM in 1988, he was the first ever from India. Now, the country has 75 GMs! Amazingly, Anand is still the highest rated of these(!), but that won't last very long. There are several teenage prodigies knocking on the doorsteps. Gukesh D is world number 18 with a FIDE rating of 2732. The kid is only 16 years old! He's about as strong as Magnus Carlsen, Wei Yi and Alireza Firouzja were at the same age Arjun Eirigaisi has shot up the rating list like a rocket in the last couple of years. He's a little older at 19, but his progress has been phenomenal. He's currently world number 21 with a rating of 2728. Praggnanandhaa is a little lower rated at 2687, but anyone who's seen him play knows he's the real deal. He's been dominating online rapid tournaments lately, and is currently second behind Magnus on the Champions Chess Tour. He's just 17. Any of these kids could become world champion within the next decade or two. And others will follow in their wake. India is becoming a superpower in chess.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Who do you think is the favorite to win the WCC, Ding or Nepomniatchi?
Answer: It's very evenly matched on paper. It's the world number two against the world number three. But it's also a clash of styles. Nepomniachtchi (2793) has improved a lot in recent years. He's on his highest rating ever right now. He has won two consecutive candidates tournaments, which is something very few players have ever been able to do. He won the last one with 9.5/14, an impressive 1.5 points ahead of second-placed Ding. Nepo's greatest strength is also his greatest weakness. He plays aggressively and confidently, using the clock as a weapon. Sometimes that works brilliantly and he goes on a tear. Other times it backfires, because he perplays too quickly and makes blunders. Ding (2811) is a totally different type of player from Nepo. He's stability personified. He rarely wins big tournaments, but then again, he rarely performs poorly either. He went on a 100-game unbeaten streak in 2017-2018, which was the world record until Magnus Carlsen beat it next year. That speaks volumes about his consistency. Ding's current rating is close to his personal best of 2816. He hasn't been rated below 2790 since 2018. Prediction: I would probably give the slightest of edges to Nepo, given that he has more experience playing for the world championship and his current form. Also, he just seems to have more of a killer instinct. But it go either way. If it goes to tie-break, the match is still wide open. Nepo is an excellent rapid and blitz player, but so is Ding.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Do you think all the top 20 chess players are geniuses?
Answer: Genius is an ambiguous term that people never seem to agree about. Here's one definition: an exceptionally intelligent person or one with exceptional skill in a particular area of activity. According to that, all the top 20 chess players are clearly geniuses. When some people think of geniuses, however, they think of a renaissance man, or polymath, like Leonardo Da Vinci. The top chess players are not like that. Modern top-level chess is such an all-consuming occupation that the elite players have little time and energy left to really excel at anything else. There's also a big difference between them. Magnus Carlsen, Levon Aronian, Fabiano Caruana, Garry Kasparov and a few others seem like they have an intellectual capacity that extends beyond the 64 squares of the chess board, but I wouldn't say that's true for all top players. Vassily Ivanchuk has often been called a genius, but sometimes he seems more like an idiot savant. Sergey Karjakin seems particularly dense to me. He's like a mouth breather that happens to be good at chess. So no, I wouldn't say that they're all geniuses, but they're all chess geniuses.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Any opinion on AI becoming global revolution as well as threat to us after Elon Musk warns about AI?
Answer: I'm with John Carmack[1] on this. I don't believe in fast takeoffs. His view is that once we have AI on the level of a learning-impaired toddler, AGI will be inevitable, and at that point we can start to worry about existential threats. We’ll have plenty of time to handle it then. I largely agree. There has been lots of talk about the superintelligence singularity. Once AI reaches human-level general intelligence, it will magically create superintelligences in a self-reinforcing loop that spins out of control in an instant. That’s a fascinating thought experiment from the science fiction literature. It’s just not how the world works in practice. In the real world, there are always engineering constraints and bottlenecks. In theory, we have the technology to build a city on Mars, or a transatlantic tunnel with trains running at hypersonic speeds. But it hasn’t happened yet. At the moment, we’re struggling to create convincing narrow AI and have succeeded in some fields, like imaging, language and gaming. We’re nowhere near general capabilities. While we clearly need to be serious about a number of ethical concerns related to AI, there is no reason to lose sleep over doomsday scenarios just yet.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is Musk a loudmouthed bullshitting ignoramus about AI? Here's a $500,000 bet he can take to prove he isn't. Will he take it though?
Answer: Is Elon a loudmouth? Certainly. Is Elon a bullshitter? Well, sometimes he makes bold claims that he believes may become true if everything goes right. Examples: And then he makes those claims with conviction, as if they were already true. This is how you generate enthusiasm around a business. All founders do it to some extent. He just does it better than everyone else. Is Elon an ignoramus? Definitely not. I used to think Elon was primarily a business person. Because how can someone conceivably run two companies like Tesla and SpaceX, be a public figure, and simultaneously have a deep understanding of the technical aspects of rocket science, AI, electrical engineering and all these other things? It just seemed too unbelievable to me. Having now seen a number of interviews and podcasts with him, I've come to the realization that the man is just wired differently. He's somehow able to combine to combine an insane work ethic with a deep understanding of physics and engineering and incredible business skills. A true genius if you ask me.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: The 2020 Tesla model 3 SR+ RWD is the slowest and least powerful Tesla on the market. It does 0-60 in 5.3 seconds with a top speed (software limited) of 227 km/h. Is this above average or impressive performance?Could it outrun most conventional cars?
Answer: Definitely above average, though my home country of Norway gives a glimpse into what the not-too-distant future will look like. Electric engines are really common here, with >80% of new cars sold being EVs. My Volvo XC90 hybrid does 0-100 kmh in 5.5 seconds despite being a 2.5 ton 7-seater, and there are tons of faster cars on the roads. Teslas and Porsche Taycan will generally smoke everything else. Jaguar I-Pace does 0-100 in 4.8. Hell, even a sensible car like the Toyota Rav4 hybrid does 0-100 in 6.2. 10 years from now, 400 hp will be as common as 150 hp used to be. Basically all cars will be much faster than they need to be. Top speed? Not so sure. Volvo has started limiting all their cars to 180 kmh, and I expect other brands to follow suit.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Why did 'House of the Dragon' change actors?
Answer: The way they did it was just awkward to me. From one episode to the next they replaced Milly Alcroft, who is 22 years old and played the young Princess Rhaenyra Targaryen, with Emma D’Arcy, who is 30. Why? To make her look 10 years older, yes, but you can easily do that with makeup. 22 and 30 is just not that different. Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Software-as-a-Service (SaaS): What are some of the skills that every SaaS startup founder must have?
Answer: Patience It takes a long time to build these things. The ironic thing is that the faster the startup grows, the faster it will lose money in the short term. There’s usually a relatively high cost associated with acquiring SaaS customers and the payback period may be a year or longer. That means a successful SaaS company will go through a cash flow trough. The company will have to crawl its way back from that hole before it can explode into the stratosphere. The upside is that SaaS customers can have very long lifecycles and bring in expanding revenue. People used to think internet companies couldn’t last, but that turned out to be wrong. Salesforce was one of the first SaaS companies back in 1999, and it’s still going strong. Some of their customer relationships have lasted over two decades. But yeah, you definitely need patience as a SaaS startup founder. You’re going to have to invest a significant portion of your life in something that may or may not succeed. And even if it does succeed, the first few years are mostly going to suck.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What do you think of Carlsen's statement on Twitter regarding Niemann?
Answer: For the record, here is the statement: Magnus is mostly just stating what the chess world has already inferred: He also discloses that he has more to say depending on explicit permission from Niemann, presumably because of legal threats. What do I think? At this point, I am convinced that Niemann has indeed cheated more than he has admitted to. I also strongly believe he has cheated over the board on several occasions, having seen the analysis from Andrii Punin [1], Yosha Iglesias [2]and Fabiano Caruana [3]. I still think that he most likely didn't cheat in the Sinquefield Cup. It's just a difficult tournament to do it in with all the security, and the win against Magnus didn't seem particularly suspicious (aside from being a win with the black pieces against Magnus). If he did cheat in that game, it must have been for just a few moves, because he played far from perfect. Of course, that could still be enough to tip the game in his favor. I think that Magnus could have handled the situation better by making a public statement earlier, to avoid all the unresolved tension we've had these last weeks. At the same time, I respect him for taking a strong stance on cheating in chess. Like he says, it is an existential threat to the game we all love. Overall, this tweet brings very little new information to the table, and I suspect there is more going on behind the scenes. This story is not over.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is it possible to become an FM (FIDE Master) when I start learning chess at the age of 25?
Answer: I don't know of anyone who actually did this, but I'll give you a perspective based on my own experience. I might have reached FM if I had continued studying chess with the same level of intensity in my late 20s as I did in my early 20s, but I don't know that for sure. Considering I started significantly younger than 25 (albeit still old by chess standards) and worked so hard at it for several years, I would say this: Unless your pattern recognition and memory capabilities are genius level, you would probably have to work as least as hard as I did (5 hours a day) over a ten-year period to reach 2300. It is really difficult to reach that level in the first place, and the vast majority of those who pull it off have the advantage that they started learning in childhood.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Which is better in chess, an anti cheat algorithm that catches 100% of cheaters but produces 0.01% false positives or one that produces no false positives but misses 0.01% of cheaters?
Answer: I think it's pretty clear that a false positive is worse than a false negative. If someone has devoted themself to chess and you take that away from them while also publicly shaming them, you could essentially ruin their life. As a side note, those are totally unrealistic numbers. It's fully possible to cheat without getting caught. It's rare that someone gets away with it, but I still believe it's a lot more common than people think. We'd probably be lucky to catch 99% of cheaters, let alone 99.99%.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Why are the estimates for the start of humanity so varied, such as 1 million years ago, 200,000 years ago or 60,000, or 10,000 B.C.? I don't think scientists are guessing, but how can they come up with these figures?
Answer: Our increasing understanding of human evolution in recent years is making it harder to put an exact date on the start of humanity. We tend to think of modern humans as an end state of evolution, but that couldn't be further from the truth. After we were able to map essentially the entire human genome in the late 1990s and early 2000s, a number of startling discoveries were made. Did you know that the “modern” humans who lived 5000 years ago were genetically closer to the last neanderthals who lived 30,000 years ago than they were to the humans who live today? [1] Yes, that's right. The people who built the pyramids and invented writing were closer to homo neanderthalis, a type of human by many considered to be a different species than us. Anatomically modern We have found more than 300,000 years old remains of what are considered “anatomically modern humans”. That just means that our skeletons look the same. Jebel Irhoud-1, who lived 300,000 years ago, may have had a face that looked like ours, but was also quite different from us genetically. Accelerating evolution Around 10,000 years ago, the last ice age ended and we started settling down in farms. Agriculture led to an explosion in population growth, and the speed of human evolution accelerated to two orders of magnitude greater than it was prior. I personally have blue eyes and can digest the lactose in milk. None of those traits existed in humans 10,000 years ago. We are now almost 8 billion people on Earth. Human evolution is happening at a breakneck speed, faster than ever before. Evolution never rests. It's not merely an adaptation to the environment, but also randomness. When you sample over 100 million new humans every year, a lot of random traits pop up indeed. So when did “humanity” start? We can put an arbitrary start date on it all we want, but evolution happens continuously, not discretely.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Would you personally prefer to watch a 2023 FIDE World Cup of Ian Nepomniachtchi vs. Ding Liren or Magnus Carlsen vs. Hans Moke Niemann?
Answer: I would prefer to watch a world championship match that has the two strongest players in the world or at the very least the strongest one against another top player with a realistic shot at the title. If it's not clear who the strongest player in the world is, the match should be between two players that could claim to be. Right now, it's clear as day who the strongest player is, so any match without Magnus is anticlimactic. Unfortunately, Ding vs. Nepo is just not that interesting. Neither of them have ever been close to Magnus, like Caruana and Aronian was in the past. Carlsen - Niemann would be sort of fine, except that Niemann isn't strong enough to pose a real challenge to Magnus. But at least that match has the world number one, so I would rather take that one.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Do startup founders and CEOs worth 1bn or more get to sit and do nothing all day?
Answer: They could if they want to, but very few of them do. There is a reason someone becomes a billionaire founder in the first place. These people are workaholics, with an intense drive and passion for their work that you'll hardly find anywhere else. So what do startup founders do when they sell their company? They move on the next one. Once someone has succeeded wildly with one startup, they have several unfair advantages when they start their next one. Some of the most successful companies ever have been started by people who were already wealthy and had already started companies before.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What do you think about Magnus Carlsen resigning after 2 moves against Hans Niemann?
Answer: Magnus is clearly making a statement. That he doesn't want to play with cheaters. The moment Magnus resigned. Niemann is a proven cheater in online tournaments. Even after getting caught, he has been a repeat offender over several years. You could say “it's only online”, but this downplays the severity of his actions too much. Some of the tournaments he cheated in had significant prize money. What he has been doing is undermining the game of chess in a bad way. Even worse, it looks quite likely that Niemann cheated in over-the -board tournaments to achieve his final Grandmaster norm and secure the GM title. Analysis has surfaced that seems to show this convincingly. If true, this means he obtained the title illegitimately, and has gotten away with it (so far). There should be some form of repercussions. On the other hand, I don't think Magnus is handling this in the most elegant way. Resigning after one move with no explanation is just passive-aggressive. It seems that Niemann got in Magnus’ head with his trash-talk, and now Magnus has seen red. What he should have done in my opinion is to come right out and say it. “Niemann is a cheater and I don't want to play with him”. I believe he would have garnered more respect from the chess community that way. This is the second top-level tournament that's being disrupted by this unresolved drama. The chess world needs some form of resolution. Even if Niemann has cheated several times, he is still young, and he should get a chance to redeem himself. All this drama can be very damaging to him, both as a chess player and as a human being. He deserves a fair trial, not to be pilloried.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Why are the most startups in Silicon Valley looking for valuable exit instead of creating the meaningful products for general public? Is it the more of reflection of our society's obsession with money?
Answer: If someone offered you a billion dollars, would you take it? Because that's what a valuable exit can actually mean for some founders. But how does a startup get there? Yes, there are a few exceptions where startups get to billion-dollar valuations without providing any value whatsoever (Theranos comes to mind). But in the vast, vast majority of cases, a company gets a valuable exit because it created something meaningful of real value. Also, an “exit” isn't actually an exit. It just means the company changed ownership. Some paper is shuffled around, but the company keeps going (again, in the vast majority of cases). One exit strategy is an IPO. It's basically just a way to raise more money for the company, so it can continue to do what it's doing, at an even greater scale. Aiming for an exit as the endgame is a perfectly reasonable strategy for a founder. You're taking a huge risk to start a company in the first place, so it only makes sense that it should pay off big if you actually succeed.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Self taught developers, how did you overcome the times of self doubt and self sabotage?
Answer: There was no self-doubt when I was teaching myself how to write code, because I wasn't trying to prove anything. I was just learning some cool stuff for fun. Then I stumbled into a job where I was getting paid to do it. There was some self-doubt there for a while, with good reason. I wasn't qualified for that job at all. So what did I do? I intensified the learning process and tried to soak up as much knowledge as possible from my new colleagues while I continued to study software development on my own. Eventually, I got to a point where I could deliver software that provided some business value, and after that there was never any doubt.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: As a very good chess player, what psychologically based tricks, tactics, and traps have you found useful?
Answer: There is only one scenario in chess I can think of where I've successfully been able to trick my opponents with psychology. The scenario: The trick: I intentionally let my clock run down even further, pretending that I'm trying to find a way to play for a win, knowing full well that I have to allow the repetition. When I finally allow the draw, I'm secretly hoping that my opponent will play on. This has a very high success rate. My opponent will usually smell blood and play the suboptimal move to try to exploit my time trouble. It's a high-risk strategy, because sometimes I'll end up blundering in time trouble and lose, but I've won many games this way.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What happens when Magnus Carlsen learns shogi? Will he also become shogi champion given enough time?
Answer: Magnus already knows how to play shogi. In a podcast with Lex Friedman, he expressed his personal opinion that the pieces aren't powerful enough in shogi, and that makes it less exciting than chess to him. I have no idea how good he is at shogi, but it's also a highly competitive game, if not as competitive as chess.
