Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How does a Norwegian react if he sees cheap prices in other countries?
Answer: That's basically what we expect when travelling. No surprise there. Norway is a high-GDP country with a 25% VAT on most goods, so things are expensive. Some things like (non-electric) cars and alcohol are also taxed through the roof. In Western European countries and the United States it's usually not so much cheaper that it makes a big difference for most things you'll buy when travelling, except alcohol. In Eastern Europe, there is a big difference for sure. If you travel to Asia, Africa and South America it can get ridiculous. If I travel to low-cost countries like China or Thailand, I'll go on a shopping spree for sure. However, it has changed a bit in recent years. Inflation and a weakening of the Norwegian currency means that the difference has been reduced a lot, especially when compared to other Western European countries. This summer, I went to Denmark. While the Danish krone (DKK) used to be worth about the same as the Norwegian krone (NOK), it was now worth 1.4. For the first time in my life, I experienced that clothes were notably more expensive in another country than Norway. When I was in New York in 2014, the USD to NOK ratio was around ~5, but now it's ~10. New York already wasn't that cheap compared to Norway back then, but I imagine it would be significantly more expensive now for certain categories of goods.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Is Stockfish coded to 'see' the board as checkered?
Answer: That's a clever question. Yes, it actually does. Sort of. Stockfish uses a position encoding that's designed to be efficient and minimal, to allow the engine to calculate millions of moves per second. The encoding it uses is called a bitboard. In Stockfish's implementation of bitboards, the concept of color pops up quite frequently. More importantly, its evaluation function explicitly uses color to, for instance, penalize the side with the “wrong” bishop in opposite-colored bishop endings, depending on the configuration of the pawns. What Stockfish doesn't have is an intuitive understanding of color complex domination. This is something that expert-level (2000+) human players use a lot when evaluating positions. The core of what Stockfish does is brute-force search with some pruning to increase the search depth and a little bit of custom flavor sprinkled on top. So while a human can look at the board and instantly recognize things like “that bishop is dead”, Stockfish will need to calculate variations to come to the same conclusion. If there is some concept that's outside its search horizon or not explicitly accounted for in the evaluation function, it will simply fail to “see” it. A more promising approach to approximate human-like intuition in chess is with artificial neural networks. The breakthrough result was DeepMind's AlphaZero that was announced in 2017. It used neural networks to estimate the strength of candidate moves and Monte Carlo tree search to evaluate them. LeelaChessZero is a open-source implementation of the same idea. Again, the board encodings that these engines use are are also very compact. An important realization with AlphaZero was that the engine became stronger when it was trained from a starting point of having zero knowledge of the game except for the rules. That's where the “zero” comes from. It was simply trained by playing against itself. The amazing result was that AlphaZero seemed to play more intuitively (and also stronger) than traditional chess engines like Stockfish. In a neural-based engine, everything it “knows” about chess is inferred implicitly from the network weights. Since then, Stockfish has also started using neural networks in its evaluation function, in the version of the engine called NNUE. So the trend is to move away from handcoded expert knowledge in chess engines and rely more on machine learning. In theory, this should allow engines to “understand” that the chess board is checkered without being explicitly told so.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How would Hakon Hapnes Strand's teaching approach be if he is teaching machine learning?
Answer: I have taught machine learning to people before, but mostly as one-off introductory courses lasting a single day or a week. It's not something I do on a regular basis. In a limited time frame there is only so much you can do. My approach has been to provide a very brief theoretical introduction and jump to practical examples as soon as possible. Even if the course attendees aren't programmers, you can still give them some small code snippets to play around with. We would usually go through some samples in a Google Colab notebook, rich with visualizations and explanations. If the course lasted over several days or weeks, I would give them small homework assignments, like to clone the notebook and complete an experiment. This has worked surprisingly well even with people who have never written any code before. I think that to truly grasp the intuition behind machine learning, you simply need to try it for yourself, so my approach has been to enable that.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Should APIs be self-documenting?
Answer: Yes, but that's standard practice now with OpenAPI. I think a better question is whether you need additional documentation beyond the auto-generated Swagger page. The answer is, sometimes. If it's a public API with lots of consumers, there should definitely be more verbose documentation. It's rare that all the endpoints are completely self-explanatory. On the other hand, if the API is just an interface between two teams who work together or between two solutions developed by the same team, I don't think it's necessary. You just ping whoever is responsible for the code and ask if you're curious about something. The self-documentation is more than enough in that case.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: How does it feel to have 20K+ followers on Quora?
Answer: Prologue: Someone requested my answer to this question, and I was surprised to find I already had a complete answer waiting for me as a draft. Well, here it is! I’m not gonna lie, it feels pretty good. Some years ago, I worked as a journalist in the local newspaper. The stories I published online would typically get a few thousand clicks. The most popular ones got 10k-20k. These days, my Quora answers routinely get thousands of views and often tens of thousands. I have several answers with over a million views each. I’m actually able to write to a larger audience on Quora than I did as a professional journalist. This feels great. To write about things I care about and actually have people read it. There are few other benefits to having many Quora followers. It doesn’t make me famous, I’m not making any money off of it and it rarely, if ever, presents me with any additional career opportunities. But that feeling of being recognized and heard is something I think we all crave.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Why do you need any kinds of "SaaS Security" if most SaaS apps live in "The Cloud" which is overall very secure?
Answer: Security needs to permeate your entire SaaS infrastructure. It’s still possible to screw up in a number of different ways even if you rely on the inherent security of managed cloud services. If you want to, you can do incredibly irresponsible things, like sending passwords in plain-text over HTTP, allowing four-digit pin codes as passwords, storing connection strings in public git repositories and so on. “The Cloud” does not prevent you from any of this. Moreover, you have a special responsibility with a multi-tenant solution like a SaaS app, because you're entrusted to handle the personal data of users across many organizations. In a previous job, we used a timesheet app where anyone could press F12 to enter Chrome DevTools and find the hourly rates of everyone in the company. Not great. You can face legal prosecution for that sort of stuff. The public cloud provides many tools that make security a lot simpler than it used to be. But you still have to use them and actually know what you're doing.

Question: If Stockfish was given 40 minutes to make 40 moves, and Magnus Carlsen 40 hours, who will win? (the machine cannot "think" while waiting for the opponent).
Answer: Stockfish would win. It's way too strong. There is a small chance that Magnus would get away with a draw, but Stockfish would win the vast majority of games. Having 40 hours for the game isn't even as big of an advantage as you'd think. There is a saying in chess: “Think long, think wrong.” It means that if you don't find the best move within the first 10-15 minutes, you probably won't find it at all. A long think is often followed by a bad move, because it means the player doesn't know what to do. You can't brute-force a complicated middlegame position. Chess is just too complex for that. Even computers can't do it. So even if you have all the time in the world, you're never going to figure out everything. Meanwhile, 40 minutes is enough for Stockfish to play way above the 3000 Elo mark. A human player has no chance to compete with that.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What is your opinion on Magnus Carlsen’s withdrawal from the Sinquefield Cup and the rumors surrounding Hans Niemann?
Answer: If Niemann cheated, then his withdrawal is totally understandable. At present, I haven’t seen any convincing evidence that suggests to me that any cheating occurred in the Sinquefield Cup. It would be pretty difficult to pull off in any case. However, Niemann has been caught cheating in online prize tournaments on several occasions. It’s also looking more and more likely that Niemann has actually cheated in over-the-board tournaments as well. This analysis is quite damning: When achieving his final GM norm in 2020, Niemann played several games where all his moves corresponded to the top line of Stockfish 12, the latest version of the strongest computer engine at the time. I should note that this guy (Ukrainian FM Andrii Punin) has an excellent track record for accurately exposing cheaters in over-the-board chess tournaments. He has previously exposed GM Max Dlugy, who coincidentally has been coaching Niemann. Alexei Shirov has also commented on this: One possibility here is that even if Niemann wasn’t cheating in the Sinquefield Cup, he has done so in classical tournaments in recent years. That would explain his extremely fast climb on the rating list. If this is true, it means that Niemann probably shouldn’t have been playing in a super tournament like the Sinquefield Cup in the first place. His rating would be artificially high because of the cheating. If Magnus already knew about this, I can understand why it would be frustrating for him to lose to someone who has cheated his way to playing for big prize money. Of course, there could be other reasons for why Magnus withdrew. We don’t know until he confirms. But it’s looking a lot like it has to do with Niemann and possible cheating one way or another.

Question: If the odds of a nuclear war is 1 in a thousand per year, then how many years would it take for the odds to occur to be 95%?
Answer: The key to setting up the equation is to flip the question on its head. How many years would it take for the probability of a nuclear war not occurring to be 5%? ( 1 − 1 / 1000 ) x = 1 − 0.95 Solving for x gives us: x = l n 0.05 / l n 0.999 ≈ 2994

Question: Why does Haskell make it so difficult to program in imperative style?
Answer: Haskell is a highly opinionated language. It's purely functional by design. Unlike multi-paradigm languages, where it's up to the programmer to choose a programming style, Haskell absolutely forces you to write functional code. This restriction gives Haskell programs some nice properties: Enforcing a certain style also ensures that programs are written in a certain way. In a more free-form language like C++, two programmers could write the same program in wildly different ways.

Question: Why do some software engineers dislike C# and .NET?
Answer: I find that C# haters generally take three forms: Java programmers They remember a time when Micro$oft was evil in some previous century. Question: What is your view about blindfold chess? Have you personally tried it to improve your chess prowess?
Answer: When I started learning chess, I would read several chess books cover to cover. I would play through all the games and every single variation move by move. To do that, I would set up every game and position on a chess board. But this was really time consuming. Reading even a single book took a very long time. For every game in a book, there are usually only a handful of diagrams. Sometimes only two or three. I realized that if I could visualize the board well enough that I could keep the game in my head between the diagrams without having to set up the position on a board, I could read books much faster. So I practiced that skill to where I could play through entire games in my head. This is useful when learning. It's actually how Magnus Carlsen has learned most of the chess he knows. Other than that, I found blindfold chess somewhat interesting in itself. It's amazing that our brain is able to do it. It's also a great party trick with friends who don't play the game at a high level.

Question: The CEO of an Indian company wrote a post on LinkedIn where he advised youngsters to put 18 hours a day (not literally) for the first few years, and then reap the rewards later in their career. Why is everyone loathing him for his bold stance?
Answer: It's complete nonsense. There are two basic ways to increase your output and income. Lets say you work 50% overtime and earn 50% more money without improving. Maybe it's the type of job where there's not much room for improvement and you just have to grind it out. So you do that for a few years until you burn out. You will have made 50% more money, but then what? This is what we would call a dead-end job. Alternatively, you could focus on improving to put yourself in a better position for the future. Realizing that your earning potential will be much higher later, you also realize that it's pointless to “cash out” by working yourself to death when your earning potential is at its lowest. So let's say you work normal 8-hour days, while improving at a rate of 50% per year. After only three years, your output has tripled. After a few years you're probably earning a lot more simply by continuing to work 8-hour days than you would have done by working 50% overtime in the dead-end job. That's compound interest, and this is where you want to be. By working sensible hours, you will keep surplus energy and a healthy work-life balance. You won't burn out. You will stay hungry and find work fulfilling. Your health and your relationships will be in a better place. All of these positive things that come from living a sustainable life. In the future, I believe 6-hour workdays and 4-day work weeks will become common. The 18-hour shifts are a thing of the distant past. We have a name for it: Slavery.
